NeuroGecko

The complete record — what was asked for, what was built, what was wrong, and what is left

A biologically-grounded leopard gecko (Eublepharis macularius) in MuJoCo. Every number in the animal is tagged PUBLISHED, DERIVED or INVENTED. Every hypothesis ever tested stays in the record, especially the wrong ones. This document is that record, assembled by machine from docs/FAILURE_MAP.md, config/proxies.yaml, git log, git blame and the evidence JSON. No figure in it was transcribed by hand.

How to read the colour

confirmed / published / working partly / uncertain refuted / not accepted invented, and says so not started

Two conventions run through every chart. A number that has been measured in this repository is drawn as a bar. A number that is published elsewhere and has not been reproduced here is drawn as a dashed marker or a shaded band, never as a bar — so a target cannot be mistaken for a result. And every chart caption names the ledger row the measurement came from, so any figure here can be traced to the run that produced it.

One thing this document deliberately does not contain

There are no time estimates anywhere in it. Not for the remaining modules, not for the blocker, not for the proof battery. That is a standing instruction on this project, and it is also the honest position: every schedule this project has implied has been wrong, usually because the blocker turned out to be somewhere nobody was looking. Work that has happened carries the date it happened. Work that has not happened carries an order and a dependency — what has to be true before it can start — and nothing else.

Part 1

What you asked for, and where each of those things stands

A real gecko, not a gecko-shaped robot

The animal has to behave the way Eublepharis macularius behaves because of what is published about it, not because a reward function was shaped until the motion looked right.

Where it stands: Every parameter carries PUBLISHED / DERIVED / INVENTED in config/proxies.yaml. 143 registered; 43 % published, 14 % derived, 43 % openly invented.

Procedural understanding, not a lookup

It should work out what prey is from what it senses — not be told “object 7 is food”. Many kinds of insect; some things move and are not prey; prey sometimes holds still.

Where it stands: Partly. The strike, the flee response and the approach criterion are procedural and published. The eye is the gap: it detects on 5.4 % of steps, and prey identity is still colour and motion, not a tuned detector.

No oracle. No privileged information.

The animal must not be handed the prey's coordinates. If it finds food, it must find it with its own senses.

Where it stands: NOT DONE, and now instrumented rather than argued about. The oracle is demoted to a shadow that reaches the logger and never the policy (brain/hunt_metrics.py refuses to be constructed any other way). It is still connected to the walker's goal.

Videos that show the animal, honestly

One fixed angle. No shaking. Real speed. All four legs visible. The walk that was accepted, not whatever checkpoint was lying around.

Where it stands: Fixed after four separate defects: half-speed playback, a camera locked to the bobbing trunk, a compass angle the animal walked into, and — the one that mattered — the wrong walker in every clip.

Never guess at how long things take

A standing instruction from the first session.

Where it stands: Honoured. This document dates what happened and orders what has not. It gives no estimate for anything, and the reason is in Part 10.

Short answers, plain words, jargon defined inline

A standing instruction.

Where it stands: Honoured in conversation. This document is the exception the user asked for, and it still defines its terms — see the glossary in Part 17.

Carry the map, always

docs/FAILURE_MAP.md is read first every session and updated before every commit that tests something. Nothing is ever deleted from it.

Where it stands: Honoured across 29 sessions and 221 numbered hypotheses. This report is generated from it.

Part 2

What NeuroGecko is

A 38-gram leopard gecko, built in the MuJoCo physics engine, with a brain assembled module by module out of published measurements. It is not a reinforcement-learning agent that happens to look like a lizard. The distinction is the whole project: an RL agent is judged by whether it gets better at the reward, and this animal is judged by whether it reproduces numbers somebody measured in a real gecko and did not tell it about.

How one step actually runs

The physics runs at 500 Hz and the control loop at 50 Hz. The only trained component anywhere in this chain is the walking residual, and in the accepted walker it is switched off — the animal walks on a hand-written rhythm, and the ledger measured the trained addition as worse (#11, #71, #183).

The eight brain modules, and what each one is for

1 · Hypothalamus working

The drives. How hungry it is, how much energy it has left, how warm it is. Nothing here decides anything; it produces the numbers the decision runs on.

2 · Basal ganglia working

The selector. Six behaviours compete — hunt, shelter, warm up, rest, flee, explore — and exactly one wins. Reproduces the published gating table to 0.103 percentage points.

3 · Spinal cord + brainstem working

The rhythm. Four coupled oscillators, one per leg, producing the walking pattern without needing rhythmic input. The brainstem turns “hunt” into a stride command.

4 · Eye half

Two jobs. Keeping the gaze stable — the published optokinetic reflex, reproduced. And finding prey — the blocker, detecting on 5.4 % of steps.

4b · Strike working

The last two centimetres. Released at 20.3 mm, peak 0.851 m/s, 80 ms. 89.7 % capture against a published 82.9 %, with nothing fitted to it.

5 · Smell built, unused

Tongue-flicking. Returns a strength per odour and never a bearing, because no gecko has been shown to find prey by smell alone. Nothing consults it yet.

6 · Day/night clock built, unused

When the animal is awake. The sleep-cycle period is stored as null on purpose, so borrowing a bearded dragon's number is impossible without declaring it.

7 · Memory specified

Where the goal was. Two decay components: route precision fades before the ability to get there at all. Both published in this species.

8 · Learning specified

Getting better with practice. 9 % per trial, ceilings 3.02× on speed and 4.59× on route. Published in this species — measured on escaping water, not on hunting.

Part 3

The road map

working, checked against something partial built and not accepted specified, not built

Five modules stand. One is built and openly recorded as not working. Three are specified and not built — and the specification for all three exists because a literature sweep in Session 10c refuted the assumption that they were too thin to build (#216, #217). The surprise of that session was that the modules deferred for lack of evidence had target-species numbers all along, and the module considered urgent — the prey detector — has no gecko measurement of any kind.

Part 4

The six rules, and the failure each one came from

None of these were decided in advance. Each one is the scar left by a specific defect, written down so the same defect costs one session instead of three.

1

Every number is PUBLISHED, DERIVED or INVENTED — and says which.

A plausible number wearing a published number's clothes is the worst defect available.

The failure it came from: cost_of_transport = 0.73 sat in the registry tagged E. macularius, verified. It is Teratoscincus przewalskii, a different family. No cost of transport has ever been measured in this species.

2

Never tune until the answer matches.

If a model needs its constants adjusted to reproduce a published result, the constants must come from a paper.

The failure it came from: The basal-ganglia dopamine curve sat 0.10 too high for three sessions. It was not scaled down; the mechanism was found to be wrong in the opposite direction to the previous correction. Error fell from 10.3 percentage points to 0.103.

3

The reward is what the model is told to want. The gates are what the animal does. Only the second counts.

A training reward can be satisfied in ways that have nothing to do with the behaviour.

The failure it came from: The trained walking residual improves the reward and fails the gates. The accepted walker runs with the residual switched off entirely.

4

A failed prediction stays in the table.

Adding a knob per failing joint is fitting the harness to the answer.

The failure it came from: Two of six locomotion gates have never passed. They are still listed as failing, in every report, including this one.

5

Measure before claiming — including your own tests and your own solver.

The instrument is part of the experiment.

The failure it came from: Five recorded failures were in the test, not the model. One was in the integration step. One test literally built a patch of the colour it read out of the model and checked the detector saw it — it passed while the detector scored 0.000 on the real rendered prey. Twice, three sessions apart.

6

One source is not a citation.

Check a parameter set against something it must independently predict.

The failure it came from: The basal-ganglia weights were settled by the gating constant they have to reproduce, not by a vote among sources.

Part 6

What was done wrong — the recurring shapes

Eight failure shapes account for most of what went wrong. Each one recurred after being “fixed”, which is why they are worth naming rather than merely counting. The count beside each is how many distinct ledger rows record it.

×5

A default won because nobody named the parameter

The goal oracle (#165), the food oracle, the gait profile (#177), and twice before that (#26, #33). Each time a constructor omitted an argument and the callee's default silently decided the science.

Now: Every one is now passed explicitly and reported in info on every step. common/walker_pairing.py warns when the measured-broken combination is assembled.

×3

The test compared the code against itself

A class literally named the detector cannot disagree with the world read the prey colour from the model, built a patch of that colour, and checked the detector saw it. It never touched the renderer. It passed while the detector scored 0.000 on the real prey — twice, three sessions apart. A world-builder guard required added bodies to be mocap, when what it needed to test was that they add no degrees of freedom.

Now: Assertions now reach the thing being guarded. The world guard tests nq and nv directly (39 → 39, 38 → 38).

×2

A fix that provably could not do anything

The tectum subtracted a scalar from the motion map to reject self-motion. argmax(clip(x−c,0,None)) == argmax(x) for any scalar c — identical on 20 000 of 20 000 random maps. It had never changed one reported bearing.

Now: Replaced first with a spatially varying surround, then — when that was also shown to assume uniform flow — with a predicted flow field subtracted from the image.

×3

A number wearing another species' clothes

cost_of_transport = 0.73 tagged E. macularius, verified; it is Teratoscincus przewalskii. The human-readable scorecard had it right and the machine-readable registry the code reads did not.

Now: Corrected, and the gap recorded rather than filled.

×4

I explained away a real observation, repeatedly

The user said the walk dragged. The answers given were: camera shake, then half-speed playback, then an under-actuated forelimb they would have to accept. Then the profile. Then the policy. All five were wrong about the cause.

Now: It was the PAIRING. Three of the four profile-policy combinations walk with a front-foot gap under 0.03; the one being filmed had a gap of 0.376.

×2

The map already contained the answer

#71 states outright that the accepted walker IS the open-loop base. #11 measured the trained residual as worse. The evidence file records its controller as zero residual. All three were read, and the checkpoint was loaded anyway.

Now: Reading the ledger is not the same as believing it. GeckoBrainEnv could not even express lab profile, no policy until use_policy=False was added.

×4

I asserted something I had not checked

A citation was invented outright — Day, Crews & Wilczynski were said to have studied leopard geckos; they never did (#215). “Nobody has filmed a gecko hunting” was said as fact; Delheusy, Brillet & Bels 1995 exists, n=6, 64 fps. “A sharper eye would find the cricket” and “geckos head-bob to range prey” were both told to the user as fact and both refuted.

Now: Every claim in this document that is not measured in this repository is marked as unverified, and the companion prompt asks an outside reader to check the bibliography specifically for this failure.

×3

I built the thing that was not the blocker

The walker was retrained for 2.1 M steps against a reach problem that did not exist — the existing walker reached a mouth-goal 75 times in 160 s, and the retrain was 8× worse (168 mm vs 20.5 mm). hunt_targeting, proposed as the approach fix, gave 0 strikes against 29.

Now: Both killed. Both kept in the ledger, and the targeting option kept in the code, defaulted off, with its measurement attached.

The one that is worst, and why it is listed separately

In Session 10c a citation was invented. Day, Crews & Wilczynski were asserted to have studied leopard geckos. They never did — their lizard work is three papers on two other families. The confusion is explicable, because David Crews did work extensively on Eublepharis macularius, but on temperature-dependent sex determination, not on the brain. The invented citation was then written into a research brief as a known starting point, where it would have been read as established.

It is recorded as ledger row #215. It is also the reason Part 14 of this document states plainly that the bibliography is a harvest of strings found in the repository and has not been verified against any database, and the reason the companion prompt asks an outside reader to check exactly that first.

The dopamine curve sat 0.10 too high #104–#108

WAS

Three sessions of a basal-ganglia model that would not match the published table.

WHY

The mechanism was wrong in the opposite direction to the previous correction. Afferent gain (1±λ) with threshold 0.2.

NOW

Mean error 10.3 pp → 0.103 pp, axis slope 1.000.

The gecko could not see its own food #112, #196

WAS

The detector tested for green; the prey had been changed to brown. Exactly 0.000 at every illumination — and the guarding test compared the code to itself.

WHY

Read the colour the renderer actually draws — the material, not just geom_rgba.

NOW

Two separate occurrences fixed, three sessions apart, and the self-referential test replaced.

The eye could not find the cricket #116–#118, #134

WAS

Four eye configurations, 64 → 512 px. Correlation with true prey bearing ≈ 0 in all four.

WHY

It was never resolution. The prey travelled 0.0 mm and was off-image on 81 % of frames.

NOW

Prey now walks 398 mm per episode. The eye had something to look at for the first time.

The eye reported the same thing with and without prey #209–#213

WAS

72 % of frames firing at salience 0.4161 with prey; 72 % at 0.4034 with no prey in the world at all. Separation d = 0.036.

WHY

A local-versus-surround comparison assumes self-motion is spatially uniform. Optic flow expands from a focus of expansion, so the local excess is large everywhere.

NOW

An efference copy — predicting the flow from the animal's own yaw and speed and subtracting it — cut false alarms to 3–7 %.

Eight gate contracts failing for four sessions #158–#164

WAS

Reported as eight separate failures; the walking evidence looked unverifiable.

WHY

One body check compared raw bytes and raised before the others could run. What differed was a comment.

NOW

All 16 pass. The physics hash matched all along: b178bf26…

Pursuit could never work #169, #175

WAS

The hunting channel had no route to success at any parameter value.

WHY

Walk 0.055 m/s, cricket 0.118 m/s. The real animal does not chase — it strikes from 2 cm at 0.851 m/s.

NOW

Strike built: 81 % capture against a published 82.9 %, unfitted.

Nothing had ever been caught #202–#204

WAS

A strike that worked in isolation and an approach that could not reach 2 cm.

WHY

Not the eye, not the walker, not the targeting — all three had been diagnosed as the blocker and all three were wrong. It was prey motion plus a speed-dependent flee radius.

NOW

26 of 29 strikes landed — 89.7 % against a published 82.9 %. The first time the animal caught anything.

The walk dragged, for six sessions of denial #182–#184, #206–#208

WAS

The user said so from the first video and was told five different reasons why it did not.

WHY

Front-foot duty gap 0.376 on the ONE combination being filmed. The other three combinations sit under 0.03.

NOW

common/walker_pairing.py now warns whenever that pairing is assembled, so the next session cannot repeat it silently.

Part 8

The measurements worth keeping

Part 9

The eye — why it still cannot find the cricket

This is the only module in the project that is built and recorded as not working, and it has been misdiagnosed four separate times. What follows is what is actually known, in the order it was found out.

What has been ruled out, and what is left

Ruled out: resolution

Held still, peak salience is 0.36 to 0.83 at every range tested — including ranges where the prey covers half a detector cell. Four configurations from 64 to 512 pixels all correlated ≈ 0 with true bearing (#116–#118).

Ruled out: bearing quality

Of 81 detections in a real hunt, 44 were usable and 37 were wrong. When the eye speaks it is right more often than not (#220).

Ruled out: the walker

The existing walker reaches a mouth-goal 75 times in 160 s. A 2.1-million-step retrain aimed at the supposed reach problem was 8× worse and was killed (#200, #201).

Ruled out: targeting

Aiming the walker at the prey gave 0 strikes against 29 for aiming past it. Arriving at a goal means stopping at it, and the mouth needs the animal to keep going (#203).

Fixed: self-motion

An efference copy cut false alarms from 72 % of frames to 3–7 % and flipped the still-versus-moving effect to the right sign for the first time (#213).

Left: the detection rate

5.4 % of steps. The same eye that peaks at 0.67–0.83 on a stationary animal averages 0.02 during a hunt, because the prey is out of view most of the time. This is the blocker, and it is the only one.

What the fix is specified to be

Two parallel detector channels over the same image, differing in receptive-field size and in what they are wired to. A coarse array of ~30° patches that only says a small thing is moving over there and gates whether a hunt starts at all; and a dense sub-16° direction-selective array that supplies the bearing error during pursuit. The published test for it is a lesion double dissociation: suppressing the wide channel should stop approaches being initiated from beyond 22 cm without harming approaches already under way, and suppressing the narrow channel should do the opposite. Every tuning constant in it is a mouse, a zebrafish larva or a toad — the full parameter list, with that stated on each row, is in Part 10.

Part 10

The three modules that are specified and not built

Memory and learning can be built on evidence, and the deferral should end. In the last eighteen months three papers on the actual target species produced usable numbers: leopard geckos improve about 9 percent per trial on a simple beacon task, reach a ceiling of roughly 3x faster and 4.6x straighter after 20 spaced trials, keep a learned location for 2 to 4 months, and are back to naive by 6 to 14 months. That is enough to build both modules honestly. But the numbers come with a timescale problem the project must face head on: the memory evidence lives at months, and a hunt lives at seconds. Nothing has ever been measured in any lizard at intervals shorter than two months, so a working-memory or within-session buffer is invention no matter how reasonable it looks. The irony is that the urgent module is the unsupported one. There is no size tuning, no speed tuning, no contrast threshold,

The prey detector — the blocker

Build two parallel detector channels over the same visual input, both tuned to small moving objects, differing only in receptive-field size and in what they are wired to. Channel A, wide-field: one unit per patch of roughly 30 to 34 degrees across (published receptive fields of 700 to 900 square degrees), tuned to objects of about 4 to 5 degrees, NOT direction-selective, and with no fine localisation. Its only output is 'something small is moving somewhere in this patch'. Channel B, narrow-field: a dense retinotopic array of units covering under 16 degrees each (under 200 square degrees), tuned to the same 4 to 5 degree object size, direction-selective, and precisely localised. Its output is a continuous bearing error. Wire them differently, because the published lesion result is a clean double dissociation: silencing wide-field cells stopped approaches being INITIATED from beyond 22 cm without hurting accuracy once an approach began, while silencing narrow-field cells degraded targeting accuracy, cut the probability of interception given an approach, made the animal pause within 5 cm of the prey, and stopped it re-initiating after a failed contact. A third class (parvalbumin cells, tuned to larger and darker stimuli) had no role in prey capture at all. So: Channel A gates whether a hunt starts and at what range; Channel B supplies the steering signal during pursuit and the terminal commitment. An independent two-channel size split is published in a fish larva with a crossover at 6 degrees: the prey-feeding retinal channel peaks at 2 to 3 degrees and falls off above 6, while a sibling channel does not respond below 6 degrees at all. Use 6 degrees as the small-versus-large crossover, route small to approach and large to avoid, and reproduce the published sign reversal: a 1 degree spot evokes a turn of about 20 degrees TOWARD, a 10 degree spot a turn of about 60 degrees AWAY. Finally, the detector is not one filter across the whole hunt. The same cricket grows from roughly 5 degrees at detection to roughly 45 degrees at the strike (a 1.8 cm cricket at the published 2.03 cm lunge distance), and separate cell populations own each end, so build a small-object detection filter and a large-object strike-commit filter as different units.

ParameterValueProvenance
Wide-field receptive field size700 to 900 square degrees, equivalent to about 30 to 34 degrees diameter. Responds to small light or dark objects moving anywhere within that region.PUBLISHED, proxy (mouse superior colliculus). No gecko equivalent exists.

Sign of the effect only; the modulation function is not published.
Multiple targets, neural mechanismDivisive normalisation across the target map, with global (not lateral) inhibition. The strongest competitor suppressed responses by 61 +/- 7 percent on average. About half the population (48 percent, n=51) signalled the strongest stimulus with a near-binary switch whose transition range was 4 deg/s or less in competitor loom-speed units; the rest (52 percent, n=56) were gradual. Discriminability at a 2 deg/s strength difference: d-prime 2.48 +/- 0.38 switch-like versus 0.8 +/- 0.18 gradual.PUBLISHED, proxy (barn owl optic tectum)
Multiple targets, selection policyWith two equal-strength competitors: 80 percent winner-take-all, 20 percent vector averaging. With unequal competitors, the stronger is chosen 70 percent of the time. Tectal cells are more switch-like than retinal cells (R=0.72 versus 0.47).PUBLISHED, proxy, AND MEASURED ON THE WRONG BEHAVIOUR. The 80/20 split and the 0.7 bias come from escape responses to competing looming stimuli, not from prey selection. The same paper shows the competition mechanism extends to prey-like stimuli only at the imaging level.
Target choice in a dense prey field, and the strike acceptance windowWith about 100 prey items present, the animal almost invariably chose the CLOSEST one, subject to an acceptance window. Hunt-initiation prey position: azimuth mean 0.7 deg, SD 48.4 deg; altitude mean 19.9 deg, SD 19.7 deg; distance mean 3.4 mm, SD 1.6 mm. Strike zone (95 percent CI during successful strikes): azimuth 0.9 deg, altitude 17.4 deg, distance 0.870 mm. Note the acceptance window is WIDE in azimuth and NARROW in elevation.PUBLISHED, proxy. The nearest-target rule is stated qualitatively, without a probability.
Motion is a gain term, not a hard gateIn a mammal, immobile fresh-frozen crickets were contacted in times indistinguishable from live crickets: 8.06 +/- 1.08 s versus 7.6 +/- 1.34 s, n=8, p>0.05. In toad and fish larva, motion is obligatory. No gecko data settles which regime applies.PUBLISHED, proxies that disagree
Configural rule: elongation axis relative to motion axisA moving stripe whose long axis lies along the direction of motion is prey; perpendicular is not. The discrimination is described as 'largely invariant, thus far investigated' to movement direction in the plane, contrast polarity, and stripe velocity. Compute the configural score independently of, and before, the speed and contrast gains, and make it blind to the sign of contrast.PUBLISHED, proxy (toad). Qualitative only; no response ratio, no stimulus dimensions, no sample size is obtainable.
Form of the toad response law, correctedTurning activity R-bar (turning reactions per minute) is characterised by THREE SEPARATE univariate relations, each measured with the others held constant: R-bar = f(angular velocity), R-bar = f'(background contrast), R-bar = f''(angular size). It is NOT a single joint function of the three. The source also says the dependence is on these 'among other things', so three is not an exhaustive parameter list. The tuning curves themselves are in paywalled figures and were not obtained.PUBLISHED form, proxy; numeric curves NOT_FOUND
Motion front end for a lizardCorrelation-type elementary motion detector array with 0.3 degrees of visual angle spacing and a 0.1 second time constant. The authors state the model is sensitive to local contrast and viewer-object distance and that additional processing is needed to separate relevant from irrelevant motion under natural conditions.PUBLISHED, proxy (distant lizard) and OPTICALLY MISMATCHED. Anolis is diurnal and foveate; a leopard gecko is nocturnal and afoveate with a large pupil and short focal length. Use the architecture, invent the constants, and say so.
Outcome statistics to calibrate against (NOT detector parameters)Eublepharid strike success 77 to 83 percent (82.9 percent on crickets, 100 percent on mealworms). Mammalian capture given contact 38 +/- 16 percent. Fish larva response rate to an optimal small stimulus 22 percent. Time to capture in a 45 x 38 cm arena: 11 +/- 2 s with vision, 36 +/- 9 s in darkness, improving about fourfold to 13 +/- 1.1 s over four days of experience.PUBLISHED, mixed proxies
False positive rateNOT FOUND anywhere. No published measurement exists, for toad, mouse, fish larva, or any lizard, of how often a predator strikes at a non-prey object.NOT_FOUND

What would have to be invented

  • Every gecko-specific tuning value. No size tuning, speed tuning, contrast tuning, elevation tuning, or detection latency has ever been measured for prey detection in ANY gecko, ANY nocturnal lizard, or any squamate other than the Anolis motion model. The whole size-and-speed specification is imported from a fish larva, a rodent and a toad.
  • Visual acuity for this species. No value in cycles per degree exists for Eublepharis macularius or any eublepharid. The only guidance is a comparative statement, itself unverified in full text, that nocturnal geckos have lower acuity than diurnal geckos. So whatever angular threshold is imported from mouse (6 to 8 degrees) or fish (3 degrees), the gecko's should probably be LARGER, and the size of that correction is unmeasured.
  • Contrast threshold and absolute-luminance dependence at low light. Nothing exists for any nocturnal lizard.
  • A false positive rate, and any distractor-rejection statistic.
  • A below-the-horizon prey prior. The two published elevation figures point the other way in eye coordinates: prey is held at about +5 degrees relative to the mouse's eye and at about +20 degrees altitude in the fish larva. Both are consequences of head posture, not a world-frame rule.
  • Any capacity limit on how many prey items can be tracked at once.
  • A prey-selection version of the 80/20 winner-take-all split. The published number is from escape from looming stimuli.
  • The Ewert worm-versus-anti-worm tuning curves and any worm-to-anti-worm response ratio. The figures are unreachable; the invariance rule is the only citable part.
  • The modulation function linking measured target speed to strike release distance. Only its sign is published.
  • Whether the leopard gecko hunts visually at all in the first place. The only quantitative sensory study on this species is about PREDATOR detection and found chemical cues dominant with vision merely modulatory. A vision-first prey detector is an explicit modelling choice, not something the target-species literature supports.

Memory

A leopard gecko learns where one goal is and keeps that knowledge for a couple of months, then loses it. Detail goes first: after four months the animal still gets to the goal but by a longer, sloppier route. After six to fourteen months it performs like an animal that never learned anything and has to be retrained from scratch. It does not carry a map. Only about one third of individuals orient by the relationship between several cues; the rest lock onto one landmark or fall back on a search pattern the authors themselves say may involve no spatial knowledge at all. It does notice when an object it knows has moved, so it holds what-and-where information about objects even without a map. Individual differences are real but tiny and they fade with age.

What would have to be invented

  • Any decay at hours, days or weeks. Nothing has ever been measured in any lizard shorter than two months, and that is exactly the window a hunt occupies. If the module remembers where a cricket was five minutes ago, that rule is invented.
  • Working memory, a short-term buffer, or any capacity limit on how many items are held.
  • Place cells, grid cells, head-direction cells, or any metric map. Zero spatially tuned single units have ever been recorded in any reptile.
  • Path integration, dead reckoning, or a homeward vector. Never demonstrated in any reptile, and explicitly rejected in the one lizard tested for it (Ellis-Quinn and Simon 1989, Sceloporus jarrovi, n=108).
  • Retreat-site fidelity, nightly return-to-shelter probability, or home range size. No field study of this species exists at all.
  • Memory consolidation or replay during sleep. The word consolidation appears zero times in the only paper that ever recorded a sleeping leopard gecko.
  • Interference, retroactive or proactive, and any reversal cost for this species.
  • A savings coefficient for relearning after full forgetting.
  • Any coupling between body temperature and forgetting rate. The single closest experiment argues against it: fire salamanders held 100 days at 4 C forgot no more than controls at 20 C (Wilkinson et al. 2017, Sci Rep 7:40079, n=9).

What the model must not claim

  • That decay is being modelled, if the simulation clock never reaches months. A tau of 115 days inside an episode measured in minutes is a term whose value is numerically indistinguishable from zero. This is the same class of defect as the scalar subtraction that could not move an argmax: the code runs, the parameter is real, the behaviour is unchanged. If the clock does not reach months, either run a compressed clock and say so, or do not ship the decay term.
  • That the gecko has a cognitive map or allocentric place memory. About two thirds of individuals showed no evidence of it, and the authors explicitly cannot rule out a non-cognitive motor search.
  • That memory duration is a reptile property. It is a species property. Tortoises retain for up to nine years, monitors for twenty months, this animal for two months. Fast forgetting is the ecologically correct default for a semi-arid seasonal habitat, not a deficiency to engineer away.
  • That the medial cortex module causes the memory behaviour. The anatomy is described in this species and the function has never been tested in it. The only two reptile lesion studies contradict each other and neither is a gecko.
  • That the retention numbers are replicated. Both papers come from one lab, one captive colony descended from about 90 wild-caught Pakistani founders, one apparatus, and one forced-swim task, with an overlapping author list. Treat them as a single evidence stream.
  • That any of this generalises across sexes. The 2023 and 2025 cohorts are 41 females to 1 male.

Learning

A leopard gecko gets better at finding a fixed goal, slowly and unevenly. On the simplest version of the task, with one landmark right next to the goal, its chance of getting there rises about 9 percent per trial. Over 20 trials it ends up roughly three times quicker and takes a route about four and a half times more efficient, and then it stops improving. Roughly a quarter of individuals never engage with the task at all. In every published analysis, how motivated the animal was on that trial predicted performance more strongly than how much it had learned. It learns places and boundary shapes far more cheaply than it learns arbitrary visual patterns. Its defensive behaviour is not learned at all: an overt threat display in this species is triggered only by smell, with vision and touch able to raise sampling but never to fire the display on their own.

What would have to be invented

  • Any learning rate for an appetitive, food-rewarded, or prey-capture task. Every learning number for this species comes from an aversive forced-swim escape task in which the animal was prodded with a swab to keep it moving. A hunting simulation is a different motivational world and no number crosses that gap.
  • Any learning rate in a fast-clock regime. The 9 percent per trial figure was measured with trials spaced a week apart. If the simulation runs many trials per simulated day, it is outside the regime the number was measured in.
  • A per-individual trials-to-criterion rule. None exists for this species in any task.
  • Reversal cost for this species. If reversal is needed, expose it as a tunable multiplier bounded by 1.3x and 10x and state that no target-species measurement exists.
  • Extinction rate, trials-to-extinction, or spontaneous recovery. Zero studies in any lizard.
  • A habituation decay constant. This is the biggest single gap. No fitted habituation curve or time constant exists for ANY lizard or ANY reptile. The only trial-indexed data in any gecko is a Tokay study (Szabo and Ringler 2025, n=20) showing habituation to a novel SPACE within about 4 exposures, NO habituation to a novel OBJECT next to food across 30 trials, and antipredator immobility staying repeatable (R=0.41-0.56) across monthly repeats. Those three facts are constraints; the rate is invention.
  • Latent or unreinforced map building rate. Directionally permitted by one lacertid study whose sample size could not be obtained; no rate anywhere.
  • Social learning, gaze following as a mechanism, and tool use. Gaze following rests on one study with six observers, one demonstrator, and a movement-versus-gaze confound the authors themselves could not resolve. Tool use has zero hits in any lizard.
  • Sex-specific learning parameters. A meta-analysis of 11 lizard species found essentially no sex effect, and the target species found none either (p=0.9626 latency, p=0.487 path). Building them would be inventing a difference that was looked for and not found.
  • Any coupling of learning rate to body temperature. A Q10 of 3.1 and 2.3 exists for maze acquisition in a diurnal desert iguana from 1968, whose full text and sample size could not be obtained and whose thermal optimum is nothing like a nocturnal gecko's.

What the model must not claim

  • That the learning rate is calibrated to this species' hunting. It is calibrated to this species' swimming away from water. Say so in the code comment.
  • That 20 trials is a trials-to-criterion. It is the length the experimenters chose. The only defensible statement is that 20 spaced trials produce a measurable group-level improvement.
  • That a learning curve measured in time-to-goal is a learning curve. In this species it is largely a motivation curve, and in the dark it goes the wrong way entirely: geckos reached the goal faster while swimming longer, faster paths. This is the direct analogue of the velocity rule finer than its own instrument. A metric that improves when the animal is doing worse is not a metric.
  • That a learning module which improves path efficiency by more than about 5x over 20 trials is modelling this animal. That outruns the published ceiling.
  • That learning is deterministic. Between-individual consistency is R=0.03 to 0.19, so roughly 81 to 97 percent of the variance is within-individual noise, and about a quarter of animals never engage. A clean monotonic learner is the wrong shape.
  • That a gain term which is always smaller than the drive term is doing anything. Motivation outweighed training phase by roughly an order of magnitude in F in every published model. If drive is modelled as a multiplier and learning as a small additive term, the learning term will never move the behaviour, and the module will look present and do nothing.
  • That an egocentric turn rule is the evidence-backed default. The claim that whiptail lizards reverse position cues faster than feature cues did not survive verification: a specialist review reports the spatial advantage held during acquisition only and NOT during reversal, and the reading of position as an egocentric response rule is an interpolation the paper does not support.
  • That vision can trigger a defensive display. In this species it cannot. If the simulated gecko has no chemical channel, it should be unable to mount an overt display at all.

Sleep

No sleep-cycle period has ever been printed for Eublepharis macularius. The animal has been recorded asleep exactly once in the history of the field, in two males, and the paper reports per-species periods only as a violin plot, with raw data available from the authors on request. What IS published is a bounded interval that contains the gecko's value by construction: median periodicities of 84 to 134.5 seconds across all individuals of the seven lizard species studied, with a mean across species of 113.2 +/- 6.8 seconds, all measured at 20 to 27 degrees C ambient. The same paper's figure legend gives a rounded visual anchor of about 100 seconds in lizards against about 50 seconds in mammals and birds. Use 100 to 113 seconds as the default and run sensitivity across 84 to 134.5 seconds. Do not state a single gecko-specific value as published, because the paper does not print one.

Part 11

The full plan, in order

No step below carries a time estimate. Each carries its position in the order and the reason it sits there — what has to be true before it can start. That is a deliberate choice and it is also the only defensible one: on this project the blocker has moved four times, and each time it moved because something nobody was measuring turned out to be the cause. A schedule built on that record would be fiction.

1

Change the success metric before changing the animal. Score hunting by path efficiency (distance travelled divpublished for this species

ided by straight-line distance to the prey at the moment of detection), not by time to capture. This is a change to the logging and fitness code, not to the brain, and it should land before the oracle is disconnected.

Why here in the order: When the oracle goes, time to capture will get worse for two different reasons at once, and time to capture cannot tell them apart. In this species the point is settled: path length tracked learning (F=24.157, p<0.0001) while latency did not (F=0.326, p=0.5686), because latency is dominated by motivation. Worse, geckos in total darkness reached the goal FASTER while swimming LONGER paths at twice the speed. A fast random search beats a slow correct one on the clock. Judging the post-oracle animal on time will reward flailing.

2

Add an approach-state detector and log it every step: approaching when absolute prey bearing is under 90 degrepublished for a proxy

es AND range is decreasing AND self-speed exceeds threshold. Log approach starts, approach-start range, approach-start bearing, terminal bearing error, contacts, and captures-given-contact as separate counters.

Why here in the order: This is instrumentation, not capability, and it is what makes everything after it debuggable. Without it, a broken detector and a broken controller produce the identical symptom (no crickets caught) and you cannot tell which one you are fixing. Build it while the oracle is still connected so it can be validated against ground truth, then keep it after.

3

Keep the oracle running as a shadow signal after disconnecting it from the policy. Feed it only to the logger.mostly invented

Report per episode the angular error between what the eye reports and where the cricket actually is.

Why here in the order: This is the only way to tell 'the eye cannot see the cricket' apart from 'the eye sees it and the body cannot get there'. It costs almost nothing and it converts the expected collapse in performance from a mystery into a measurement. It is also the guard against shipping a detector that looks present and does nothing: if the eye's error is at chance, no downstream module can be working, whatever the behaviour looks like.

4

Build the strike gate: release the lunge at about 2 cm range, peak velocity 0.85 m/s, peak acceleration 47 m/spublished for a proxy

squared, with peak acceleration about 16 ms before contact and peak velocity about 9 ms before contact. Scale the release distance up for faster-moving targets. Check against a strike success rate of 77 to 83 percent.

Why here in the order: This is the only part of the hunt with numbers from a gecko in the same family, and it is the part that turns a successful approach into food. It is also cheap to validate: the success rate is a published number the simulation can be scored against directly. Do it before the detector, because a working detector feeding a broken strike still catches nothing, and you will blame the detector.

5

Build the two-channel wide-field / narrow-field detector as specified: a coarse 30 degree patch array that onlpublished for a proxy

y says 'small thing moving here' and gates whether a hunt starts, plus a dense sub-16-degree direction-selective array that supplies the bearing error during pursuit. Both tuned to small objects with a 6 degree small-versus-large crossover, a 90 deg/s speed peak with near-zero response below 12 and above 360 deg/s, a probabilistic release of about one in five for an optimal stimulus, and a separate large-object filter for the strike commit.

Why here in the order: This is the module that makes the oracle removable. Build it after the metric, the scoring rule and the strike gate so that its failures are visible and attributable. Its correctness test is the published lesion dissociation: silencing the wide-field channel should stop long-range approaches while leaving accuracy intact, and silencing the narrow-field channel should degrade accuracy and cause pauses close to the prey. If a simulated lesion does not reproduce that, the two channels are decorative.

6

Add target selection for multiple prey: filter candidates by a wide-in-azimuth, narrow-in-elevation acceptancepublished for a proxy

window, take the nearest survivor, and implement competition as divisive normalisation across the target map with global inhibition and roughly 60 percent suppression by the strongest competitor, with a thresholded switch on top.

Why here in the order: Only worth doing once one cricket can reliably be caught. Adding competition to a detector that cannot find a single target just produces a more elaborate failure. Note the selection split (80 percent winner-take-all, 20 percent averaging) was measured on escape from looming stimuli, not on prey, so treat that number as a starting value rather than a constraint.

7

Give the animal a chemosensory channel, and gate the defensive display behind it as a hard AND, with vision anpublished for this species

d substrate vibration allowed to raise tongue-flick rate and arousal but never to fire the display alone. Combine modalities additively.

Why here in the order: This is the only quantitative sensory-hierarchy result that exists for the target species, and removing the oracle is exactly the moment it matters: if the simulated gecko has no chemical channel, it should be unable to mount a defensive display at all, and it will be missing the sensory modality this species actually leads with. A self-deposited scent field is also the only evidence-backed way for a nocturnal animal to get home in the dark. Caution: the target-species result is about detecting predators, not finding prey.

8

Build learning: update on path efficiency, at about 9 percent gain per reinforced trial, with a hard ceiling opublished for this species

f roughly 3x on speed and 4.6x on route efficiency over 20 trials, gated multiplicatively on a drive or arousal state, with about a quarter of individuals never engaging and a per-individual competence offset explaining only 7 to 19 percent of success variance.

Why here in the order: Learning cannot be evaluated until there is a metric that tracks it, a detector that gives it something to learn about, and a strike that turns learning into reward. It comes seventh for that reason, not because the evidence is weak. Make drive an explicit state rather than folding it into the learning rate, because in every published model motivation outweighed learning phase by roughly an order of magnitude, and a learning term smaller than the drive term will never move the behaviour.

9

Build memory decay as two components with different rates: route precision decaying with a time constant of abpublished for this species

out 115 days and coarse goal knowledge with about 131 days. Ship it ONLY if the simulation clock actually reaches months; otherwise ship the store without the decay and say so.

Why here in the order: Last, because it is the module most likely to be present and inert. Every measured retention point in this species is at 2 months or beyond, and inside an episode measured in minutes a 115-day time constant is numerically indistinguishable from zero. That is the same defect as a subtraction that cannot move an argmax. Decide the clock question first, then either run a compressed clock deliberately or leave the term out.

10

Add sleep as a single two-phase oscillator with a period of about 100 to 113 seconds at 20 to 27 C, scaled by published for this species

body temperature with Q10 = 2.3, timed to the LIGHT phase, with sleep pressure driving slow-wave amplitude and never the period. Modulate heart rate, breathing and muscle tone with cycle phase. Leave it completely uncoupled from memory.

Why here in the order: Cheap, well specified, and low risk as long as it stays disconnected from the memory module. It goes near the end because it changes nothing about hunting. The one thing that would make it wrong is wiring it to consolidation: no reptile has ever been shown to consolidate memory during sleep, and the word consolidation appears zero times in the only paper that ever recorded a sleeping leopard gecko.

Loose ends that are not in the ordered plan

  • Smell exists and nothing consults it. brain/vomeronasal.py is built and tested and no behaviour reads it. Published: tongue-flick rate rises from 3.0 to 14.57 per minute (n=7); defensive response 0.21 to chemical cues against 0.07 to visual (n=42).
  • The day/night clock exists and nothing consults it. brain/arousal.py is built. Its sleep_cycle_period_s is deliberately null.
  • Temperature affects nothing. The animal is thigmothermic — it takes heat by contact with a warm surface, not from light — so bask as currently modelled is the wrong mechanism.
  • There is no physical strike lunge. The strike's outcome is decided at launch and is ballistic. The body does not actually move through it.
  • The proof battery is 1 of 15. Fourteen checks that were listed as the acceptance criteria for the whole animal have never been run.
  • The oracle is still connected to the walker's goal. The shadow logger is in place and refuses to be switched into the policy; the disconnection itself has not happened.

Part 14

The bibliography

Read this before the table. What follows is a harvest, not a curated reading list. It is every author-year string and every DOI that appears anywhere in this repository's own text, with the parameter or ledger row that mentions it. None of it has been verified against a bibliographic database. This project has invented a citation once (#215) and has overstated the absence of a real one. A name appearing here means the repository leans on it — not that it exists. Checking that is the first task in the companion prompt.

What cannot be built honestly

Things that must not be built, and why

  • Place cells, grid cells, or head-direction cells. Zero spatially tuned single units have ever been recorded in any reptile, and the search returned nothing. Such a layer would be a rodent import wearing a gecko label.
  • Path integration, dead reckoning, or a homeward vector. Never demonstrated in any reptile. The one lizard tested for outbound-route information had it explicitly rejected in favour of familiar-area landmark recognition.
  • A sun or sky compass. The only demonstrated reptilian outbound-course mechanism runs through the parietal eye in daylight, in diurnal lizards. A crepuscular gecko active after sunset cannot run it.
  • Long-range homing. The only gecko translocation experiment ever run found the opposite: 10 of 11 geckos displaced 1 km simply stayed where they were released.
  • A nightly loop in which the gecko leaves a shared retreat at sunset and returns before dawn. This is the most tempting navigation claim for this project and it traces to a hobbyist magazine article recirculated through Wikipedia and care sheets. No sample size, no method, no peer review. If a return-to-shelter behaviour is implemented, it must be labelled invention.
  • Sleep-dependent memory consolidation or replay. Not demonstrated in any reptile. Do not cite the 2026 gecko sleep paper as support: it runs no learning task and never mentions consolidation.
  • A habituation module with a numeric decay constant. No fitted habituation curve or time constant exists for any lizard or any reptile. The three qualitative constraints that do exist (fast habituation to a novel place, none to a novel object near food, and none at all for the antipredator response) also rule out a single global habituation rule.
  • Any coupling of memory decay to body temperature. It has never been studied in any reptile, and the one ectotherm experiment that exists points the other way.
  • A defensive display that can be triggered by vision or vibration. In this species those modalities never fired a display on their own; only chemical cues did.
  • Sex-specific learning or spatial parameters. A meta-analysis of 11 lizard species and the target species itself both looked and found nothing.
  • A per-individual trials-to-criterion learning curve presented as published. Every learning result in this species is a group-level contrast between the first three and last three trials.
  • The Ewert response law written as a single joint function of velocity, contrast and size. The source defines three separate univariate relations measured with the others held constant; writing it as one surface invents interaction terms nobody measured. And do not invent the worm versus anti-worm tuning numbers to fill the gap.
  • An egocentric turn-rule architecture justified by the whiptail position-versus-feature study. That claim failed verification: a specialist review with full-text access reports the spatial advantage held during acquisition only and not during reversal, and the reading of position as an egocentric rule is an interpolation the paper does not support.
  • Allocentric place learning justified by the turtle medial cortex lesion result. It is the cleanest place-versus-cue dissociation in any reptile and it is a turtle, outside Squamata entirely, and it is directly contradicted by the only lizard lesion study. Do not pick whichever of the two supports the design you already wanted.
  • Any home range, daily movement distance, or foraging loop geometry for this species. No field study of wild leopard geckos exists at all. Set the enclosure scale from the physics and the task and call it a design choice.
  • A below-the-horizon prey prior in world coordinates. The published elevation figures are positive in eye coordinates and are consequences of head posture.
  • A prey detector calibrated with mammalian or fish acuity numbers taken at face value. Nocturnal geckos have systematically lower spatial acuity, so any imported angular threshold is probably too fine, and the correction size is unmeasured. If the threshold is imported unchanged, say so.

What the literature sweep actually turned up

Twelve findings that changed the plan. Several of them reverse a decision this project had already made.

  • The brief's founding citation was a species confusion. Day, Crews and Wilczynski never studied leopard geckos. Their entire lizard output is three papers on two other families. The confusion is understandable, because David Crews did work extensively on Eublepharis macularius, but on temperature-dependent sex determination, not spatial cognition. A memory module built on 'the Day et al. leopard gecko numbers' would have been built on nothing.
  • The modules that were deferred as too thin turned out to be the buildable ones, and the module needed most urgently turned out to be the unsupported one. Memory and learning now have real target-species numbers. The prey detector has none, for any gecko, ever.
  • Only about one third of leopard geckos orient by the relationship between cues. The authors state plainly that the rest may have used a non-cognitive motor search and that they cannot rule it out. The default for a single simulated animal should therefore be the majority strategy, not the flattering one.
  • Geckos found the hidden platform FASTER in complete darkness than at the end of normal training, while swimming LONGER paths at roughly twice the speed. A fast undirected search solves the task without any spatial memory at all. Any learning curve measured in time is contaminated by exactly this.
  • In every published statistical model of this species, the number of prods needed to keep the animal moving predicted performance more strongly than the training phase did, often by an order of magnitude in F. The published leopard gecko learning curves are partly motivation curves.
  • Fast forgetting is the correct answer for this animal, not a defect. Two months, against nine years in giant tortoises and twenty months in monitors. The authors' own explanation is the seasonal semi-arid Pakistani habitat: the landscape gets rearranged, so an old map is worse than no map.
  • The defensive display in this species is chemosensory AND-gated. Vision and touch can raise sampling but never fire the display. If the simulated gecko has no chemical channel, the honest consequence is that it should be unable to display at all.
  • The two reptile lesion studies of the hippocampal homologue directly contradict each other. Turtles lost place learning and kept cue learning; whiptail lizards never used a place strategy at all, lesioned or intact. Neither animal is a gecko, and the gecko's own medial cortex has never been lesioned, inactivated or recorded from.
  • Zero place cells, grid cells or head-direction cells have ever been recorded in any reptile. That search returned nothing at all, which is unusual and worth stating plainly rather than softening.
  • Three items from the verification pass should be carried forward as corrections. The Ewert response law is three separate univariate relations, not one joint function of velocity, contrast and size. The whiptail position-over-feature reversal advantage is contradicted by a specialist review with full-text access. And the claim that every Ewert paper is paywalled is false: at least two Bufo primary papers with quantitative neuronal tuning data are freely readable, one of them with 104 single neurons showing configural-motion selectivity.
  • The single best-transferring quantitative data for this animal's hunting covers only the last two centimetres. A gecko in the same family has published lunge distance, velocity, acceleration and success rate. Everything upstream of that lunge, all the finding and approaching, has to be imported from a fish larva, a mouse and a toad.
  • The entire target-species literature on memory and learning is one laboratory, one captive colony descended from about 90 wild-caught Pakistani founders, one apparatus, one aversive task, and an overlapping author list. Three papers, but a single evidence stream.
Part 16

What must be checked or clarified

Open questions, in the sense that the project cannot answer them from anything it currently holds. Several are decisions rather than measurements, and they are listed because they are sitting underneath work that has already been done.

Is lab or legacy the right gait profile? must be settled

lab is gate-validated and limps under the trained policy. legacy is un-gated and looks correct. Whether the gate battery ever scored front-foot symmetry has never been established. Looking better is not the same as being right, and this decision sits underneath every video and every hunt measurement.

Does the leopard gecko hunt visually at all? unresolved in the literature

The only quantitative sensory study on this species is about PREDATOR detection, and it found chemical cues dominant (0.21 chemical vs 0.07 visual, n=42). The whole visual prey-detection module is built on a mouse, a fish larva and a toad. If the answer is no, a large part of the eye work is aimed at the wrong sense.

What does the animal do between 2 cm and 30 cm? no data exists

The best-transferring numbers in the entire corpus — lunge distance, velocity, acceleration, success rate — cover only the last two centimetres, and they come from a different genus in the same family. Everything upstream has to be imported.

Is the memory module going to be present and inert? must be decided before building

Every measured retention point in this species is at two months or beyond. A time constant of 115 days inside an episode measured in minutes is a term whose value is numerically indistinguishable from “no decay”. Ship the store without the decay and say so, or do not ship it.

What is the simulation's clock actually worth? unexamined

The learning rate was measured with trials one WEEK apart. The memory numbers live at months. The hunt lives at seconds. Nothing in this project has established what one simulated second is supposed to be, and three modules now depend on the answer.

Was the gate battery ever a locomotion validation? worth re-deriving

Two of six gates have never passed. The accepted walker is accepted on four. Whether four-of-six is a meaningful bar, or whether the two failing gates are the ones that matter, has never been argued in writing.

Does the registry's confidence field mean anything? audit needed

75 of 143 parameters are tagged uncertain and 30 verified. The policy text says verified means checked in the primary source. One entry tagged verified was the wrong species. The field has never been audited end to end.

Are the 212 harvested citations real? explicitly unverified

This project has invented a citation once (#215) and overstated the absence of one (Delheusy 1995). The bibliography in Part 14 is a HARVEST of every author-year string in the repository. It has not been checked against any database. That check is the first thing the companion prompt asks for.

Part 18

The analysis brief that goes with this document

This report is also meant to be handed to a second reader with web access — another model, or a person — whose job is to check it rather than agree with it. The brief below is that instruction set. It is reproduced here so it cannot get separated from the document it is about; it also ships as NeuroGecko_Analysis_Prompt.md.

The single most important rule of this project

Every number in the simulation is tagged PUBLISHED, DERIVED or INVENTED, and says which. The project's stated position is that an invented number labelled as invented is fine, and a plausible number wearing a published number's clothes is the worst possible defect. Everything you do should serve that rule: move numbers from invented to published where a real measurement exists, and move them from published to invented where the citation does not support what is claimed.

A second rule matters for how you answer: the project never accepts time estimates. Do not give any. Give orderings and dependencies.

Task 1 — Verify the bibliography. Do this first.

Part 14 of the PDF lists 212 author-year strings and 51 DOIs harvested from the repository's own text. The document states plainly that none of them has been checked against a bibliographic database. Check them.

For each entry, especially the ones the project leans on most (Jagnandan 2014 and 2017, Fuller 2011, McElroy 2008, Delheusy 1995, Vollin 2021, Kröhnke 2023, Bergel 2026, Frýdlová 2026, Masseck 2008, Rawat 2019, Zaaf 2001, Autumn 1994 and 1997, Ewert 1969, Han & Carr 2024, Prescott 2024, Girard 2005, Hoy 2019, Yilmaz & Meister 2013, Whitford 2022, Wainwright 1991, Werner 1998/2005/2008, Wever 1964):

  1. Does it exist? Search Google Scholar, PubMed, Crossref (api.crossref.org), Semantic Scholar, and the publisher directly. Resolve every DOI at https://doi.org/<the DOI>.
  2. Is the species right? This project has already been caught attributing leopard-gecko work to authors who studied other families. For every citation used to justify a parameter tagged E_macularius, confirm the paper's actual study species.
  3. Does the paper say what the parameter claims? Where you can reach the full text or a preprint, check the specific number. The project's registry entries carry a source field with journal, volume and pages — verify those too.
  4. Flag every entry you cannot resolve. "Could not retrieve" is a valid and useful answer. Do not fill a gap with something plausible.

Report as a table: citation | exists? | species studied | number checked | verdict where verdict is one of CONFIRMED / WRONG SPECIES / MISQUOTED / NOT FOUND / PAYWALLED.

Task 2 — Attack the named gaps

Part 15 lists quantities the project says have never been measured and has therefore refused to invent. For each, search hard before accepting the gap. Search in English and, where relevant, in the languages of the herpetological literature (German, Czech, Russian, Chinese) and in the grey literature: theses, zoo and husbandry research, conference abstracts, preprints on bioRxiv.

The gaps, in the order they would unblock the most work:

  1. Visual prey detection in any gecko. Receptive field size, size tuning, speed tuning, contrast threshold, detection latency, acuity in cycles per degree. The project claims nothing exists for any gecko and is currently importing all of it from a mouse superior colliculus, a zebrafish larva and a toad. Look for optic tectum recordings in any gekkotan, any nocturnal lizard, any squamate.
  2. Whether this species hunts visually at all. The only quantitative sensory study on E. macularius is about predator detection and found chemical cues dominant. If a study exists showing visually guided prey capture in this species or a close relative, it changes the whole architecture.
  3. Anything between 2 cm and 30 cm of a gecko prey-capture sequence. The project has good numbers for the final lunge (from Coleonyx, same family) and nothing at all for the approach.
  4. Cost of transport, sprint maximum, endurance, thermal performance curve, CTmin for E. macularius or any eublepharid.
  5. Any field study of wild leopard geckos — home range, activity budget, diet, microhabitat. The project believes none exists.
  6. A fitted habituation curve or time constant for any lizard or any reptile. The document calls this the single biggest gap in the learning module.
  7. Memory decay at hours, days or weeks in any lizard. Everything published is at two months or beyond, and a hunt lasts seconds.
  8. A false-positive rate for any biological prey detector — toad, mouse, fish larva, lizard. The document says no such measurement exists anywhere.
  9. Cricket walking-vibration spectrum on sand, for a substrate-vibration sense.
  10. A sleep-cycle period for E. macularius specifically. The project has a published bracket of 84–134.5 s across lizard species and refuses to pick a number inside it. The source paper reportedly gives per-species values only as a violin plot with raw data on request — see whether the raw data, supplementary material or a later paper prints it.

For each: either give the measurement with its citation and sample size, or state clearly that you searched and found nothing, and say where you searched.

Task 3 — Adjudicate the contested claims

The document flags several places where the evidence disagrees with itself. Read the primary sources and take a position.

  • The two reptile hippocampal-homologue lesion studies contradict each other. Turtles lost place learning and kept cue learning; whiptail lizards never used a place strategy at all. Neither animal is a gecko. Which, if either, should a gecko model follow, and on what grounds other than convenience?
  • The Ewert prey-recognition response law. The document says it is three separate univariate relations (velocity, contrast, size, each measured with the others held constant) and not one joint surface, and that the worm/anti-worm tuning curves are unreachable. Confirm or correct this from Ewert's actual papers, and find the numeric curves if they are reachable.
  • The whiptail position-over-feature reversal advantage. The document says this claim failed verification — that the advantage held during acquisition only, not reversal. Check it.
  • The nightly retreat loop. The document says the claim that leopard geckos leave a shared retreat at sunset and return before dawn traces to a hobbyist magazine article recirculated through Wikipedia and care sheets, with no sample size, method or peer review. Trace it yourself and say where it actually comes from.
  • The "tight hide" rule. Every care sheet states geckos prefer a snug crevice. The document says there is zero primary support in this species. Find the primary source or confirm its absence.
  • Whether the 82.9 % strike success rate transfers. It comes from Coleonyx, a different genus in the same family. The simulation reproduces 89.7 %. Is that a validation or a coincidence?

Task 4 — Check the arithmetic that was DERIVED

These numbers are not printed in any paper. The project computed them and says so. Recompute them from the published points and say whether the derivation holds.

  • Memory decay constants τ ≈ 3.79 months (route precision) and τ ≈ 4.32 months (goal-finding). Derived by interpolating between two published retention points and assuming an exponential form that was never tested, and by treating a hazard ratio as a linear index of memory strength. Is that defensible? If not, what should it be?
  • The learning curve shape. The per-trial hazard ratio (1.09) and both ceilings (3.02× latency, 4.59× path) are published. The trajectory between them is drawn as an exponential and is invented. Does any published data constrain the shape?
  • The approach speed floor, 0.018 m/s. Scaled from a mouse figure of 0.05 m/s against a 0.164 m/s locomotor speed, applied to this animal's 0.055 m/s walk. Is proportional scaling right here?
  • The angular size at which vision starts guiding approach, 6–8 degrees. Derived geometrically from a 2 cm cricket at 15–20 cm. The document calls it the most load-bearing and weakest number in the whole prey rule.

Task 5 — Challenge the architecture, not just the numbers

Read Part 2 (how one step runs), Part 9 (the eye) and Part 11 (the plan), then answer these as an outside reader who is allowed to say the plan is wrong.

  • The blocker is that the eye reports something on 5.4 % of steps during a hunt. The proposed fix is a two-channel wide-field/narrow-field detector borrowed from mouse superior colliculus. Is that the right fix for a low detection rate, or does a low detection rate point at something else — the field of view, the head not being pointed at anything, the prey being out of frame, the sampling rate?
  • The animal is nocturnal, afoveate, with a large pupil and short focal length. Every imported tuning constant comes from diurnal, foveate animals. How big is that correction, and does anyone know?
  • The walking rhythm is hand-written and the trained residual is switched off because it was measured as worse. Is a hand-written CPG a defensible scientific choice, or a convenience? What would it take to show it is right?
  • The document says only about one third of leopard geckos orient by the relationship between cues, and the rest may be running a non-cognitive motor search. Should a single simulated animal model the majority strategy or the interesting minority one?
  • The learning numbers come from an aversive forced-swim escape task, and the simulation is about hunting. Is there any principled way to carry a learning rate across motivational systems, or should the module say it cannot?

Task 6 — Find what the project has not thought of

Search for recent work (2023 onward, and check for anything in 2026) on:

  • Reptile or lizard neuroscience relevant to any of the eight modules.
  • Simulated animals built the same way — physics-engine models validated against published biology rather than trained to a reward. Note what they did about the same problems (provenance, gaps, oracle removal, validation).
  • MuJoCo or physics-simulation work on sprawling-posture locomotion.
  • Anything on Eublepharis macularius at all. It is a common laboratory and pet species and the project may simply have missed papers.

How to report back

Write one document with these sections, in this order:

  1. Verdicts on the bibliography — the table from Task 1, with counts: how many confirmed, wrong species, misquoted, not found.
  2. Gaps closed — every quantity from Task 2 you found a real measurement for, with citation, sample size, study species, and the exact value.
  3. Gaps confirmed — every one you searched for and could not find, with where you searched. This is as valuable as the previous section.
  4. Contested claims, adjudicated — Task 3, with your position and the primary source you based it on.
  5. Derivations checked — Task 4, with your recomputation.
  6. Architecture challenges — Task 5. Be direct. If the plan is aimed at the wrong problem, say so and say what the right one is.
  7. What the project missed — Task 6.
  8. The ten things you would change first, in order, with the dependency for each. No time estimates.

For every claim you make, give the source. Mark anything you could not verify as unverified. If you are not sure, say you are not sure — this project would rather have a recorded gap than a confident guess, and it has the ledger to prove why.

What not to do

  • Do not accept a number because the PDF states it confidently. The PDF is the output of the system being audited.
  • Do not fill a gap with a value from a related species without saying so, and without naming the species and the distance between it and Eublepharis macularius.
  • Do not cite a paper you have not opened. The project has already been burned by exactly that.
  • Do not reproduce long passages from any paper. Summarise, cite, and quote at most a short phrase.
  • Do not give schedules, timelines or effort estimates for anything.

These are not unit tests. Corrections and limits the audit records against itself

  • The model has 32 hinge joints, not the 26 asserted in parts of the supplied documents.
  • Fuller Table1 femur/tibia is 1.54/1.51=1.0199, not 0.98. The requested 0.90–1.06 pass band is retained explicitly.
  • Fuller Table1 tibia SEM is 0.02 cm, not the 0.04 cm transcribed in the supplied scorecard.
  • Interorbital distance is approximated by the inner spherical-eye gap, not center-to-center separation.
  • The source limb total includes fourth toe. MJCF ankle-to-digit geometry is a proxy, not a measured metatarsal segment.
  • Static zero-control heights are engineering gates using walking reference values; they do not establish dynamic posture validity.
  • A root spawn-height edit alone cannot set the eventual mechanically settled hip height.
  • Gate tolerances are engineering choices. Passing them is not a statistical claim about individual animals.
  • Tail CoM exclusion holds all remaining segments in the same neutral pose and is not an autotomy behavior experiment.

Part 22

The surface: what was added, and what it cost the physics

The animal had 23 rigid shells that visibly slid past one another. It now has one continuous deformable surface of 21,663 vertices bound to 23 bones, an eyeball with a vertical pupil and a lid that closes, and a tongue on a slide joint. The question that matters is not whether it looks better. It is whether the animal the gates measured is still the animal that walks.

It is. Measured three ways, not assumed (#318). A lab body rebuilt from a mesh-free, skin-free copy of the same source has bit-identical body_mass, body_inertia, body_ipos, jnt_range, dof_damping and actuator_gainprm — maximum absolute difference exactly 0.000e+00 on every array, total mass 0.038 kg both ways. After 300 steps from the stand keyframe the two worlds' qpos agree to the last bit. And the 64×64 image the animal's own head_cam delivers to its retina differs in 0 of 4096 pixels. This was checked rather than argued because the assumption was not safe: the retina is a camera ON the animal, and in legacy mode it draws geom group 1 — the group every new mesh and the skin sit in.

The six steps, in the one order that works

Forgetting the fifth step twice left a body that compiled, rendered, and passed 14/14 gates while three reproducibility tests failed with an unrelated-sounding message (#332). tools/rebuild_body.py exists so that order cannot be got wrong again.

1generate the swept body, limb and toe meshes
2generate the eyeball, lid and rim meshes
3bind one surface to the 23 bones and emit the skin
4patch the source XML (idempotent)
5refit lab body v1 — the step that gets skipped
6refit lab body v2 with --fit-com, then the world, then the furnished world
Two renderer facts that cost this project several sessions, recorded so they are not rediscovered. (a) Mesh UVs require a type="2d" texture; a cube texture is addressed by POSITION and ignores texture coordinates entirely, which renders the whole animal flat grey (#315). (b) A mesh geom's texture rows count from the BOTTOM of the image and a skin's count from the TOP, so the same v coordinate lands on opposite ends of the same PNG — measured: the texture at v = 0.10 is yellow (237, 200, 59) and at v = 0.90 is white (228, 225, 218), which is exactly the white eyelid that appeared (#344). And one that does not work at all: MuJoCo accepts <layer role="normal"> in a material and the renderer ignores it — measured, 0 of 57600 pixels changed (#329). Bumps have to be baked into the colour.
Part 22 · continued

Every constant in the surface generators

These are appearance numbers. Almost none of them is published, and the project's first rule applies to them exactly as it applies to the physics: the ones that are INVENTED say so in their own source. They are reproduced here in full because the surface is the one part of this animal that was built by eye, and a reader checking the work needs to see which dials exist.

The swept surface — tools/make_gecko_mesh.py, 13 constants

One surface is swept along the animal's own axis, sampling the envelope of the gated collision primitives at every station, so the skin cannot be a different animal from the one the gates measured.

A fractional wrap leaves the texture discontinuous at the seam, and a wrap that changes from ring to ring shears that discontinuity along the body -- which is why the tail came out as a barber's pole. Two tiles round a ~60 mm girth keeps the spots roughly as wide as they are long.

Part 23

The agents, and what survived them

Every piece of biology in this animal was found by a research pass, and every research pass in this project is adversarial by construction: one agent per question finds a claim, then independent agents are told to REFUTE it and to reject anything they cannot confirm from a source they have personally opened. The refutation rate is the point. A pass that confirms everything it looked for has not checked anything.

233agent runs recorded
276published measurements
10 / 36surface claims survived
