The 167 figure is the tally carried in docs/FAILURE_MAP.md's standing summary and has not been independently recounted here; the 12, 42 and 24 are each stated in the ledger row or the document that pass produced. 167 + 12 is the pre-existing count, and 42 + 24 were added in the most recent session, giving 233 recorded agent runs in total. Treat 167 as reported rather than verified.
The surface pass is PARKED, NOT APPLIED. The appearance work was called off by the user before this research returned, and a pass in which 26 of 36 claims died is exactly the reason not to have built first and checked afterwards. The skin that exists was built from reference photographs, not from this document. Applying it is unstarted work.
Part 23 · continued

Surface anatomy — the 10 claims of 36 that survived

42 agents. Each claim below was confirmed from a source the verifying agent opened and read. The last line of each is the instruction the pass wrote for whoever eventually builds it.

ear

The tympanic membrane of the leopard gecko is externally visible on the side of the head, with no scale cover or flap over it.

[verified] Vedurmudi et al. use the leopard gecko as their type example of an internally coupled ear. Fig. 1 caption: the location of the eardrum / tympanic membrane on the side of its head is highlighted; a close-up of the head shows the eardrum and the embedded extracolumella can be 'discerned clearly'; a third panel is a close-up of the eardrum itself. This is photographic evidence for the species, not a verbal description. I extracted and read the PDF text directly. Caveat: the caption names only 'Leopard gecko', not the binomial, though that vernacular is standard for E. macularius.

Source: Vedurmudi AP, Goulet J, Christensen-Dalsgaard J, Young BA, Williams R, van Hemmen JL (2016) Internally coupled ears: mathematical structures and mechanisms underlying ICE. Biological Cybernetics 110: 359–382, Fig. 1 caption (p. 360). PDF: https://www.atsu.edu/research-portal/uploads/78040790-Internally%20coupled%20ears-mathematical%20structures.pdf

For the model: Model the ear as a real aperture in the head silhouette with a visible membrane at its floor — not a painted-on spot and not a scale-covered depression.
eye

Eublepharids have genuinely movable eyelids; the family name is descriptive, not just etymological.

[verified] Boulenger's family diagnosis for Eublepharidae states the eyes are moderately large and are protected by thick, movable, lids that meet ("connivent"). Smith's genus diagnosis for Eublepharis independently states both eyelids are well developed and movable. Two independent primary taxonomic sources, ~50 years apart, agree. Smith elsewhere lists "connivent eyelids" as one of the three characters separating eublepharids from typical gekkonids (with opisthocoelous vertebrae and united parietals).

Source: Boulenger, G.A. 1885. Catalogue of the Lizards in the British Museum (Natural History), 2nd ed., Vol. 1, p. 229 (Fam. Eublepharidae). Archive.org id catalogueoflizar01brituoft. AND Smith, M.A. 1935. The Fauna of British India... Reptilia and Amphibia Vol. II, Sauria, pp. 125-126 (genus Eublepharis). Archive.org id in.ernet.dli.2015.207328.

For the model: Model two real lid flaps as separate deformable geometry over the globe, not a painted-on ring. The lids are described as THICK, so they need volume — a fleshy fold with its own scale texture, not a thin membrane.
eye

Leopard geckos have NO spectacle / brille. The cornea is bare and directly exposed when the lids are open.

[verified] Smith states that in Eublepharis the eyeball "has lost the fixed membranous covering" that other geckos have. Hellebuyck & Solanes Vilanova state that a true transparent rigid spectacle is present in all Gekkota except the eublepharid clade, which has fully moveable eyelids. Reavill & Schmidt say it species-specifically: the leopard gecko "belongs to a family of geckos that have eyelids and not a spectacle" — and warn that the caseous corneal plug clinicians see in this species is commonly misdiagnosed as a retained spectacle. Three independent sources, one of them naming E. macularius directly.

Source: Smith 1935, Fauna of British India, Sauria, pp. 23-24. AND Hellebuyck, T. & Solanes Vilanova, F. 2023. Animals 13(6):1108, doi:10.3390/ani13061108. AND Reavill, D. & Schmidt, R.E. 2012. Pathology of the Reptile Eye and Ocular Adnexa. Proc. ARAV 2012, p. 89.

For the model: Do NOT put a glossy transparent scale disc over the eye. The cornea is a wet, directly exposed, strongly specular dome — shade it as bare cornea with a sharp specular highlight, sitting inside a soft skin aperture, not behind a flat scale.
eye

The pupil is vertical.

[verified] Smith's genus diagnosis for Eublepharis lists flatly: "Pupil vertical." Boulenger's family diagnosis calls it an "elliptico-vertical pupil" — i.e. a vertically-elongate ellipse rather than a mathematical hairline. Two independent primary sources.

Source: Smith 1935, Fauna of British India, Sauria, p. 126. AND Boulenger 1885, Cat. Liz. Brit. Mus. Vol. 1, p. 229.

For the model: Pupil axis is vertical in head space (perpendicular to the long axis of the eye aperture), so it stays vertical regardless of how the eye aperture is tilted on the skull.
feet

Each of the four feet bears five digits; there is no digit reduction.

[verified] Zhuang et al. (2019) figure 1B is a schematic of a gecko left pes in dorsal view explicitly 'based on a radiograph of the left pes of Eublepharis macularius', labelling five metatarsals MTI-MTV. Corroborated at genus level by congener descriptions that report subdigital lamellae as five per-digit counts for each autopodium (E. jhuma: right manus 10-15-17-18-15; right pes 11-16-21-23-22) and relative lengths for digits I-V.

Source: Zhuang, M.V., Russell, A.P. & Higham, T.E. (2019) Evolution of pedal digit orientation and morphology in relation to acquisition and secondary loss of the adhesive system in geckos. Journal of Morphology 280. PDF: https://biomechanics.ucr.edu/Zhuang_et_al-2019-Journal_of_Morphology.pdf — figure caption, p.4 of PDF text

For the model: Model 5 toes per foot, 20 total. Digit I (innermost) is shortest on both hand and foot and sits noticeably offset from the others.
feet

Leopard geckos have NO adhesive toe pads: no expanded scansors, no adhesive pads, and no documented setae.

[verified] Peattie (2008) abstract, read verbatim via Europe PMC: 'Subdigital adhesive setae have previously been documented in all legged gecko families except the Eublepharidae.' The single exception she reports is Aeluroscalabotes felinus, 'the only arboreal eublepharids', with setae up to 9 micrometres — a different genus, not Eublepharis. Independently, Smith (1935, p.~119) states that Teratoscincus, Stenodactylus, Alsophylax, Gymnodactylus, Cnemaspis, Agamura, Pristurus 'and Eublepharis have the primitive, non-dilated form of digit. All the other genera mentioned in this work have adhesive expansions by means of which they are able to ascend vertical walls.' Smith's family key entry for the genus reads simply 'Digits not dilated, clawed ... Eublepharis, p. 125.'

Source: Peattie, A.M. (2008) Anatomical Record 291:869-875, DOI 10.1002/ar.20706 (abstract via Europe PMC REST API); Smith, M.A. (1935) The Fauna of British India, Reptilia and Amphibia Vol. II — Sauria, pp. 119, 125-128, https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.207328

For the model: CRITICAL: do not model the fanned, flattened, pad-like toe undersides seen in Gekko or Hemidactylus references. The underside of each toe is a narrow, rounded strip, not a broadened paddle. No setal fringe, no leaf-like terminal pads.
feet

They DO have subdigital lamellae — the widespread claim that leopard geckos 'have no lamellae' is imprecise. What they lack is ADHESIVE pads/scansors/setae, not lamellae.

[verified] Boulenger (1890) genus diagnosis: 'Digits short and cylindrical, with a row of lamellae below, clawed...'. Smith (1935) genus diagnosis: 'Digits short, cylindrical, with transverse lamellae beneath, clawed...'. So a single ventral row of transverse plate-like scales runs the length of each toe; they simply are not adhesive scansors. This distinction is the single most commonly garbled fact about this animal.

Source: Boulenger, G.A. (1890) The Fauna of British India, Reptilia and Batrachia, Genus Eublepharis, p. 107, https://archive.org/details/TheFaunaOfBritishIndiaReptiliaAndBatrachia ; Smith, M.A. (1935) op. cit., p. 125

For the model: Model a single row of transverse ventral scale-plates down each toe — visible as stacked bands on the sole of the toe. Roughly 15-23 per long toe based on congener counts. This is surface detail, not silhouette.
head_scales

The nostril is a lateral opening on the side of the snout very close to, but NOT touching, the rostral scale.

[verified] Boulenger (1885), in the family account for Eublepharidae, states the nostril is rather large, directed slightly upwards though lateral, and separated from the rostral and the labial plates. Smith (1935) states for E. hardwickii — and the E. macularius account on the following pages is written purely as a list of differences from hardwickii, none of them cranial — 'rostral broader than high, not in contact with the nostril'. Corroborated a third time by the modern Eublepharis descriptions, which place the naris inside a discrete nasal scale rather than on a suture. Three independent sources, two of them museum/fauna-level taxonomic works, agree. NOTE: the strongest statement (Boulenger) is a family-level diagnosis, and Smith's is inherited by E. macularius through the difference-only convention rather than being written out for it.

Source: Boulenger, G.A. 1885. Catalogue of the Lizards in the British Museum (Natural History), 2nd ed., Vol. I, family Eublepharidae, pp. 229–230 (read via archive.org OCR, item catalogueoflizar01brituoft); Smith, M.A. 1935. Fauna of British India, Reptilia and Amphibia Vol. II — Sauria, pp. 126–129 (archive.org item in.ernet.dli.2015.62460)

For the model: Place the nostril aperture on the LATERAL face of the snout, roughly one scale-width behind the rostral plate, with the opening canted slightly dorsally rather than facing straight sideways. Critically: do NOT let the nostril hole touch or notch the rostral, and do not let it sit on the lip line. It is a hole within a single swollen scale, set above the first supralabial.
tubercles

The dorsal integument is built from exactly two visible element types: a pavement of small flattened scales, and larger raised tubercles set into that pavement.

[verified] Russell et al. (2014) SEM-surveyed skin from head, trunk, hindlimb and tail of adult leopard geckos (SVL 89-120 mm, n=5 for body regions, 7 original + 2 regenerated tails) and describe the dorsum as clad in "two general types of integumentary derivative": scales (granular, semi-imbricating or imbricating) and tubercles. Corroborated independently by Smith (1935, p.126-127), who describes the genus as "back with small juxtaposed scales and larger tubercles", and by Boulenger (1885, p.230-232), whose key splits Eublepharis into "back with enlarged tubercles" (incl. macularius) vs "back uniformly granular".

Source: Russell AP, Lai EK, Powell GL, Higham TE (2014) Journal of Morphology 275:961-979, doi:10.1002/jmor.20269 (PDF: https://biomechanics.ucr.edu/Russell_etal_2014.pdf), Results "Scale Descriptions"; Smith MA (1935) Fauna of British India, Reptilia & Amphibia Vol. II Sauria, pp.126-128; Boulenger GA (1885) Catalogue of the Lizards in the British Museum (Nat. Hist.) Vol. I, pp.230-232

For the model: Two-layer surface: a continuous fine base tiling plus a sparse scattering of discrete raised bumps. Do not model the bumps as a modulation of the base tiling - they are separate, larger elements that displace it.
tubercles

The specific number of dorsal tubercle rows at midbody for E. macularius sensu stricto is not in any source I could open; the nearest figure is 18 rows, for the Rajasthan/Delhi population.

[likely] Mirza (2024) describes the Aravalli/Delhi population (as E. madarensis, resurrected; The Reptile Database still treats madarensis as a synonym of E. macularius and disputes the revalidation) with "large unkeeled tubercles in 18 longitudinal rows" and, in the specimen description, "the large scales are arranged in 18 longitudinal rows at midbody". Comparative counts in the same papers: E. satpuraensis 20 rows; E. hardwickii and E. pictus 23-26 rows of flat tubercle-like scales. The likely source of a macularius count, Mirza et al. (2014) Phyllomedusa 13(2):75-90, was unreachable (revistas.usp.br refused connection from this network), so I did not open it and do not cite it.

Source: Mirza ZA (2024) Taprobanica 13(1):9-15, Diagnosis and Description (PDF: https://www.taprobanica.org/~file/318_eublepharis_madarensis_taprobanica_13_1_2024_mirza_9_15-99e7c-3349_1243.pdf); Reptile Database account for E. macularius, https://reptile-database.reptarium.cz/species?genus=Eublepharis&species=macularius (Comment section, on the status of madarensis)

For the model: Budget roughly 18-20 tubercle rows spanning the dorsum from flank to flank at midbody. Treat this as the right order of magnitude, not a verified count for macularius.
Part 23 · continued

Surface anatomy — the 26 that did not

This is the more valuable half. Each of these was a plausible, confidently-worded statement about this animal that turned out to be a congener's trait, an absolute where the source hedged, or a number nobody has actually measured.

Tubercles never touch each other: each is isolated from its neighbours by intervening small scales.

-- REFUTED AS WORDED, BY ITS OWN CITED SOURCE. I opened both sources (source_opened = true for both).

1. THE HEDGE THE CLAIM DROPS. Russell, Lai, Powell & Higham (2014) J. Morphol. 275:961-979, Results ("Scale Descriptions", p. 968) reads exactly: "Tubercles juxtapose neighboring scales and are usually isolated from other tubercles by intervening scales." The qualifier "usually" is the authors' own. It entails exceptions. The claim converts this into "never" and "each", which is a strictly stronger assertion than the source makes. I searched the full text for "never", "always", "exclusive", "without exception" — the authors never make an absolute statement about tubercle isolation. The submitted DETAIL actually quotes "usually" correctly, then the CLAIM headline silently strengthens it; the failure is in the claim, not the transcription. PDF opened at https://biomechanics.ucr.edu/Russell_etal_2014.pdf and text-extracted locally to C:\Users\ziyad\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-ziyad\920e259d-472d-4210-945a-591bc20b749a\scratchpad\russell2014_flow.txt

2. SCOPE ERROR. That sentence sits in the paragraph describing the DORSAL BODY (referencing Fig. 2c), not a whole-animal rule. Russell et al. state separately that "The ventral regions of the body are devoid of tubercles."

3. REGIONS WHERE "EACH IS ISOLATED" HAS NO PURCHASE. Russell et al.: ventrally on the tail "the tubercles also lose their identity along this transitional gradient"; in segment 5 "distinction between tubercles, imbricating scales and ventral plates is lost"; and "The regenerated tail lacks tubercles and bears scales that are more homogeneous than those of the original." A regenerated tail is common in both wild and captive animals, so a universal quantifier over "each tubercle" fails outright there.

4. A WORDING SLIP THAT INVERTS THE ANATOMY. Russell et al. use "juxtapose" to mean abut/lie edge-to-edge (contrast their imbricating scales, which overlap). So a tubercle IS in direct contact with the small scales around it ("Tubercles juxtapose neighboring scales"); what it is usually separated from is OTHER TUBERCLES. The claim's "isolated from its neighbours by intervening small scales" garbles this — the intervening scales are the neighbours, not a gap between the tubercle and its neighbours.

5. WHAT DOES HOLD, AND IT CORROBORATES TWICE. The weaker, hedged observation is genuinely supported by two independently opened sources. McLean KE & Vickaryous MK (2011) BMC Dev Biol 11:50 (opened at the PMC URL given): "Along the dorsal and lateral surfaces this pavement of flattened scales is interrupted at regular intervals by large cone-like tubercles" and "Close inspection reveals that adjacent, slightly enlarged scales surround each tubercle." The DETAIL's characterisation of McLean & Vickaryous is accurate. Russell et al. add that on the tail tubercles are "spaced dorsoventrally in columns, at relatively regular intervals" and (Fig. 4 caption) "arranged in columns ... within whorls, and rows ... along the tail" — regular spacing, consistent with usual separation.

6. SPECIES CONFUSION — CHECKED, NONE FOUND. Both papers genuinely study E. macularius; I found no sign the observation was imported from another gecko. The E. pictus material (Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022, rosette of 10-12 small scales) is a congener transfer and the submitter already flags it as such, which is correct practice. I did NOT open Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022, so the 10-12 rosette count is UNVERIFIED here and must not be cited as E. macularius.

7. CAPTIVE-BRED VS WILD-TYPE — A REAL UNRESOLVED CAVEAT. McLean & Vickaryous state explicitly: "All E. macularius were captive bred and obtained from one of two commercial suppliers (Pat Wise Lizards, Calgary, Alberta, Canada; Global Exotic Pets, Kitchener, Ontario, Canada)." They give no wild-type or morph designation. Russell et al. give NO provenance at all — only "Seven original tails and two fully regenerated ... tails were removed from specimens (snout-vent length 89-120 mm) of leopard geckos" under Calgary protocol BI07R-32; no wild-caught/captive-bred statement, no locality, no morph. So neither opened source documents wild-caught wild-type animals, and the tail half of the claim rests wholly on captive-bred commercial pet-trade stock. COULD_NOT_VERIFY: whether wild E. macularius show the same tubercle spacing, and whether captive selective breeding alters tubercle arrangement — I have no source open on either, and I am not filling that gap. Treat any "wild-type" framing of this trait as UNVERIFIED. - correction: Replace the absolute with the sourced hedge, and fix the neighbour/tubercle inversion:

"On the dorsal body, tubercles abut the surrounding small scales directly and are USUALLY — not invariably — separated from OTHER TUBERCLES by those intervening scales (Russell et al. 2014, J. Morphol. 275:961-979, Results: 'Tubercles juxtapose neighboring scales and are usually isolated from other tubercles by intervening scales'). On the original tail the same pattern holds: a pavement of small flattened scales is interrupted at regular intervals by large cone-like tubercles, with adjacent slightly enlarged scales surrounding each tubercle (McLean & Vickaryous 2011, BMC Dev Biol 11:50), the tubercles being spaced in columns within whorls and in rows along the tail (Russell et al. 2014). This description does not extend to the whole animal: the ventral body is devoid of tubercles, tubercles lose their identity ventrolaterally on the tail and are indistinguishable from other scales near the tail tip, and regenerated tails lack tubercles entirely (Russell et al. 2014)."

Confidence: the hedged version is MODERATE-to-GOOD (corroborated by two opened, peer-reviewed sources). The original absolute ("never", "each") is UNVERIFIED and contradicted by the qualifier in its own primary source. Provenance caveat to carry forward: both sources used captive animals (McLean & Vickaryous explicitly captive-bred commercial stock; Russell et al. unstated), so wild-type applicability is UNVERIFIED.

On the trunk the tubercles are in longitudinal rows, but loosely so - regular enough that taxonomists count them as a character, irregular enough that no author describes them as a lattice.

-- REFUTED as a statement about E. macularius, because every row-statement in the cited sources belongs to a congener, not to macularius.

WHAT I OPENED AND CONFIRMED VERBATIM 1. Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022, Evolutionary Systematics 6(1):77-88 (opened: Pensoft full text/XML, local copies C:\Users\ziyad\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-ziyad\920e259d-472d-4210-945a-591bc20b749a\scratchpad\pictus_plain.txt and mirza2022.xml). Methods sentence is exactly as quoted: "Dorsal longitudinal tubercle rows (DTR) were counted from across the dorsum of the trunk". The pictus holotype description reads "the large tubercle-like scales are fairly arranged in 26 longitudinal rows at mid-body, each large scale is enveloped in a rosette of 10-12 small scales". CONFIRMED — but this is E. pictus. 2. Mirza 2024, Taprobanica 13(1):9-15 (opened: journal PDF, local copy ...\scratchpad\mirza2024.txt / madarensis.pdf). Same DTR Methods sentence verbatim. "These tubercles are nearly equidistant from each other and cover the dorsum of the animal"; "the large scales are arranged in 18 longitudinal rows at midbody". CONFIRMED — but the paper's whole purpose is to REMOVE this Aravalli population from E. macularius and name it E. madarensis. Calling it "a macularius-complex population" conceals that the author is describing a different species; its comparison section explicitly contrasts it with E. macularius. 3. Russell, Lai, Powell & Higham 2014, J. Morphol. 275:961-979 (opened: local PDF text ...\scratchpad\russell2014.txt). Genuinely E. macularius, SEM of trunk skin. For the body it says tubercles "juxtapose neighboring scales and are usually isolated from other tubercles by intervening scales" — no row structure, in any direction. Row/column language appears only for the tail: tubercles "spaced dorsoventrally in columns, at relatively regular intervals" and "arranged in longitudinal rows along the length of the tail" (Fig. 4). So the claim reports Russell accurately, but this is an argument from silence and cannot show that rows exist-but-loosely.

RELATED-SPECIES TRANSFER (the core defect) Every published longitudinal-row count I could open is for a congener, never for E. macularius: E. hardwickii 24 rows and E. pictus 23-26 (Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022); E. satpuraensis "~20 rows" (Mirza, Sanap, Raju, Gawai & Ghadekar 2014, Phyllomedusa 13(2):75-90, opened, ...\scratchpad\satpura.txt); E. madarensis 18 (Mirza 2024). These are congeners in the same genus but different species, and the transfer is especially unsafe here because row-describability tracks exactly the character that separates them: Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 diagnose hardwickii + pictus as having flat tubercle-like scales with "interspaces much less than the size of the scales", versus "interspaces much more than the size of the tubercles in E. angramainyu ..., E. fuscus ..., E. macularius (Blyth), E. satpuraensis ... and E. turcmenicus". Densely packed rosette-set tubercles are countable in rows; the widely spaced macularius condition is what the row-count was not applied to.

NO ROW DESCRIPTION FOR E. MACULARIUS IN ANY SOURCE I OPENED - Boulenger 1885, Cat. Lizards Brit. Mus. I:232 (opened, ...\scratchpad\boulenger1885.txt): macularius diagnosed only by tubercle size/spacing ("the granular interspaces being as wide as the tubercles themselves; these are subconical or slightly keeled"). No rows on the trunk. - Boulenger 1890, Fauna Brit. India p.107-108 (opened, ...\scratchpad\fbi1890.txt): body "covered above with small, irregular, flat scales, intermixed with numerous roundish, subconical tubercles"; rows are mentioned only for the tail ("above with small flat scales and rows of enlarged subconical tubercles"). - Smith 1935, Fauna Brit. India, Reptilia & Amphibia II:126-128 (opened, ...\scratchpad\smith1935.txt): back with "small, irregular, juxtaposed scales intermixed with larger rounded or oval subconical or keeled tubercles"; again rows only on the tail. macularius is separated from hardwickii solely by tubercle-to-interspace ratio and pore count. - Reptile Database compilation of Anderson 1999 / Grismer 1988,1991 diagnoses for E. macularius (opened, ...\scratchpad\rd_macularius.txt): tubercle size and spacing, no row character. - Rawat, Thapa, Bhattarai & Shah 2019, IRCF Reptiles & Amphibians 26(1):58-61 (opened, ...\scratchpad\rawat2019.txt): the one place I found DTR applied to animals identified as E. macularius. Table 1's legend defines "number of rows of granular dorsal tubercles at midbody (DTR)" after Mirza et al. 2014 — and then the table reports no DTR value at all (it jumps from PP to FLL). Weak source (semi-popular journal, photo vouchers), used only as corroboration.

THE SECOND HALF OF THE CLAIM ALSO FAILS "No author describes them as a lattice" is an unverifiable universal negative, and the evidence inside the genus runs the other way: "nearly equidistant from each other and cover the dorsum" (Mirza 2024, madarensis) is a statement of even spacing, and "each large scale is enveloped in a rosette of 10-12 small scales" (Mirza 2022, pictus) — matched by "10-12 smaller scales surround each dorsal tubercle" in an E. angramainyu description (opened, ...\scratchpad\arc_angramainyu.txt) — is a regular repeating unit, i.e. as lattice-like as this literature gets. The absence of the word "lattice" is a fact about vocabulary, not about the skin. The gloss of "fairly arranged" as "approximate, not strict" is also the claimant's, not the author's: Mirza uses the same stock phrase for geckos with genuinely regular rows, e.g. "enlarged, keeled, tubercles, fairly regularly arranged in 15-16 longitudinal rows on dorsum ... individual tubercle row separated from the adjacent by three transverse scale rows" in a Hemidactylus description (opened, ...\scratchpad\arc.txt), explicitly contrasted there with congeners whose tubercles are "irregularly arranged". In his usage "fairly (regularly) arranged" means regular enough to score, not loose.

COULD NOT VERIFY - Any published DTR/longitudinal-row count for E. macularius sensu stricto. Confidence: unverified. - Whether the trunk tubercles of wild-type E. macularius do or do not fall into countable longitudinal series. Unverified in either direction; I found no source that examines it. - Provenance of Russell et al.'s geckos: the Methods give only a University of Calgary animal-care protocol and cite a lab diet study (Lynn et al. 2013); the paper states nothing about wild-caught vs captive-bred origin, locality, morph, or vouchers. So no morph confusion is demonstrable, but the one source that actually looked at macularius trunk skin rests on undocumented laboratory animals. Confidence: unverified. - Anderson 1999 (Lizards of Iran), Khan's Pakistan works, Borner 1976/1981: not opened; not cited above.

Corroboration status: the DTR Methods sentence is doubly corroborated (both Mirza papers, opened). The absence of trunk-row description for E. macularius is corroborated four times (Boulenger 1885, Boulenger 1890, Smith 1935, Russell et al. 2014). The row counts for congeners each rest on a single source per species. - correction: What the opened sources actually support, restricted to E. macularius: the trunk bears small, irregular, juxtaposed scales intermixed with enlarged rounded-to-subconical, smooth or feebly keeled tubercles whose interspaces are as wide as or wider than the tubercles themselves (Boulenger 1885:232; Boulenger 1890:108; Smith 1935:127-128), and under SEM those trunk tubercles "juxtapose neighboring scales and are usually isolated from other tubercles by intervening scales" (Russell et al. 2014:968). None of these authors describes the trunk tubercles as forming rows of any orientation; all row and column language in this literature — Boulenger 1890, Smith 1935 and Russell et al. 2014 alike — is reserved for the tail, where tubercles sit in dorsoventral columns within each caudal whorl "at relatively regular intervals" and in longitudinal rows along the tail's length.

Counting longitudinal tubercle rows (DTR, "counted from across the dorsum of the trunk") is indeed a standard meristic in modern Eublepharis taxonomy (Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022; Mirza 2024), but every published count I could find is for another species: E. hardwickii 24, E. pictus 23-26, E. satpuraensis ~20 (Mirza et al. 2014), E. madarensis 18 (Mirza 2024 — a taxon that paper removes from E. macularius). The only publication I found that defines DTR for animals identified as E. macularius (Rawat et al. 2019, Nepal) leaves the value unscored. Notably, Mirza & Gnaneswar's own diagnosis places E. macularius in the widely-spaced-tubercle group (interspaces much greater than tubercle size), opposite the closely packed, rosette-set tubercles of the species for which row counts are given.

So: whether E. macularius trunk tubercles form countable longitudinal series — loosely or otherwise — is UNVERIFIED. Do not assert rows on the trunk of this species; do not carry the "nearly equidistant" wording over from E. madarensis or "fairly arranged in 26 longitudinal rows" from E. pictus, and drop the unverifiable "no author describes them as a lattice", which in any case sits awkwardly with the even-spacing and rosette wording that does appear for congeners.

On the original tail the arrangement is strictly geometric: tubercles sit in dorsoventral columns, one column per caudal whorl, and those columns line up into longitudinal rows along the tail.

WHAT CHECKS OUT (confidence: verified, single-sourced) The DETAIL's quotations from Russell et al. are verbatim accurate, and the method description is right. Methods: fine entomological pins were inserted transversely through the mid-point of each whorl at the dorsal extremity of the tail, the specimens radiographed on a Kubtec Xpert 80, and intervertebral joints and intravertebral autotomy planes mapped against the marker pins. Results: the original tail bears scales in whorls around its circumference, the breadth of each whorl corresponds to the length of an underlying vertebra, "indicating a 1:1 correspondence of whorls and autotomy planes" (repeated in the abstract). Tubercles are "spaced dorsoventrally in columns, at relatively regular intervals", are "located close to the center of each whorl", and "are arranged in longitudinal rows along the length of the tail". The Fig. 4 caption does state both axes: tubercles "arranged in columns (vertical dotted line) within whorls, and rows (horizontal dashed line) along the tail". So the two-axis geometry itself is real and correctly cited.

WHY THE CLAIM NEVERTHELESS FAILS AS WRITTEN

(a) "Strictly geometric" is the claimant's word, not the source's, and the source says the opposite twice. Russell et al. hedge both axes: "relatively regular intervals" and "close to the center of each whorl". They then describe the scheme actively dissolving. Ventrally, tubercles "diminish in prominence"; as dorsal semi-imbricating scales grade into polyhedral ventral plates "the tubercles also lose their identity along this transitional gradient"; on the body the ventral regions are outright "devoid of tubercles". So a "dorsoventral column" is not a complete ring - it fades out before reaching the venter. Longitudinally, in the posterior fifth of the tail (their segment 5) "distinction between tubercles, imbricating scales and ventral plates is lost". So the arrangement does not hold over the whole original tail. Inspecting Fig. 4 directly confirms this: tubercles are visibly offset from the drawn dotted and dashed guide lines rather than sitting on them.

(b) "One column per caudal whorl" is not stated anywhere in Russell et al. The paper gives no count of columns per whorl, and the Fig. 4 caption's wording is plural-in-plural ("columns ... within whorls"), which is ambiguous. My own reading of Fig. 4 is consistent with one centred column per whorl (inter-tubercle spacing along a row roughly equals the whorl width marked by the "whorl" brace; the dotted line sits mid-whorl between demarcation furrows), but that is my inference from the image, not a documented statement. Confidence on this sub-clause: unverified.

(c) SPECIES CONFUSION in the second citation - this is the substantive error. Mirza (2024) is not a paper about E. macularius. Its title and abstract state that the Rajasthan population is a distinct taxon from E. macularius (following the molecular phylogeny of Agarwal et al. 2022) and assign it the name Eublepharis madarensis (Sharma, 1980). The Description section - the very section containing the tail sentence - opens "Based on the female holotype (SMF 60980) of E. macularius smithi", a Delhi specimen (Börner 1981) that Mirza explicitly synonymises into E. madarensis; the synonymy list runs Cyrtodactylus madarensis Sharma 1980 / Eublepharis macularius smithi Börner 1981 / Eublepharis macularius - Das 1992 / Eublepharis sp. Rajasthan - Agarwal et al. 2022. Mirza's Comparison section then lists characters separating E. madarensis FROM E. macularius (reticulate-then-striped vs. spotted pattern; vertebral stripe present vs. absent; feebly vs. strongly tuberculate lamellae). The tail count is quoted correctly - the original-tail dorsum bears small juxtaposed scales intermixed with large sub-conical tubercles in a whorl of about 9-10 rows on the first segment, reducing on subsequent segments - but it is a datum for E. madarensis, NOT E. macularius. TRANSFER FROM A RELATED SPECIES, STATED EXPLICITLY: E. madarensis is a congener in the same genus Eublepharis, and Mirza calls it "most similar to E. macularius", so it is a close relative - but under his arrangement it is a separate species, and the whole point of the paper is to remove that Rajasthan/Delhi population from E. macularius. Offering it as corroboration for E. macularius inverts the source's conclusion.

(d) TERMINOLOGY MISMATCH that makes the two counts non-comparable even setting species aside. Russell et al.'s "segment" is one-fifth of the tail's length, and they state "Several whorls were present in each segment sampled." Mirza's "caudal segment" is a single whorl-bearing annulus. The "9-10 rows on the first segment" and Russell's "segment 1" are not the same unit.

COULD NOT VERIFY - Wild-type vs. captive-bred morph status of the Russell et al. animals. The paper gives only SVL 89-120 mm, n = 7 original tails plus 2 regenerated, and University of Calgary animal-care protocol BI07R-32. There is no mention of captive, wild, colony, breeder, supplier, strain or colour morph anywhere in the text. So the lineage of the animals that produced this geometry is undocumented; I mark it unverified rather than guess. (No evidence the tubercle geometry is a morph artefact either - I simply cannot check it.) - Whether the column/row geometry has been replicated. I found and opened no second source describing it. Per the "one source is not a citation" rule: this geometry rests on Russell et al. (2014) alone, and Mirza (2024) does not corroborate it - it describes whorl composition in a different species, not alignment of columns across successive whorls. - correction: Accurate restatement: On the original tail of Eublepharis macularius, Russell et al. (2014) found scales arranged in whorls around the circumference, with marker-pin radiography showing each whorl's breadth matching one underlying vertebra, i.e. a 1:1 correspondence of whorls with autotomy planes. Within that framework, tubercles are spaced dorsoventrally in columns at RELATIVELY REGULAR (not strict) intervals, sit close to the centre of each whorl, and align into longitudinal rows along the tail. The regularity is approximate and regionally limited: tubercles are prominent dorsally, diminish in prominence ventrally and lose their identity where dorsal imbricating scales grade into ventral plates, so the columns are not complete dorsoventral rings; and over the posterior fifth of the tail the distinction between tubercles, imbricating scales and ventral plates disappears altogether, so the scheme does not apply there. The regenerated tail lacks tubercles entirely.

Drop "strictly geometric" - it is the claimant's word and contradicts the source's own hedges. Drop or downgrade "one column per caudal whorl": Russell et al. never state a count of columns per whorl; the figure is consistent with one centred column per whorl but that is an inference from Fig. 4, not a documented statement.

Drop the Mirza (2024) leg entirely, or relabel it. Mirza ZA (2024) Taprobanica 13(1):9-15 redescribes Eublepharis madarensis (Sharma, 1980) and explicitly removes the Rajasthan/Delhi population from E. macularius; its Description is based on the Delhi holotype of E. macularius smithi Börner, 1981, reassigned to E. madarensis. Its "about 9-10 tubercle rows in a whorl on the first caudal segment, reducing on subsequent segments" is a character of E. madarensis - a congener in the same genus that Mirza calls most similar to E. macularius, but a distinct species under his arrangement. If cited at all it must be labelled as a related-species datum, and note that Mirza's "caudal segment" (one annulus) is not Russell's "segment" (one-fifth of tail length, containing several whorls).

Remaining gaps to declare rather than fill: the column/row geometry is single-sourced (Russell et al. 2014 only), and that paper does not state whether its geckos were wild-type or captive-bred morphs.

Tubercles are largest on the hindlimb, mid-sized on the trunk and tail base, and smallest on the head.

-- SOURCE OPENED = TRUE. I opened the publisher-typeset PDF of Russell AP, Lai EK, Powell GL, Higham TE (2014) "Density and Distribution of Cutaneous Sensilla on Tails of Leopard Geckos (Eublepharis macularius) in Relation to Caudal Autotomy", J. Morphol. 275:961-979, hosted on coauthor Higham's lab site (https://biomechanics.ucr.edu/Russell_etal_2014.pdf). I did NOT rely on the text-flow extraction, which scrambles the table: I reconstructed Table 2 (printed p. 968) from PDF word x/y coordinates with PyMuPDF, so every row/value pairing below is read off the printed page, not inferred.

NO SPECIES CONFUSION AND NO MORPH SUBSTITUTION FOUND. The paper is explicitly on E. macularius (Blyth) 1854, and its caudal whorl/tubercle description is consistent with that species. That is not where the claim fails.

WHAT THE TABLE ACTUALLY SAYS (tubercle mean area, mm2 +/- sd, area = longest dimension x perpendicular dimension, 10 scales per focal area, ImageJ, from SEM images): dorsum thigh 3.092 +/- 1.72; dorsum crus 2.473 +/- 1.72; dorsum pes 1.534 +/- 0.36; between hips 1.434 +/- 0.23; original tail segment 1 0.914 +/- 0.08, segment 2 0.823 +/- 0.07, segment 4 0.716 +/- 0.46, segment 3 0.551 +/- 0.12; between eyes 0.644 +/- 0.06; between shoulders 0.141 +/- 0.15; upper labials = no tubercle entry. So the six numbers in the DETAIL and their row assignments are correct - I confirm them independently. The claim still fails.

CLAUSE 1 ("largest on the hindlimb") - weakly supported at best. The three hindlimb point estimates are the three largest values, so the direction is right. But the paper runs no statistical comparison of scale areas among regions; n = 10 scales per focal area; and the sds are enormous and overlapping (thigh 3.092 +/- 1.72 vs crus 2.473 +/- 1.72 are indistinguishable; pes 1.534 +/- 0.36 overlaps between-hips 1.434 +/- 0.23). Any ordering within the hindlimb, and hindlimb-pes vs trunk-hips, is unresolvable from this table. Confidence: unverified as a ranking.

CLAUSE 2 ("mid-sized on the trunk") - false as printed. The trunk was sampled twice and spans the whole range, not the middle: between hips 1.434 (effectively tied with the pes for second-largest) and between shoulders 0.141 (the smallest tubercle value in the table). Neither trunk sample is mid-sized.

CLAUSE 3 ("smallest on the head") - false as printed, and it fails even after the DETAIL's own repair. Between the eyes is 0.644. That is larger than between shoulders (0.141) AND larger than original-tail tubercles in segment 3 (0.551). So discarding the suspect between-shoulders cell does not rescue the clause: mid-tail tubercles are still smaller than head tubercles. The paper's prose does assert the smallest occur on the dorsum of the head between the eyes (p. 967-968), but that sentence contradicts its own Table 2 in two places, not one.

ON THE DETAIL'S CAVEAT - one factual correction and one unverified inference. (a) The between-shoulders tubercle value 0.141 +/- 0.15 is NOT identical to the adjacent granular scale value; the dorsal-scale cell on that same row reads 0.142 +/- 0.04. Near-identical, different sd. (b) "Probably 1.41" is a reconstruction, not a documented correction: I searched for an erratum/correction to 10.1002/jmor.20269 and found none indexed, so the 0.141 stands uncorrected in the literature and cannot be silently replaced. The block does contain at least one further evident typo (the dorsum-thigh dorsal-scale sd is printed as "218"), which shows the table was poorly proofed but does not license substituting a guessed value.

PROVENANCE, NOT DOCUMENTED (could_not_verify). Methods state seven original and two regenerated tails were taken from specimens of SVL 89-120 mm, and that body skin was excised from five of those same specimens, cross-referenced to Lynn et al. 2013 (a juvenile diet-ration study). The text I read never states whether the animals were captive-bred, commercially sourced, or wild-caught, nor sex, nor morph. I could not open Lynn et al. 2013 (journals.uchicago.edu returned HTTP 403). So: absolute mm2 values come from sub-adult/juvenile animals of unstated origin and cannot be transferred to adult wild-type animals. Confidence: unverified.

CORROBORATION - none found; this is a one-source claim. I opened two independent descriptive sources: Boulenger 1885 (Cat. Lizards Brit. Mus. vol. 1, E. macularius account, p. 232) and Smith 1935 (Fauna of British India, Reptilia and Amphibia II, E. macularius account, p. 127). Both treat the enlarged tubercles as a feature of the BACK, and both make the diagnostic comparison tubercle size vs granular interspace; neither mentions limb tubercles at all, and neither ranks head tubercles as smallest. RELATED-SPECIES NOTE: Mirza and Gnaneswar 2022 (Evol. Syst. 6:77-88) and Mirza 2024 describe limb and trunk scalation in CONGENERS (E. hardwickii, E. pictus, and a newly described Eublepharis - same genus, different species, so distance is congeneric, not conspecific); their limb descriptions mention lamellae but no enlarged limb tubercles. I cite that only as absence of corroboration, not as evidence about E. macularius.

METHOD CAVEAT: these "areas" are bounding-rectangle products (longest dimension x perpendicular dimension) of domed/sub-conical tubercles, i.e. planar footprint approximations that overestimate area and are not comparable to true surface areas from other studies. The paper itself notes tubercles have a small perimeter relative to enclosed area. - correction: Supportable version: In the only measurements I could open (Russell et al. 2014, J. Morphol. 275:961-979, Table 2, printed p. 968; captive lab specimens of SVL 89-120 mm, origin not stated), the largest tubercles measured are on the dorsum of the hindlimb - thigh 3.092 +/- 1.72 mm2 and crus 2.473 +/- 1.72 - with dorsum pes 1.534 +/- 0.36 and dorsum between the hips 1.434 +/- 0.23 next. Beyond that, no clean head-to-tail size gradient exists in the data: original-tail tubercles run 0.914 (segment 1) down to 0.551 (segment 3), the dorsum of the head between the eyes is 0.644 +/- 0.06, and the dorsum between the shoulders is printed as 0.141 +/- 0.15, the smallest value in the table. So "mid-sized on the trunk" is wrong (the trunk supplies both the second-largest and the smallest values) and "smallest on the head" is wrong (mid-tail tubercles, 0.551, are smaller than the between-eyes value, and the printed between-shoulders value is smaller still). The paper's prose claims the smallest are between the eyes, but that sentence contradicts its own table in two places and no erratum exists; flag the conflict rather than resolving it. Treat all of this as point estimates only - 10 scales per region, no statistical comparison among regions, sds that overlap almost completely, a bounding-rectangle area approximation, and juvenile/sub-adult animals of undocumented (possibly captive-bred) origin. Single source, uncorroborated: Boulenger 1885 and Smith 1935 describe E. macularius tubercles only as a dorsal-trunk feature and say nothing supporting a hindlimb-largest, head-smallest ordering. Confidence: unverified.

What I actually opened (full texts downloaded and read myself): 1.
