Smith does state that in all reptiles the lower lid is the movable one, that closure is by upward movement of the lower lid, and that the upper lid is immovable or very restricted. The user's characterisation of this passage is accurate. NOTE the context: this sentence sits inside a discussion of how skinks/lacertids (Leiolopisma, Mabuya, Ablepharus, Cabrita, Ophisops) build a transparent window in the lower lid. It is a generalisation drawn from those groups. - p.23-24 (Gekkonidae family account) — a page the claimant did NOT consult, and it is decisive: Smith writes that in Eublepharis both lids are well developed and movable, and that the eyeball has lost the fixed membranous covering. So Smith himself exempts Eublepharis from his own p.10 generalisation, in the same volume. - pp.125-126 (genus diagnosis): both eyelids well developed, movable; and eublepharids are distinguished from typical gekkonids by opisthocoelous vertebrae, united parietals, and "connivent eyelids" (i.e. lids that converge to meet — that gloss of the term is my reading, not something I verified in a dictionary). 2. Boulenger 1885, Catalogue of the Lizards in the British Museum, 2nd ed., vol. I, Fam. Eublepharidae (p. ~228) — archive.org catalogueoflizar01brituoft_djvu.txt, saved at ...\scratchpad\boulenger1885.txt. source_opened = true. The family diagnosis says the eyes are protected by thick, movable, connivent lids — plural, with no statement that one lid is the mover. This is a second, older source saying the same thing, though not fully independent of Smith (Smith cites Boulenger). 3. Walls 1942, The Vertebrate Eye and Its Adaptive Radiation — archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.206157, saved at ...\scratchpad\walls1942.txt. source_opened = true. This is the strongest independent corroboration of the GENERAL rule, and it also shows the rule is not absolute: p.419 (Sauropsida) says the lower lid characteristically does the work of closing the eye; p.423 (Lizards) says that in lizards, as a rule, only the lower lid has a tarsal plate and moves — but immediately gives an exception, an anole (Walls's "Anolis alligator") in which the two lids move equally; pp.421-422 make crocodilians an explicit exception, with the upper lid larger and more mobile. Walls's own footnote on eublepharids describes them as having mobile lids (plural) fringed with lash-like scales; he never says which lid does the closing in them. 4. Kosanke/van Doorn-type modern review: "Anatomy, Physiology, and Disorders of the Spectacle, Subspectacular Space, and Its Lacrimal Drainage System in Squamates", Animals (Basel) 2023, PMC10044692 (full text fetched from Europe PMC). source_opened = true. It states that among Gekkota only Eublepharidae has fully moveable eyelids (plural), and — important for the logic — that most Gymnophthalmidae have moveable UPPER eyelids and immobile LOWER eyelids. That is a squamate counterexample to Smith's "in all reptiles" claim, so the premise the claim leans on is demonstrably not universal within lizards. 5. Wyneken 2012, "Reptilian Eyes and Orbital Structures", ARAV 2012 Proceedings, p.75 ff. I read a text extraction of this paper that was already present in this session's shared scratchpad (...\scratchpad\arav2012_43.txt); I could NOT re-download it from ARAV myself (cdn.ymaws.com returned 403), so treat its provenance as partially verified. Its p.76 content does match the claimant's paraphrase: the lower lid of lizards contains a cartilaginous tarsus, and in general the upper lid is mostly smooth muscle and less mobile than the lower lid, which has striated muscle. Crucially this is framed as "in general" for lizards; Eublepharis is never mentioned, and Wyneken's own adjacent example (crocodilians) is one where the lower lid moves up despite lacking cartilage — i.e. the muscle/tarsus argument is a tendency, not a law.

Species/morph-confusion check, as instructed: - No evidence the claim came from a different gecko species or from a captive-bred morph. Morph identity is irrelevant to lid anatomy and nothing in the sources touches it. - There IS a taxonomic-scope problem, in the other direction. The "both lids movable" statements are family/genus-level, not E. macularius-level: Smith's 1935 Eublepharis explicitly subsumes Goniurosaurus, and Boulenger's Eublepharidae contained Psilodactylus (now Holodactylus), Eublepharis and Coleonyx. So those statements cover a broader taxon than E. macularius, though E. macularius sits squarely inside it. - The actual transferred fact in the claimant's reasoning is the cross-taxon one they half-flagged: the "lower lid sweeps upward" mechanism is documented for lizards generally (Walls p.423; Wyneken p.76) and for amphibians/sauropsids at large (Walls p.419), not for Eublepharis.

Could not verify: no source I opened measures or even describes the relative excursion of the upper versus lower lid during a blink in E. macularius, or names which lid is the principal mover in any eublepharid. The one paper that would most likely settle it, Bellairs, A. d'A. 1948, "The eyelids and spectacle in geckos", Proc. Zool. Soc. Lond. 118:420-425, doi 10.1111/j.1096-3642.1948.tb00387.x, is paywalled and I did NOT open it — I only saw it in the 2023 review's reference list. It should be the next thing pulled. Underwood 1970 ("The eye", Biology of the Reptilia vol. 2) is the other unopened candidate. Europe PMC returns no study of eyelid kinematics in any gecko. - correction: Split the claim in two and downgrade both halves.

(a) "Lower lid is the principal mover, sweeping upward" — plausible but UNVERIFIED for E. macularius. Confidence: unverified. It is the documented rule for lizards generally (Walls 1942 p.423; Wyneken 2012 p.76, corroborated twice), and it has a mechanical rationale (tarsal cartilage plus striated muscle in the lower lid). But Walls states it as "as a rule" and records a lizard exception, and no source I opened applies it to Eublepharis. Phrase it as: in lizards generally the lower lid is the larger, tarsus-bearing, more mobile lid and closure is effected mainly by its upward movement; whether this holds for E. macularius is not documented in any source I could open.

(b) "The upper lid moves little" — DROP THIS. It is contradicted by the only taxon-specific statements available, including one on a page of the very source cited. Smith 1935 p.23-24 says that in Eublepharis both lids are well developed and movable; Smith's genus diagnosis (pp.125-126) says both eyelids well developed, movable, and makes "connivent eyelids" a diagnostic character of the family; Boulenger 1885 (Eublepharidae) says thick, movable, connivent lids; Walls 1942 calls eublepharid lids mobile (plural); the 2023 Animals review says Eublepharidae alone among Gekkota has fully moveable eyelids. Confidence: the "both lids movable" statement is documented (three sources, though Smith derives partly from Boulenger); the degree of upper-lid excursion is unverified.

Also remove "almost certainly". The premise it rests on — Smith's blanket "in all reptiles the lower lid is the movable one" — is false as stated: crocodilians have the larger, more mobile upper lid (Walls 1942 pp.421-422), and most gymnophthalmid lizards have a moveable upper lid and an immobile lower lid (Animals 2023 / Guerra-Fuentes et al. 2014). A generalisation with known exceptions inside Squamata cannot license "almost certainly" for a taxon its own author treated as exceptional.

Suggested replacement wording: "Eublepharid geckos, uniquely among Gekkota, retain functional eyelids; both the upper and lower lids are described as well developed and movable, and are 'connivent', i.e. they converge to meet (Boulenger 1885; Smith 1935, pp. 23-24 and 125-126). In lizards generally the lower lid is the larger, carries a cartilaginous tarsus and striated muscle, and does most of the work of closing the eye (Walls 1942, p. 423; Wyneken 2012, p. 76), so the lower lid is likely the main mover in E. macularius as well, but no source examined states this for the species, and the relative contribution of the two lids during a blink is undocumented."

The lids meet and the eye closes completely — the term used in both primary sources is 'connivent'.

-- The bibliographic half of the claim is correct; the inferential half is not, and the "two primary sources" are not two.

VERIFIED (sources actually opened, full scanned text of the originals): 1. Boulenger 1885, Catalogue of the Lizards in the British Museum vol. 1 (Internet Archive copy catalogueoflizar01brituoft, OCR of the original). Running head "EUBLEPHARIDÆ. 229" sits immediately above the family diagnosis, which reads that the eyes are moderately large, with elliptico-vertical pupil, and are protected by thick, movable, connivent lids. So the word is there, at the stated page, at family rank. Correct. 2. Smith 1935, Fauna of British India, Reptilia and Amphibia vol. II (Sauria) (Internet Archive copies in.ernet.dli.2015.207328 and in.ernet.dli.2015.62460). Running page "126" sits immediately above the sentence in the genus Eublepharis account saying that, as shown elsewhere (Smith, 1933), the Eublepharids differ from the typical Geckonids in having opisthocoelous vertebrae, united parietal bones, and connivent eyelids. The 1933 citation is also in the genus synonymy: Smith, Rec. Ind. Mus. xxxv, 1933, p. 16. The same term appears in Smith's family key, couplet "II. Eyelids movable, connivent" leading to Eublepharis. So that is correct too.

WHY IT STILL FAILS:

(a) The "eye closes completely" part is the claimant's gloss, not a statement in either source. Both authors use 'connivent' as a presence/absence diagnostic separating eublepharids from typical geckos with a fused brille and rudimentary lids. Neither says anything about how far the lids travel, whether the aperture is fully occluded, or what the animal does in life. Boulenger demonstrably had separate wording for degree of coverage and did not use 'connivent' for it: in the same volume, in the Geckonidae introduction (pp. 4–5), he writes that in Ptenopus the upper lid is sufficiently developed to cover the eye nearly completely, while in Aelurosaurus (= Aeluroscalabotes, the Malayan cat gecko, a different animal) there are connivent movable lids. Degree of closure gets a measured phrase; 'connivent' does not. Treating 'connivent' as "a statement of full closure, not partial" reads a quantitative finding into a taxonomic adjective.

(b) The two attestations are not independent. Boulenger 1890 (Fauna of British India, Reptilia and Batrachia; Internet Archive copy TheFaunaOfBritishIndiaReptiliaAndBatrachia), family Eublepharidae, p. 107, gives the formula: they differ from the Geckonidae in having the vertebrae opisthocoelous and the parietal bones united, and are distinguished externally from all Indian Gekkonidae by the presence of connivent eyelids, a character in which they agree with the normal Lacertilia. Smith 1935 p. 126 reproduces that same three-character formula in the same order (opisthocoelous vertebrae, united parietals, connivent eyelids). Smith also cites Boulenger 1885 p. 230 and Boulenger 1890 p. 107 directly in his genus synonymy. So Smith is carrying Boulenger's wording forward, not corroborating it from independent observation. Under the project rule about corroborating twice, this is one descriptive tradition, not two sources.

(c) Boulenger 1890 also applies "movable, connivent eyelids" to Agamidae in the same family key, opposite "no movable eyelids" for Geckonidae. That confirms 'connivent' in this literature simply denotes the ordinary lizard lid condition — lids that converge and meet — rather than any observation specific to Eublepharis. It supports "the lids meet"; it does not support "the eye closes completely" as a sourced finding.

(d) Rank problem. Neither statement is about E. macularius. Boulenger's is a family diagnosis covering Coleonyx and Psilodactylus (= Holodactylus, West Africa) as well; Smith's is a genus diagnosis for a genus that at the time still contained lichtenfelderi, now Goniurosaurus. I read both species accounts for macularius (Boulenger 1885 p. 232; Smith 1935 pp. 127–129) and neither mentions the eyelids at all — they are entirely about tubercles, preanal pores, colour pattern, measurements and range.

(e) Lexically, 'connivent' is not unambiguous. Wiktionary (weak, tertiary — used only as a lexical check, opened) gives the biological sense as both "arched inward so that the points meet" and "brought close together or in close contact; converging". The second reading does not entail complete meeting.

NO SPECIES OR MORPH CONFUSION FOUND, and this cuts in the claimant's favour on that axis: the material behind Boulenger 1885 p. 232 is wild-caught British Museum specimens (Kashmir–Murree, Rajanpur Punjab, Hyderabad and Karachi in Sind), which predate captive morphs entirely. The only adjacent-taxon issue is that the same term is applied by Boulenger to Aelurosaurus/Aeluroscalabotes felinus and to Agamidae, which shows the term is generic rather than that macularius was mistaken for something else.

COULD NOT VERIFY: Smith 1933, Rec. Indian Mus. xxxv, p. 16 — I could not locate a scan of Records of the Indian Museum vol. 35, so I have confirmed only that Smith 1935 cites it, not what it says about the lids. Unverified. I also found no measurement of lid excursion, closure speed or blink rate in any source I opened, which matches the claimant's own could_not_verify note. - correction: Sourced version, confidence: the terminology is verified, the interpretation is unverified.

Boulenger 1885 (Cat. Liz. Brit. Mus. 1, p. 229) describes the family Eublepharidae as having thick, movable, connivent lids, and Smith 1935 (Fauna Brit. India, Sauria, p. 126) describes the genus Eublepharis as having connivent eyelids, citing Smith 1933. Both statements are diagnostic characters at family and genus rank, contrasting eublepharids with typical geckos, which have rudimentary lids and a transparent spectacle. Boulenger 1890 (Fauna Brit. India, Reptilia and Batrachia, p. 107) makes the point explicitly: connivent eyelids are the character in which eublepharids agree with the normal Lacertilia — and he applies the same phrase to Agamidae.

What is therefore supportable: E. macularius, as a eublepharid, has two well-developed movable eyelids whose margins converge and meet, unlike typical geckos. What is NOT supportable from these sources: that they state the eye closes completely. Neither author describes degree of closure, lid excursion, occlusion of the aperture, or eye-closing behaviour, and both species accounts for macularius (Boulenger 1885 p. 232; Smith 1935 pp. 127–129) are silent on the eyes. Boulenger used a separate, explicitly quantitative phrase when he meant degree of coverage (Ptenopus, "cover the eye nearly completely", pp. 4–5), and did not use it here.

Also do not present these as two independent sources. Smith 1935 p. 126 reproduces Boulenger 1890 p. 107's three-character formula in the same order and cites Boulenger 1885 and 1890 in the same synonymy. One tradition, one term. Full closure in E. macularius remains unverified and needs a functional-morphology or behavioural source, not a taxonomic key.

In bright light the pupil constricts to a narrow vertical slit roughly 8% of the eye's width and ~80-85% of its height — aspect ratio about 7:1.

-- REFUTED on the claimant's own source, plus no published corroboration for any of the numbers.

1) THE CITED SOURCE CONTRADICTS THE DETAIL. I opened the Commons file page and its raw wikitext (File:EUBLEPHARIS-MACULARIUS Leopard-Gecko Leopardgecko 201705276003.jpg). The file exists, is 8688x5792, CC BY 4.0, Christian von Faber-Castell, 2017-05-27 18:37:14. But the description reads "EUBLEPHARIS MACULARIUS, Juvenile, ca. 6 Month old ... Sex not identified" (German: "Junger, ca. 6 Monate alter Leopardgecko"). The DETAIL says "an adult." It is a ~6-month-old juvenile. Ontogeny is exactly the wrong thing to get wrong here: eye and pupil dimensions scale allometrically with head growth, so a ratio from a juvenile cannot be presented as the adult/species condition.

2) "IN DAYLIGHT" / "IN BRIGHT LIGHT" IS UNDOCUMENTED. The file page records a terrarium animal ("Snatschi") kept by Alexandra von Faber-Castell and Sebastian Pilz in Zurich, photographed at 18:37. Nothing on the page states daylight, illuminance, or any light level. The entire claim is conditioned on "in bright light," and that premise is unverified — terrarium lighting at an unknown intensity, possibly with flash, is not a characterized photopic condition.

3) "CAPTIVE HIGH-YELLOW ANIMAL" IS NOT IN THE SOURCE. The file page says nothing about any colour morph. That attribution was supplied by the claimant, not the source — a filled gap.

4) THE DENOMINATOR IS NOT "THE EYE." The DETAIL measures against the PALPEBRAL APERTURE (445 x 295 px), then the CLAIM reports it as a fraction of "the eye's width" and "its height." Those are different structures. Hellebuyck & Solanes Vilanova 2023 (Animals, PMC10044692, opened, peer-reviewed) states that eublepharids are the only Gekkota with fully movable eyelids and no spectacle, naming E. macularius as the exemplar; the Reptile Database entry (opened) lists 46-57 eyelid fringe scales as a diagnostic character. So in this species the palpebral aperture is a MOVING boundary set by lid position and arousal, not a fixed anatomical reference. Both percentages therefore have an unstable denominator. The 83% height figure is the most fragile: partly closed lids simultaneously crop the dorsal/ventral tips of the pupil (shrinking the numerator) and shrink the aperture (shrinking the denominator), so 0.83 is close to uninterpretable. This normalization would be defensible in a spectacle-bearing gekkonid; in Eublepharis it is not.

5) NO PUBLISHED NUMBER CORROBORATES THE RATIO. Banks, Sprague, Schmoll, Parnell & Love 2015, "Why do animal eyes have pupils of different shapes?" (Sci Adv, PMC4643806, opened) classifies constricted pupils only qualitatively — horizontally elongated / circular / vertically elongated, the latter split into subcircular vs vertical slit — and gives an aspect-ratio example only for domestic cat (12 x 1.5 mm, ~8:1). It publishes no species-level aspect ratios, and I could not confirm E. macularius appears in its Table S1 (the supplementary table did not render). I found no source, in any literature I opened, giving a slit width, aspect ratio, or pupil-to-eye ratio for E. macularius.

6) RELATED-SPECIES TRANSFER HAZARD (flagging explicitly, per standing rules). The often-quoted gecko pupil literature is about OTHER geckos. Roth, Lundstrom, Kelber, Kroger & Unsbo 2009, "The pupils and optical systems of gecko eyes" (J Vis 9(3):27; abstract opened via PubMed 19757966; paywalled, not open access) studied Tarentola chazaliae (helmet gecko) and Phelsuma madagascariensis grandis (day gecko) — both spectacle-bearing, neither a eublepharid. Banks et al.'s "when constricted, it creates three or four vertically aligned pinholes" is written of geckos generically (citing Murphy & Howland) and cannot, on what I opened, be attributed to E. macularius. Eublepharidae is a separate family from Gekkonidae/Phyllodactylidae within Gekkota, differing fundamentally in bearing movable eyelids and lacking a spectacle. Neither the "pinhole" picture nor its absence may be transferred to E. macularius from these animals.

7) SPECIES-ID AND MORPH CHECKS, AS ASKED. The identification is a hobbyist photographer's self-label on Commons, not a curated determination — weak by this project's source standard. The file's own common names, "spotted fat-tailed gecko" / "Pakistanischer Fettschwanzgecko," use "fat-tailed gecko," a name far more strongly associated with Hemitheconyx caudicinctus (African fat-tailed gecko), a different eublepharid genus common in the same pet trade; that is a live confusion risk even though the binomial and the Commons category both say E. macularius. Congeners (E. angramainyu, E. fuscus, E. hardwickii, E. turcmenicus) are similar. And a captive Swiss terrarium animal has no locality data and unknown lineage, so it cannot be tied to wild-type E. macularius regardless of morph.

8) n=1 WITH UNCALIBRATED GEOMETRY. Beyond the single-individual caveat the claimant does make, nothing documents that the eye was orthogonal to the lens axis. Oblique viewing foreshortens width or height differentially, and a 7:1 slit ratio measured off-axis can be substantially wrong in either direction.

WHAT WEAKLY SURVIVES: only the qualitative shape. Animal Diversity Web's E. macularius account (opened) states the species has movable eyelids and a "vertical slit pupil" — but ADW's cited references for that account are husbandry/pet-trade books (Henkel & Schmidt 1995; Hunziker 1994, TFH; de Vosjoli 1990, Advanced Vivarium Systems), i.e. weak sources, and it is a single source, not corroborated twice. So even "vertical slit pupil" should be carried as single-source/weak, and the quantitative claim is unsupported outright.

COULD NOT VERIFY: (a) any of the pixel figures — 445, 295, 30-38, 245 — are the claimant's alone; I did not re-measure, because re-measuring requires downloading the 8688x5792 original and downloading a file needs the user's explicit permission, which I cannot obtain as a subagent; (b) whether the image genuinely shows maximal photopic constriction; (c) whether E. macularius appears in Banks et al. Table S1; (d) the Roth et al. 2009 full text (paywalled — abstract only); (e) whether the constricted E. macularius pupil margin is smooth/tapering as described or crenellated, which no source I opened addresses for this species. - correction: Restated to what the evidence actually supports: "Eublepharis macularius has a vertical pupil that narrows to a slit under bright illumination [single, weak source: Animal Diversity Web, whose account rests on husbandry books; not corroborated in peer-reviewed literature I could open]. No published quantitative values for the constricted slit's width, its aspect ratio, or its size relative to the eye exist in any source I opened, so the figures '~8% of eye width', '~80-85% of eye height' and '~7:1' are unverified [confidence: unverified]."

On the specific measurement offered: it should be reported as, at most, "in one Wikimedia Commons photograph of a CAPTIVE JUVENILE (~6 months old) of unknown provenance, photographed in a terrarium under unrecorded lighting, the dark pupillary slit measured ~30-38 px wide by ~245 px tall within a palpebral aperture of ~445 x 295 px (slit aspect ~7:1)" — with these caveats attached and not dropped: (i) the subject is a juvenile, not an adult, per the file's own description; (ii) illumination is undocumented, so 'in bright light' is an assumption; (iii) the normalizing denominator is the PALPEBRAL APERTURE, not the eye — and because eublepharids uniquely among Gekkota have fully movable eyelids (Hellebuyck & Solanes Vilanova 2023), that denominator varies with lid position, so the 8% and 83% figures should be dropped entirely rather than restated against 'the eye'; (iv) only the slit's own ~7:1 aspect ratio is normalization-independent, and it remains n=1, uncalibrated for viewing angle, and unverified by me; (v) 'high-yellow' should be struck as unsourced; (vi) the identification is a photographer's self-label on Commons, not a curated determination.

To actually establish this ratio, the right evidence would be direct measurement of multiple wild-type or locality-known adult E. macularius under recorded illuminance, with the eye orthogonal to the lens and pupil dimensions normalized to corneal diameter or lens diameter rather than the palpebral aperture — note Yamashita & Tsuihiji 2022 (J Morphol, PMC9545706, opened) gives a usable hard scale for one museum E. macularius (FMNH 176870): lens diameter 3.37 mm, internal scleral ossicle ring diameter 4.39 mm.

Taxonomic keys for E. macularius use the external ear as a measurable structure, giving a species-specific scale anchor: the height of the auditory meatus is about 1.5 times the internostril distance.

-- SOURCE OPENED: yes — the live Reptile Database account for Eublepharis macularius (https://reptile-database.reptarium.cz/species?genus=Eublepharis&species=macularius), fetched and parsed to text on 2026-09-12. The Diagnosis block is NOT stripped on the live page; it is still there in full, so I did not need the archived snapshot and the user's premise that the live page strips it is wrong. The string is real and verbatim: "height of auditory meatus 1.5 times internostril distance", inside "Additional diagnostic characters (Grismer, 1988:442-450; 1991: 251-252)". So the QUOTE checks out. Everything the claim builds on top of the quote does not.

WHAT REFUTES IT:

(1) It is not a key character. The Diagnosis paragraph has two halves. The key half — the part tied to an actual identification key — is "Subdigital lamellae each with several distinct small tubercles (Fig. E in key, Anderson 1999: 117); mid-dorsal tubercles generally larger than intertubercular spaces; chin shields usually in contact with first lower labials (Fig. C in key, page 117); elements of dorsal color pattern not linearly arranged." The ear ratio sits in the SECOND half, explicitly flagged as "Additional diagnostic characters" — a supplementary descriptive list, not a key couplet. The claim's headline ("taxonomic keys ... use the external ear as a measurable structure") is contradicted by the same paragraph it cites: the key couplets referenced use lamellae, tubercles, chin shields and colour pattern, and no ear character at all.

(2) The citation chain is longer and different from what the user states. The user says "one remove from the primary". It is two. The whole Diagnosis block, additional characters included, closes with "(Anderson 1999: 120)" and its figure references are to Anderson ("Fig. 56 in Anderson 1999: 120", "Fig. E in key, Anderson 1999: 117"). So the chain is Reptile Database <- Anderson 1999 (The Lizards of Iran, SSAR Contributions to Herpetology 15) <- Grismer. The user is reading a compilation of a compilation, and I did not open Anderson 1999 or Grismer either.

(3) The source work treats the animal as only tentatively E. macularius. The same Reptile Database page's synonymy list contains the line "Eublepharis cf. macularius — ANDERSON 1999". "cf." means Anderson was not confident the Iranian material he described was true E. macularius. The ear ratio therefore traces back, via Anderson, to a population the describing author himself flagged as uncertainly assigned. That is the species-confusion problem the task asked me to look for, and it is present in the source's own metadata.

(4) It is a regional diagnosis, not a species-wide one. Anderson 1999 covers Iran, where only two Eublepharis occur. I also opened the Reptile Database account for the other one, E. angramainyu (https://reptile-database.reptarium.cz/species?genus=Eublepharis&species=angramainyu): its Diagnosis reads "Mid-dorsal tubercles not as large as intertubercular spaces; subdigital lamellae smooth, without tubercles; some elements of dark color pattern of head and body linearly arranged; females with discernable preanal pores." No ear character, no competing ratio. So nothing in either account shows the 1.5 value discriminating E. macularius from anything. Calling it "species-specific" is unsupported by the cited text.

(5) The taxon concept behind Grismer 1988 is broader than today's E. macularius. The same page's Comment states that Grismer (in Estes & Pregill 1988) synonymised E. gracilis and E. afghanicus into E. macularius, that E. m. fuscus was later raised to species rank by Das 1997, and that Mirza 2024 proposed revalidating E. madarensis. A 1988 character therefore describes a composite that has since been split, so it cannot be assumed to characterise E. macularius as currently circumscribed.

(6) "Scale anchor" is a category error. A ratio of two head dimensions is dimensionless: it fixes no absolute size and cannot anchor scale. It is also a single point value with no range, no sample size, no specimen list and no age class stated, and head proportions in lizards are allometric, so a single ratio is not usable as a measurement reference even in principle.

(7) The long-axis inference is invented. "Height of auditory meatus 1.5 times internostril distance" reports one dimension of the ear opening against an unrelated dimension of the snout. It says nothing whatever about the meatus's width, so it cannot imply that the vertical axis is the long one. That inference is the user's, not the source's.

COULD NOT VERIFY: I did not open Grismer 1988 (Estes & Pregill eds., Stanford University Press) or Grismer 1991, so I cannot confirm the 1.5 figure against the primary text, confirm the page ranges, or confirm what Grismer intended the character to distinguish. I specifically could not resolve "Grismer 1991": the Reptile Database bibliography on this species page lists Estes & Pregill 1988 and Anderson 1999 but contains no Grismer 1991 entry at all, so that citation is unresolvable from the source the user actually opened. I also could not verify the actual shape or orientation of the ear opening in E. macularius from any source — treat that as unverified.

WEAK-SOURCE NOTE: none used. No pet-care or breeder material was consulted.

MORPH CAVEAT: this particular claim is not a morph artefact — it derives from museum-based descriptive work on wild material. But the reverse caution applies: selectively bred captive leopard geckos (giant lines especially) have head proportions that need not match wild-caught stock, so this ratio should not be used to validate a pet animal.

CONFIDENCE: the quote's existence and its context are verified directly from an opened page. The inferences the claim draws from it are refuted on the text of that same page. The underlying morphological fact remains unverified. - correction: The quoted string is genuine but the claim misdescribes it on four counts. Accurate version: the Reptile Database account for Eublepharis macularius carries the sentence "height of auditory meatus 1.5 times internostril distance", but it appears under "Additional diagnostic characters", not in a key — the key characters the same paragraph cites (Anderson 1999: 117) are subdigital lamellae tuberculation, relative mid-dorsal tubercle size, chin-shield contact with the first lower labials, and non-linear dorsal colour pattern, none of which involve the ear. The text is quoted by Reptile Database from Anderson 1999 (The Lizards of Iran), who in turn cites Grismer 1988/1991, so it is two removes from the primary, not one; Grismer 1991 cannot even be resolved from that page's bibliography. Anderson's Iranian material is listed in the same page's synonymy as "Eublepharis cf. macularius", i.e. only tentatively assigned to the species, and Grismer's 1988 concept of macularius subsumed E. gracilis and E. afghanicus, part of which has since been split off again (E. fuscus, Das 1997). The value is a single unranged dimensionless ratio, so it anchors no absolute scale and demonstrates no species-specificity — the congener in the same regional work, E. angramainyu, is diagnosed without any ear character. Nothing in the sentence licenses the further inference that the meatus's long axis is vertical: only its height is reported, never its width.

The gap between eye and ear opening in Eublepharis is approximately equal to the snout length.

-- I opened all three historical works in full OCR plus two primary descriptions and two modern papers. The submitter's transcription of the hardwickii passages is accurate, but the claim fails on three independent grounds.

(1) NOT STATED FOR E. MACULARIUS ANYWHERE. Boulenger 1885 p.232, Boulenger 1890 p.108 and Smith 1935 p.127 give macularius only a differential account. Boulenger's macularius text opens "Differs from the preceding by..." and lists tubercle size, granular interspaces, more elongate body and digits, 9-14 preanal pores, and colour - no head, snout or ear character. Smith's macularius account is even thinner than the submitter says: it differs "in the following particulars: - Enlarged dorsal tubercles smaller, as broad as or smaller than their interspaces; male with from 9 to 14 preanal pores." Smith does NOT carry over the "more elongate body/digits" point, so the submitter's description of Smith's framing is wrong on that detail. I also opened the two primary descriptions of the taxon: Blyth 1854 (JASB 23: 738, the original description of Cyrtodactylus macularius, a footnote) is pure colour pattern with no head proportions, and Gunther 1864 (Ann. Mag. Nat. Hist. (3) 14: 429, the original description of the synonym E. fasciolatus from Sind) mentions only tubercles, a wide ear opening, labials, chin shields, ventral series and pores. No author has ever stated the character for macularius. It is an inference from differential-diagnosis convention, not a documented fact.

(2) THE CHARACTER IS SPECIES-DIAGNOSTIC WITHIN THE GENUS, BY BOULENGER'S OWN KEY - so it cannot be assumed constant. In the same Catalogue key (p.231, section II) Boulenger separates two species precisely on this character: variegatus has the snout as long as the orbit-to-ear distance, while fasciatus (p.234) differs "in the larger and more elongate head, the length of the snout exceeding the distance between the orbit and the ear-opening." The submitter cites the character as a fixed genus attribute from the very page where its author uses it as a variable one.

(3) SCOPE ERROR - "Eublepharis" in these sources is not the modern genus. Boulenger 1885 places five species in Eublepharis, three of them American; his own synonymy for E. variegatus reads "Coleonyx variegatus, Cope," and dovii and fasciatus are Central/North American. Boulenger 1890 repeats that three of the five are American. Smith 1935 explicitly sinks Goniurosaurus Barbour into Eublepharis and treats E. lichtenfelderi (now Goniurosaurus lichtenfelderi) as the third species. So a genus-level generalisation drawn from these works covers Eublepharis + Coleonyx + Goniurosaurus, not modern Eublepharis - and the one American species measured in that comparison contradicts it.

FURTHER: Smith's wording is a range, not an equality - "as long as or shorter than the distance between the eye and the ear-opening" - which explicitly permits the snout to be the shorter of the two. "Approximately equal" flattens that.

ON THE NUMERIC CORROBORATION. I opened Mirza 2024 (Taprobanica 13(1): 9-15, DOI 10.47605/tapro.v13i1.318). The values are real: Table 1, SE 8.1 / EE 7.6 mm. But the specimen is SMF 60980, the female holotype of Eublepharis macularius smithi Borner 1981, and the entire point of that paper is that this animal is NOT E. macularius - it is reassigned to E. madarensis (Sharma, 1980), distinguished from macularius on reticulate versus spotted pattern, a vertebral stripe, and feebly versus strongly tuberculate lamellae. So the corroboration is from a species deliberately separated from the claim's target. Two further cautions: the second column of that same table (SMF 60979) is internally implausible (orbital diameter 10.3 mm against head length 15.4 mm; internarial 8.5 mm at SVL 95 mm), so the table is not a firm anchor; and the Reptile Database entry for E. macularius carries a published reservation that Mirza 2024 provides neither type information nor proper specimen sources for his sequences, leaving reproducibility unclear. I am reporting that reservation as I read it, not endorsing it.

WHAT DOES CHECK OUT. Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 (Evolutionary Systematics 6: 77-88, DOI 10.3897/evolsyst.6.83290), Table 2, with SE defined as snout tip to anterior eye and EE as posterior eye margin to anterior ear edge - exactly the historical character - gives E. hardwickii holotype NHMUK 1946.8.26.6: SE 9.4, EE 9.6 mm, ratio 0.98. That is genuine numerical confirmation of Boulenger and Smith, for E. hardwickii. The same table gives E. pictus 10.3/9.3 (1.11) and 11.2/11.6 (0.97). No table in any source I opened contains SE or EE for E. macularius. Total sample supporting the proportion: one hardwickii, two pictus, two madarensis - and zero macularius.

CONFUSION CHECK REQUESTED BY THE TASK. Species confusion: yes, this is the central defect - the statement belongs to E. hardwickii, a different species that Smith 1935 restricts to Chota Nagpur, Orissa, adjacent Bengal, Madras, and the Central and United Provinces, doubting records outside that area, whereas macularius is a north-western desert species. Boulenger 1890 and Smith both note that Murray 1884 misidentified macularius as hardwickii, so the two have a documented history of conflation. Genus confusion: also yes, as in point 3. Captive-morph confusion: I found no evidence the claim derives from a pet-trade morph; it traces cleanly to the historical hardwickii literature. Worth noting only in passing that Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 Table 1 does use pet-trade captives ("German line", "Germany bloodline") as genetic vouchers for Eublepharis sp. Himalaya, so provenance caution is warranted in this literature generally, but it is not the source of this particular claim.

COULD NOT VERIFY: Mirza et al. 2014 (Phyllomedusa 13(2): 75-90), which may contain E. macularius morphometrics, is unreachable - revistas.usp.br refused connection and then timed out. Whether SE is approximately equal to EE in actual E. macularius therefore remains unverified in either direction; I am not asserting it is false for macularius, only that it is undocumented. Confidence: unverified for E. macularius; well supported for E. hardwickii.

(1) NOT DOCUMENTED FOR E. MACULARIUS. Every ear-opening statement I found is for a different species. Sources opened and grepped in full text: - Boulenger 1885, Cat. Liz. Brit. Mus. vol. 1, p. 231 (archive.org id catalogueoflizar01brituoft, OCR full text): the phrase "latter large, suboval, vertical" sits inside the account of E. hardwickii. The E. macularius account on p. 232 opens "Differs from the preceding by..." and names only tubercle size/spacing, body and digit proportions, 9-14 preanal pores and colouration. No ear character. - Boulenger 1890, Fauna Brit. India Rept. & Batr., p. 107-108 (archive.org id TheFaunaOfBritishIndiaReptiliaAndBatrachia): same wording, same placement — ear character under E. hardwickii (sp. 112), nothing on the ear under E. macularius (sp. 113). - Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022, Evol. Syst. 6: 77-88 (JATS XML downloaded): exactly two ear-opening descriptions, both "large, sub-oval, obliquely oriented" — one in the description of the E. hardwickii specimen NHMUK 1946.8.26.6 (EL/OD 0.77), one in the E. pictus holotype description NCBS NRC-AA-0015 (EL/OD 0.51). E. macularius is named in the paper but never gets an ear character. - Mirza 2024, Taprobanica 13: 9-15 (publisher PDF): E. madarensis redescription — "ear opening large, suboval, obliquely oriented, smaller than orbital diameter (EL/OD ratio 0.43)", plus three large conical tubercles on the anterior wall of the ear. Only two mentions of "ear opening" in the whole paper (this and the EE measurement definition); none for E. macularius. - Mohapatra et al. 2026, Herpetozoa 39: e183441 (JATS XML downloaded): "Ear-opening large (EL/OD ratio 0.87), sub-oval, vertically oriented, lobules absent" — in the E. jhuma holotype description. The Comparison section contrasts E. jhuma with E. macularius on SVL, regenerated-tail scale shape and postcloacal spurs, not on the ear. So the cited wording is accurate but it is a transfer from congeners. E. hardwickii is the most distant relevant one: per the phylogeny summarised in Mirza 2024 (from Agarwal et al. 2022), the E. hardwickii group is sister to the whole E. macularius clade, so Boulenger's character is being carried across the deepest split in the genus apart from E. angramainyu.

(2) "LARGE" IS POSITIVELY CONTRADICTED WITHIN THE GENUS. I opened Mirza et al. 2014, Phyllomedusa 13: 75-90 (revistas.usp.br PDF, extracted text) — the E. satpuraensis holotype is "Ear opening deep, oval in shape, small (EL/HL = 0.15)". The submitted detail quotes this as "simply 'oval in shape'" and drops both "deep" and "small". That matters: E. satpuraensis sits inside the E. macularius clade (closer to macularius than E. hardwickii is), and it is the one congener described as having a small ear. A genus-wide "large" therefore does not hold.

Two further problems with the framing. Boulenger's 1885 genus Eublepharis is not the modern genus — his synopsis on p. 231 runs hardwickii, macularius, dovii, variegatus, fasciatus, i.e. it contains taxa now in Coleonyx and Hemitheconyx — so his text cannot support a statement about modern Eublepharis as a whole. And E. madarensis, one of the sources of the "obliquely oriented" wording, was until recently treated as E. macularius smithi Börner 1981 or as a synonym of E. macularius (Das 1992) and was only separated by Mirza 2024; quoting its ear character as if it were macularius is exactly the confusion to guard against.

No captive-morph contamination found — every statement above comes from a holotype, lectotype-era museum specimen or catalogued specimen. I did not open Agarwal et al. 2022 (Mol. Phylogenet. Evol. 168: 107414), Anderson & Leviton 1966, Börner 1974/1981, Smith 1935 or Khan's Pakistan works, any of which could in principle carry a macularius ear description; treat "no source anywhere describes it" as unverified rather than established. - correction: For wild-type Eublepharis macularius specifically, the shape and orientation of the ear opening are undocumented in every source I opened, including both Boulenger accounts that the submission leans on — mark it unverified.

What the opened sources do support, at genus level and with the species named: - Sub-oval outline is corroborated four times, in four congeners: E. hardwickii and E. pictus (Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022), E. madarensis (Mirza 2024), E. jhuma (Mohapatra et al. 2026). Boulenger 1885/1890 gives "suboval" a fifth time, again for E. hardwickii. - Orientation is genuinely split: obliquely tilted in E. hardwickii, E. pictus and E. madarensis; vertical in E. jhuma and in Boulenger's E. hardwickii. Boulenger and Mirza & Gnaneswar disagree about the same species, E. hardwickii, which suggests the character is at least partly observer-dependent. - Size is not "large" across the genus. Where measured it is always smaller than the orbit (EL/OD 0.43 in E. madarensis, 0.51 in E. pictus, 0.77 in E. hardwickii, 0.87 in E. jhuma), and E. satpuraensis is explicitly described as deep, oval and small (EL/HL = 0.15). Note the denominators differ between papers (EL/OD vs EL/HL), so these are not directly comparable.

Suggested rewording: "In described congeners of Eublepharis the ear opening is sub-oval and smaller than the orbit, with the long axis reported as vertical in some species and obliquely tilted in others; relative size varies and at least one species (E. satpuraensis) is described as having a small ear. No source I opened states the ear-opening shape or orientation for E. macularius itself." Anything more specific about E. macularius would need a source that actually describes its type or catalogued wild specimens.

(1) THE SMITH QUOTE IS ACCURATE BUT IS NOT ABOUT MACULARIUS. I opened Smith 1935 (archive.org OCR of the DLI scan, item in.ernet.dli.2015.207328). The sentence on p. 126 is verbatim in the E. hardwickii account: snout "as long as or shorter than the distance between the eye and the ear-opening, the diameter of which is more than half that of the orbit." Smith's own E. macularius account (pp. 127–128) is purely differential — "Closely allied to E. hardwickii, differing in the following particulars: — Enlarged dorsal tubercles smaller... male with from 9 to 14 preanal pores" — and never mentions the ear. So the transfer is inheritance-by-silence, not a statement about macularius. The same is true of every work in that lineage I opened: Boulenger 1885 (Cat. Liz. BM I: 231–232) describes the hardwickii ear only as "large, suboval, vertical" and gives macularius no ear character at all; Boulenger 1890 (Fauna Brit. India: 107–108) repeats this; Sharma 2002 (Fauna of India, Sauria, account 89) again says macularius is "like that of E. hardwickii except" tubercles and pores.

(2) THE SOURCE PAGE IS A TWO-SPECIES COMPOSITE, AND THE DONOR SPECIES IS A DISTANT RELATIVE. Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 (Evol. Syst. 6: 77–88, Pensoft XML) list "Smith 1935: 126 (in part)" in the synonymy of BOTH E. hardwickii AND their new E. pictus. So the very page quoted covers two species that differ on this character (holotype EL/OD 0.77 vs 0.51 — both verbatim in that paper). And Mohapatra et al. 2026 (Herpetozoa 39: 161–176, Table 2) give ND2 p-distance E. hardwickii vs E. macularius 24.6–27.2%, among the largest in the genus. Smith's "closely allied" premise, which is the only thing licensing the transfer, is obsolete.

(3) PUBLISHED EAR-VS-EYE DATA FOR E. MACULARIUS DO EXIST, AND THEY ARE HIGHER THAN THE CLAIM. Minton 1966 (Bull. AMNH 134(2): 72–73, West Pakistan series, 10 adult males + 7 females measured, native range) describes E. macularius: "ear opening crescentic, slightly smaller than eye, margined with tubercles" — i.e. roughly 0.8–0.95 of eye, not half. Rawat et al. 2019 (Reptiles & Amphibians 26(1): 58–61, Table 1; PDF fetched from journals.ku.edu), two wild adult males from Banke, Nepal, tabulate tympanum diameter TD = 4, 4 mm against eye diameter ED = 6, 7 mm → 0.67 and 0.57. Two sources, four animals, all at or above "half", one clearly approaching parity.

(4) THE CITED "0.43 IN E. MADARENSIS" IS A MACULARIUS-NAMED SPECIMEN, AND ITS OWN PARATYPE GIVES 0.83. In Mirza 2024 (Taprobanica 13(1): 9–15, publisher PDF) the 0.43 is measured on SMF 60980, the female holotype of Eublepharis macularius smithi Börner 1981 (Delhi) — referred to E. macularius by Das 1992 and only moved to E. madarensis in 2024, a move Mohapatra et al. 2026 say "remains unresolved" because the madarensis holotype V/1215 is untraceable. Table 1 of that same paper gives the paratype SMF 60979 EL 8.5 / OD 10.3 = 0.83. One taxon, one type series, one author, one set of calipers: 0.43 and 0.83. That spread is the entire "genus range" the claim builds on, so no single value can carry the precision claimed. (That paratype column also has HL 15.4 < HW 18.3 and IN 8.5 mm, which look internally inconsistent — flagging, not resolving.)

(5) LANDMARK CONFLATION. The claim slides between "eye size" and "orbit diameter" as if identical. OD is defined in all these papers as "greatest diameter of orbit"; Rawat's ED is "greatest eye diameter"; Minton says "eye". For the Nepal pair ED/HL = 0.19–0.21, versus OD/HL 0.20–0.39 in the congener descriptions — not the same landmark, and a ratio taken against the eye is not transferable to the orbit.

WHAT CHECKS OUT. The measurement definition is right: Mirza's papers define EE as "distance from anterior edge of ear opening to posterior margin of eye"; Mohapatra et al. 2026 word it "posterior point of eye". All five numeric values are real and correctly transcribed, each stated verbatim in its source as "EE/OD ratio": 1.37 (E. pictus holotype NCBS NRC-AA-0015), 1.99 (E. hardwickii holotype NHMUK 1946.8.26.6), 1.43 (Mirza 2024), 1.69 (E. satpuraensis holotype), 1.38 (E. jhuma holotype ZSI-R-29431). All four bibliographic citations are correct, including page ranges. The specimens are wild-collected museum types, so this is NOT a captive-morph contamination problem.

WHY IT STILL FAILS. (a) The stated range contradicts its own data. 1.37 and 1.38 are below 1.4. Two of five values fall outside the claimed lower bound. (b) Non-holotype specimens break the upper bound badly. The claim silently uses one holotype per species. The same tables contain other measured specimens. Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 Table 2, E. pictus paratype NHMUK 1962.238: EE 11.6, OD 4.7 = 2.47. Mirza et al. 2014 type series, one paratype: EE 8.7, OD 4.3 = 2.02. Recomputed per-specimen, the published spread is roughly 1.37-2.47, not 1.4-2.0. E. jhuma's three types give 1.38, 1.39, 1.42; E. satpuraensis's five give 1.64, 1.69, 1.69, 1.70, 2.02. (c) The ratio is not a stable character. Within E. pictus, the two type specimens in one table of one paper differ by 80% (1.37 vs 2.47). That paratype column also carries an anomalous head length (HL 24.3 mm at SVL 103.7, HL/SVL 0.23, versus 0.15 in both the pictus holotype and the hardwickii holotype), so either the range is wrong or that source's data are unreliable — neither reading supports the claim. The high values all come from long-preserved NHMUK/SMF material where a sunken or shrunken eye deflates OD. (d) No E. macularius data exist. I checked every measurement table in all four papers: Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 Table 2 (hardwickii + pictus only), Mirza 2024 Table 1 (two SMF specimens only), Mohapatra et al. 2026 Table 4 (three E. jhuma types only), Mirza et al. 2014 (satpuraensis types only). None measured an E. macularius specimen. The user is right that no EE/OD is published for E. macularius — which is precisely why the claim cannot be asserted of it. (e) The E. madarensis proxy is weaker than presented. TRANSFER FROM A RELATED SPECIES: 1.43 is not from E. macularius. Mirza 2024's Description explicitly states it is "Based on the female holotype (SMF 60980) of E. macularius smithi" — a Delhi specimen (EE 7.6, OD 5.3 = 1.43; paratype SMF 60979, EE 14.8, OD 10.3 = 1.44). The nominal holotype of madarensis (Jodhpur V/1215, immature male from Madar, Ajmer) was NOT measured. Mirza notes that SMF 60980 "appears emaciated". The Table 1 paratype column contains implausible figures (ear length 8.5 mm and internarial 8.5 mm at SVL 95 mm, versus 2.3 and 3.1 at SVL 85 mm), so I do not regard that table as clean. The detail's background is otherwise accurate and I confirmed it: madarensis is a resurrection of Cyrtodactylus madarensis Sharma, 1980, synonymised with macularius by Das 1992, and Mirza 2024 does treat Börner's E. m. smithi types as the same species under Priority. But its validity is contested — the Reptile Database still lists 8 Eublepharis species without madarensis and states that Mirza 2024 "neither provides type information nor proper specimen sources for his sequences", while Mohapatra et al. 2026 do accept it. And Mirza's own diagnosis separates madarensis from macularius on several characters, so its ratio is a related-species inference, not an E. macularius fact. (f) Minor: OD is defined in all four papers as "greatest diameter of orbit", not eye diameter, though the running text loosely says "diameter of eye".

COULD NOT VERIFY: whether the Reptile Database has since accepted E. madarensis (Mohapatra et al. 2026 cite Uetz et al. 2025 in a list that includes it, but the live genus page I opened does not list it) — treat madarensis's status as contested, confidence unverified. Also unverified: any EE/OD for E. macularius, E. fuscus, E. angramainyu or E. turcmenicus — no such published values were found in any source I opened. - correction: Do not state a 1.4-2.0 band, and do not attach it to E. macularius. Supportable version: In Eublepharis, eye-to-ear distance (EE, anterior edge of the ear opening to the posterior margin of the eye) divided by greatest orbital diameter (OD) spans at least 1.37-2.47 across published type specimens — E. pictus 1.37 (holotype) and 2.47 (paratype), E. jhuma 1.38-1.42 (n=3), E. madarensis 1.43-1.44 (n=2), E. satpuraensis 1.64-2.02 (n=5), E. hardwickii 1.99 (holotype, n=1). Most published figures are single holotypes, mostly from old preserved museum material in which orbit diameter is sensitive to shrinkage, and the within-species spread in E. pictus (1.37 vs 2.47 in one table) shows EE/OD is not a diagnostically stable ratio. No EE/OD value has been published for E. macularius itself. The nearest available figure, 1.43, is from Mirza (2024) and was measured on SMF 60980, the female holotype of Eublepharis macularius smithi Börner, 1981 from Delhi, assigned to E. madarensis (Sharma, 1980) — a closely related Aravalli taxon whose validity is itself contested, and which Mirza diagnoses as distinct from E. macularius. If you use it, label it as a related-species figure, not an E. macularius measurement.

WHAT REFUTES "SPECIES-DIAGNOSTIC": (a) Mohapatra et al. (2026) — the very paper cited in the DETAIL — diagnose their NEW species E. jhuma with, verbatim, "subdigital lamellae tuberculate (vs. subdigital lamellae smooth in E. angramainyu, E. fuscus, E. hardwickii and E. pictus)". So the tuberculate state is a character E. jhuma SHARES; the four smooth species are what jhuma is being contrasted against. Mohapatra et al. separate jhuma from macularius by a different character entirely — regenerated-tail scales "flat and rectangular (vs. circular scales in E. angramainyu, E. macularius and E. turcmenicus)". The DETAIL reads the list backwards: E. macularius is absent from the smooth list because it is in the same (tuberculate) bin as the new species, not because the state singles it out. (b) Mirza (2024) states that E. madarensis "is most similar to E. macularius and a putative synonym E. macularius afghanicus ... in bearing tuberculate lamellae", and separates them only by DEGREE — "feebly tuberculate lamellae (strongly tuberculate in E. macularius afghanicus and E. macularius)". A character that differs by degree between two taxa is not diagnostic in the binary sense the claim asserts. (Note the taxonomic tangle: the Reptile Database account I opened treats madarensis as unresolved/synonymous, commenting that Mirza 2024 "neither provides type information nor proper specimen sources".)

WHAT REFUTES "THREE INDEPENDENT CORROBORATIONS": - Rawat et al. (2019) is not independent. I read the sentence; it ends "(Mirza et al. 2014)". Their entire character set is lifted from Mirza et al.'s key. And in that key the couplet is nested — 4a "Subdigital lamellae tuberculate ... macularius" is only reached after hardwickii, turcmenicus and fuscus have already been eliminated at couplets 1-3. It separates macularius from angramainyu and satpuraensis at that node in a 6-species genus; it was never framed as a genus-wide autapomorphy. - The Reptile Database entry is not independent either. Its diagnosis is explicitly attributed in-line: "(Fig. 56 in Anderson 1999: 120) Subdigital lamellae each with several distinct small tubercles (Fig. E in key, Anderson 1999: 117)", with the remainder credited to Grismer 1988/1991. Anderson 1999 is The Lizards of Iran — a regional key, where the only congeners in play are E. angramainyu and E. turcmenicus. So this is one source (Anderson), and a geographically restricted one. - Rawat et al. also transcribed Mirza loosely: they write "circular dorsal scales", whereas Mirza et al. specify circular dorsal scales ON THE REGENERATED TAIL — and Mirza gives that state for macularius, angramainyu AND turcmenicus, so it is not exclusive either.

ALSO CHECKED, PER THE BRIEF: - Confusion with another gecko species: yes, but within Eublepharis, not outside it — the overlap is with E. madarensis (Mirza 2024) and E. jhuma (2026). I found no evidence of confusion with a non-eublepharid gecko. - Confusion with a captive-bred morph: I found no evidence of this. The diagnosis traces to Anderson 1999 / Grismer 1988-1991, i.e. wild-caught Iranian and Afghan material, and Mirza's and Mohapatra's statements are from museum specimens (BNHS, SMF types). Nothing I opened derives the character from pet-trade animals.

COULD NOT VERIFY: - Anderson 1999 (The Lizards of Iran) itself — I did not open it; I only read the Reptile Database's attributed paraphrase. Grismer 1988 and 1991 likewise unopened. - The lamellar condition of E. turcmenicus. It is not in Mohapatra et al.'s smooth list, and Mirza et al. 2014's key eliminates it at couplet 2 before lamellae are scored, so I cannot say whether it is tuberculate. If it is, the claim weakens further. Unverified. - Whether Rawat et al. could genuinely score subdigital tubercles: two Nepalese animals were measured in hand (their Table 1), but the Sunwal and Surkhet records are photographic vouchers only. Whether lamellar tubercles are resolvable in those field photographs is my own doubt, not something any source states. Unverified. - Historical baseline, as context rather than refutation: Smith (1935) keys Eublepharis on dorsal tubercle size and preanal pore counts and does not mention subdigital lamellar tubercles for E. macularius at all. Single source, so treat as weak corroboration that the character is a modern addition, not a classical one. - correction: E. macularius does have tuberculate subdigital lamellae — "Subdigital lamellae each with several distinct small tubercles" per the Reptile Database diagnosis, which credits Anderson (1999: 117, 120), and per the couplet "4a. Subdigital lamellae tuberculate ... E. macularius" in Mirza et al.'s (2014) key. That half of the claim stands.

But it is a shared character state, not a species-diagnostic one. Mohapatra et al. (2026) diagnose the new E. jhuma as having "subdigital lamellae tuberculate", contrasting it with the smooth-lamellae species E. angramainyu, E. fuscus, E. hardwickii and E. pictus; they distinguish jhuma from macularius by regenerated-tail scale shape instead. Mirza (2024) likewise says E. madarensis shares tuberculate lamellae with E. macularius, separating them only as "feebly" versus "strongly" tuberculate. Within the genus the state is at best one step in a nested key (macularius vs. angramainyu/satpuraensis, after three prior couplets), and as of 2026 it no longer even does that cleanly.

The "three independent corroborations" should be dropped. Rawat et al. (2019) cite Mirza et al. (2014) directly for the character set, and the Reptile Database diagnosis is Anderson (1999), a key to the lizards of Iran where only two congeners are in play. That is effectively two source-lineages, one of them regional; the third source, Mohapatra et al. (2026), argues against the claim rather than for it.

Usable form: "Subdigital lamellae in E. macularius bear several small tubercles rather than being smooth (Anderson 1999, via Reptile Database; Mirza et al. 2014). This helps separate it from E. angramainyu, E. fuscus, E. hardwickii and E. pictus, but it is not unique to the species — E. madarensis and E. jhuma are also tuberculate, and E. turcmenicus is unscored here — so it cannot be used alone as a diagnosis."

The terminal (most distal) subdigital lamella is cleft/divided.

(1) RDB itself brackets it. It is the ONLY character in that whole list wrapped in quotation marks and flagged "(see remarks below)". There are no such remarks. Nothing about lamellae. The cross-reference is dangling in both versions, i.e. the caveat RDB intended to attach to this character is not readable by anyone using the page. (2) The citation behind it points partly at a different species. So part of the character list RDB pastes into the macularius account comes from a three-page paper whose subject is E. turcmenicus. That is exactly the shape of error you asked me to look for: a state that may belong to, or be contrasted against, a congener. I cannot say which — I could not open Grismer 1991, Grismer 1988 (book chapter in Estes & Pregill, Phylogenetic Relationships of the Lizard Families), or Anderson 1999 (The Lizards of Iran, p. 117-120). Also worth noting: the RDB macularius page's own reference list contains no Grismer entry at all, so the citation is untraceable from the page.

(3) No corroboration anywhere, and some contrary evidence. - Exact-phrase web search for "cleft terminal subdigital lamellae" returns nothing but unrelated anatomy literature. The phrase appears to live only on this page. - Karamiani, R. 2022, "Systematics and distribution of the Leopard Geckos Eublepharis Gray, 1827 (Sauria, Eublepharidae): A review", Iranian Journal of Animal Biosystematics (OPENED full PDF: https://ijab.um.ac.ir/article_43277_d85f7ffd34969c63e0146c6ac8bc518f.pdf). This review is built on the same sources RDB cites (Grismer 1988; Grismer 1991; Anderson 1999) and its diagnostic list for E. macularius is: subdigital lamellae each with several distinct small tubercles; mid-dorsal tubercles larger than intertubercular spaces; chin shields usually contacting first lower labials; dorsal pattern not linearly arranged; 46-47 eyelid fringe scales; 21-30 ventral scale rows. No cleft/divided lamella. The word "cleft" occurs zero times in the paper. Its summary of the genus's key characters treats subdigital lamellae only as smooth vs. tuberculate. - RELATED-SPECIES EVIDENCE, flagged as such: Mirza, Z.A. 2024, Taprobanica 13(1): 9-15 (OPENED full PDF: https://www.taprobanica.org/~file/318_eublepharis_madarensis_taprobanica_13_1_2024_mirza_9_15-99e7c-3349_1243.pdf) redescribes E. madarensis from the holotype of "E. macularius smithi" — a population treated as part of E. macularius until this 2024 split, so about as close a proxy as exists without being E. macularius sensu stricto. It describes the digits as "bearing horizontally oriented smooth, un-notched lamellae on ventral surface" and says "Lamellae beneath the digits tuberculate, except for the 2-3 terminal ones". I.e. the distal-most lamellae are singled out for LACKING tubercles, not for being split. The same author uses the identical "un-notched lamellae" wording for E. hardwickii and E. pictus in Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022, Evolutionary Systematics 6(1): 77-88 (OPENED, JATS XML: https://evolsyst.pensoft.net/article/83290/download/xml/) — those two are congeners in a different, eastern-Indian clade, not E. macularius. - The genus-level diagnosis (Leviton et al. 1992), which I read both on the RDB E. hardwickii account and quoted in Karamiani 2022, describes the digit as "clawed, the claw partly concealed beneath two or four lateral scales and an upper scale" — a claw sheath, with no cleft or divided terminal lamella mentioned. I also pulled the RDB accounts for E. angramainyu, E. turcmenicus, E. hardwickii, E. fuscus and E. satpuraensis: "cleft" occurs zero times in all five.

MORPH / CAPTIVE-STOCK CHECK: I found no evidence this is a captive-morph artifact. The character is presented in a wild-type taxonomic context and traces to museum-specimen literature, so morph confusion is not the likely failure mode here; species-level compilation error is.

COULD NOT VERIFY (do not fill these in): whether Grismer 1988:442-450, Grismer 1991:251-253, or Anderson 1999:120 actually assert a cleft terminal lamella for macularius, and if so for which taxon the state was scored; and what RDB's missing "remarks" said. All three primary sources were inaccessible to me. Two plausible but UNVERIFIED origins I will name without asserting: (a) the paired lateral claw-sheath scales of Eublepharis being loosely described as a "cleft" terminal lamella, and (b) carry-over of a character framed for pad-bearing gekkonids, where a divided terminal scansor is a standard diagnostic — I did not open a source for (b), so treat it as a hypothesis only.

CONFIDENCE: unverified. Per the default rule, holds=false — not because I proved the lamella is entire, but because one compiled database entry, self-flagged, citing a paper about another species, with no corroboration in any source I could open and with the nearest peer-reviewed descriptions saying "un-notched", is not enough to stand. - correction: Do not state as fact that the terminal subdigital lamella of E. macularius is cleft or divided. Defensible version: "The Reptile Database account for E. macularius lists, among characters compiled from Grismer (1988, 1991), a quoted character 'cleft terminal subdigital lamellae', flagged by the database with a cross-reference to remarks that are absent from the page; the state is not corroborated in any other source I could open, one of the two cited Grismer papers concerns E. turcmenicus rather than E. macularius, and recent descriptions in the genus instead describe the subdigital lamellae as smooth and un-notched, with the 2-3 terminal lamellae distinguished by lacking tubercles (Mirza 2024, for E. madarensis, split from E. macularius in 2024). The solidly corroborated digit character for E. macularius is that the subdigital lamellae bear several distinct small tubercles (strongly tuberculate), versus smooth in E. angramainyu, E. fuscus, E. hardwickii, E. pictus and E. satpuraensis — that one is carried by both the Reptile Database account and Karamiani (2022).

Claws are present on every digit, and are partly enclosed at the base by a sheath of scales — two lateral scales plus one upper scale.

-- I opened Boulenger 1890 and Smith 1935 in full OCR and the quoted sentences are real and on the cited pages — but they do not support the claim as worded, for four reasons.

(1) WRONG TAXONOMIC LEVEL. Both sentences are GENUS (not species) diagnoses. Boulenger 1890 p.107 is under "Family II. EUBLEPHARIDAE / Genus EUBLEPHARIS": "Digits short and cylindrical, with a row of lamellæ below, clawed, the claws only partially retractile into a small sheath." Smith 1935 p.125 (sentence breaks across to p.126) is under "Genus EUBLEPHARIS": "Digits short, cylindrical, with transverse lamellae beneath, clawed, the claw partly concealed between two lateral scales and an upper scale." Neither author says anything about claws in his E. macularius species account (Boulenger p.108; Smith pp.127–129 — I read both in full; they cover tubercles, pores, colour, size, range only). Boulenger's Eublepharis then held five species, three of them AMERICAN; Smith's included Goniurosaurus hainanensis and E. lichtenfelderi. So the sheath character was written for a genus concept much broader than, and partly outside, modern Eublepharis.

(2) THE TWO SOURCES ARE NOT INDEPENDENT. Smith 1935 is the successor volume of the same Fauna of British India series and cites "Boulenger, ... Fauna Brit. Ind. 1890, p. 107" in the genus synonymy immediately above that very sentence. Sharma 2002 (Fauna of India, Reptilia Vol. II: Sauria, ZSI, p.148) repeats it again almost verbatim: "The digits are short, cylindrical, clawed (claws are partly hidden between two lateral scales and an upper scale)". That is a copy-chain down one series, not two independent observations 45 years apart.

(3) THE "TWO LATERAL + ONE UPPER" CONFIGURATION IS SINGLE-SOURCED. Boulenger says only "a small sheath" and makes a functional statement (partially retractile); he gives no scale count. Only Smith gives 2+1. Also, Smith uses a near-identical stock formula for unrelated genera in the same book — "the claw between two enlarged scales" for Cyrtodactylus/Geckoella (p.~52), Agamura and Pristurus — so this reads as genus boilerplate, not a measured observation on macularius material.

(4) "EVERY DIGIT" IS UNVERIFIED. Neither cited source says all/every digit. Smith's key entry for the genus reads only "Digits not dilated, clawed"; elsewhere in the same key he writes "All the digits clawed" (Platyurus) and "Inner digit clawless" (Ptychozoon, Ptyodactylus group), so the omission for Eublepharis is meaningful, not shorthand. I found no opened source stating claw presence on all five digits of E. macularius.

SPECIES-CONFUSION CHECK (asked for explicitly): the "E. macularius" of Boulenger and Smith is a composite. Boulenger p.108 gives range "Punjab and Sind; also recently found in the ruins of Nineveh"; Smith p.128 gives "N.W. India to S. Transcaspia and Mesopotamia" and cites a "Persian specimen". Those western populations are now covered by later-named taxa (E. angramainyu, E. turcmenicus) — I did NOT open those original descriptions, so treat that referral as unverified. What I did verify: Mohapatra et al. 2026 (opened PDF, pp.162, 174) state that Indian "E. macularius" has been progressively split (E. satpuraensis 2014; E. pictus, Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022; E. madarensis resurrected by Mirza 2024) and that the status of the Himachal Pradesh population — "the only known population of 'E. macularius' in India" — "remains unresolved". No captive-morph contamination is involved; these are 19th/20th-century wild museum specimens.

MOHAPATRA ET AL. 2026 QUOTE CHECKS OUT BUT DOES NOT HELP: p.168, holotype description of E. jhuma: "Limbs short, stout; digits dilated, clawed, with tuberculate lamellae on the ventral surface, oriented horizontally; claw much smaller than length of the lamellar region". Correct verbatim, correct citation (Herpetozoa 39: 161–176, DOI 10.3897/herpetozoa.39.e183441). But it describes E. jhuma sp. nov. (congener, same genus, described 2026 from Kaimur Hills, Bihar), not E. macularius, and the word "sheath" does not occur anywhere in that paper — it gives no support for a claw sheath at all. - correction: What is actually documented, stated at the level the sources support:

"In the genus Eublepharis (as diagnosed in the Fauna of British India series), the digits are short and cylindrical with transverse subdigital lamellae and bear claws that are only partially retractile, the claw base partly concealed between two lateral scales and an upper scale (Smith 1935: 125; the retractile-into-a-small-sheath wording goes back to Boulenger 1890: 107, which does not specify the scales; repeated almost verbatim by Sharma 2002: 148). This is a genus-level character; neither Boulenger nor Smith describes claws in his E. macularius species account, and I found no source that verifies the scale configuration on E. macularius material specifically."

Drop from the claim, or re-label: - "on every digit" — could_not_verify. No opened source states all/every digit for E. macularius. Confidence: unverified. - "two independent sources ~45 years apart" — false. Smith 1935 cites Boulenger 1890 p.107 directly; both are volumes of the same series; Sharma 2002 continues the copy-chain. One source lineage, three restatements. - "two lateral scales plus one upper scale" — single-sourced (Smith 1935, echoed by Sharma 2002). Boulenger says only "a small sheath". Confidence: low/single-source. - Attribute the sheath character to genus Eublepharis sensu Boulenger/Smith, and flag that that genus concept then included American eublepharids (Boulenger) and Goniurosaurus/E. lichtenfelderi (Smith), and that their "E. macularius" spanned Mesopotamia and Transcaspia. - The E. jhuma line is fine but must be labelled as a transfer from a congener: E. jhuma Mohapatra et al. 2026, same genus, described 2026, phylogenetically nested near E. satpuraensis — not E. macularius, and it says nothing about a sheath.

To actually settle this you need a modern specimen-based redescription or a digit/claw morphology study on verified E. macularius (Salt Range, Punjab, Pakistan topotypes — ZSI-R-6224 is listed as the holotype in Mohapatra et al. 2026's comparative material, p.175). I did not find or open one.
