The naris sits within a single enlarged nasal scale, and that nasal scale — not the naris — is what contacts the rostral.

-- SOURCES I ACTUALLY OPENED (source_opened = true for all of these): 1. Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022, Evolutionary Systematics 6(1): 77–88 — full article XML pulled from https://evolsyst.pensoft.net/article/83290/download/xml/ and read locally. 2. Mirza 2024, Taprobanica 13(1): 9–15 — PDF pulled from https://www.taprobanica.org/~file/318_eublepharis_madarensis_taprobanica_13_1_2024_mirza_9_15-99e7c-3349_1243.pdf, text extracted and read. 3. Boulenger 1885, Cat. Liz. Brit. Mus. (N.H.) vol. 1, Eublepharis pp. 230–233 (archive.org catalogueoflizar01brituoft). 4. Boulenger 1890, Fauna Brit. India, Reptilia & Batrachia, Eublepharis pp. 107–108 (archive.org reptiliabatrachi00boul). 5. Smith 1935, Fauna Brit. India, Reptilia & Amphibia vol. II Sauria, Eublepharis pp. 125–129 (archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.207328). 6. Minton 1966, Bull. AMNH 134, E. macularius pp. 72–73 (archive.org bulletin-american-museum-natural-history-134-029-184). 7. Reptile Database entry for E. macularius (compilation, weak; quotes Anderson 1999 / Grismer 1988 diagnoses).

WHAT CHECKS OUT The quoted wording is real and I verified it verbatim, so the claimant did not invent or garble it. In Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 it appears twice: in the redescription of the E. hardwickii holotype NHMUK 1946.8.26.6 ("rostral in contact with nasal, first supralabial and internasals; two large and a slightly smaller internasal between nasals, nostrils large situated medially in the nasal scale") and in the description of the E. pictus holotype NCBS NRC-AA-0015, which adds the clause "nasal bordered by rostral, internasal, supralabial I and 8 small scales". Mirza 2024 repeats it for E. madarensis. The claimant was also right to flag this as a species transfer.

WHY IT STILL FAILS FOR E. macularius (a) No documentation at all for E. macularius sensu stricto. I checked every classical and museum-based description I could open. Boulenger 1885 and Boulenger 1890 do not mention the nostril, nasal or rostral for either Eublepharis species — Boulenger's head-scale sentence for E. hardwickii stops at "rostral subpentagonal, twice as broad as high, with median cleft above; three or four internasals", and his E. macularius entry is purely differential (tubercle size, pore count, colour). Minton 1966, describing Pakistani wild-caught E. macularius from the heart of its range, gives labial and ventral scale counts but says nothing about the nasal region. So the claim is undocumented, not documented-and-transferred.

(b) The "apparent tension with the classical sources" that the DETAIL says this resolves does not exist in anything I opened. The only classical statement I found on this character is Smith 1935 for E. hardwickii: rostral broader than high, NOT in contact with the nostril, three or four internasals. That agrees with Mirza; it does not conflict with him. The rationale offered for the claim is therefore built on a conflict I could not locate.

(c) The three Mirza statements are one source, not three. They are the same author's reused description template, near-verbatim across two papers, varying only in the internasal count (hardwickii: two large + one slightly smaller; pictus: two large + one much smaller middle; madarensis: two large + two slightly smaller). Under the project's corroborate-twice rule this counts as a single observation formula, not independent corroboration.

(d) "Medially" is being over-read. In strict anatomical usage medial means toward the midline, not "in the middle of". On that reading the naris would sit at the rostral-facing edge of the nasal, which undercuts rather than supports the inference that it is "separated from the rostral by scale surface". Mirza nowhere writes that the naris does not touch the rostral. The word "enlarged" in the claim is also the claimant's, not Mirza's — Mirza says the nostril is large, and only for E. pictus implies a relatively large nasal by listing 8 small scales around it.

(e) Factual error in the claimant's sourcing of the madarensis wording. That sentence is not from a Rajasthan animal. Mirza 2024 states the description is "Based on the female holotype (SMF 60980) of E. macularius smithi" Börner 1981, collected at DELHI on 30 July 1965. The Rajasthan type of madarensis (Jodhpur V/1215, Madar near Ajmer) is an immature male and is not the described specimen. This cuts both ways: it corrects the claimant's framing, but the specimen actually measured had been a named subspecies of E. macularius.

(f) Phylogenetic distance — the claimant is right, and can be stated more strongly. Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 recover the E. hardwickii group as sister to the E. macularius clade, and place "E. cf. smithii" (which Mirza 2024 synonymises with E. madarensis) INSIDE the E. macularius clade alongside E. macularius, E. fuscus, E. satpuraensis, E. sp. Himalayas and E. sp. Pakistan. Same paper notes relationships within that clade have poor to moderate support.

MORPH / MISIDENTIFICATION CHECK (the thing you asked me to look for) No morph confusion in the scalation wording itself — every sentence traces to a preserved museum type (NHMUK 1946.8.26.6, NCBS NRC-AA-0015, SMF 60980). Related caution worth recording: the molecular sampling in Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 does include captive pet-trade stock as terminals ("Eublepharis sp. Himalaya German line" OK563705, "Eublepharis sp. Himalaya female, Germany bloodline" OK563706), so captive-origin material is embedded in the genus's molecular framework even though it is not the basis of these scale descriptions.

COULD NOT VERIFY (confidence: unverified) I could not open the places where a macularius-specific statement would most plausibly sit: Grismer 1988 (eublepharid phylogeny, head-scale character coding), Anderson 1999 The Lizards of Iran, Börner 1974/1976/1981, Szczerbak & Golubev 1996, Khan 2006, Blyth 1854 original description, and Mirza et al. 2014 (E. satpuraensis, Phyllomedusa 13(2): 75–90 — the USP server refused connection; this one matters most, because E. satpuraensis sits inside the E. macularius clade and if Mirza used the same template there it would move the transfer much closer). My web-search budget ran out before I could chase these.

Note in fairness: nothing I opened asserts the opposite either — no source I read says the naris contacts the rostral in any Eublepharis. So the claim is plausible and the evidence leans its way. It is simply not documented for E. macularius, and per the standing rule that means holds=false. - correction: What is documented, and what should be said instead: "Mirza gives, in identical boilerplate for three congeners — E. hardwickii and E. pictus (Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022, from holotypes NHMUK 1946.8.26.6 and NCBS NRC-AA-0015) and E. madarensis (Mirza 2024, from SMF 60980, the female holotype of E. macularius smithi Börner 1981, a Delhi specimen) — that the rostral contacts the nasal, the first supralabial and the internasals, and that the nostril is large and situated medially in the nasal scale; for E. pictus he adds that the nasal is bordered by rostral, internasal, supralabial I and eight small scales. Smith 1935 independently states for E. hardwickii that the rostral is not in contact with the nostril. TRANSFERRED FROM RELATED SPECIES: E. hardwickii and E. pictus belong to the E. hardwickii group, the sister clade to the E. macularius clade; E. madarensis is nested inside the E. macularius clade itself (as 'E. cf. smithii' of Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022), so it is the closest of the three. No source I opened states this for E. macularius sensu stricto — Boulenger 1885, Boulenger 1890 and Minton 1966 do not describe the nasal region of E. macularius at all, and Smith 1935 treats E. macularius only by difference from E. hardwickii (smaller dorsal tubercles, 9–14 preanal pores), which by that work's convention implies but does not state the shared nasal condition. Confidence: unverified." Two specific fixes to the original wording: drop "enlarged" (Mirza says the NOSTRIL is large, not the nasal scale), and drop the inference that the naris is "separated from the rostral by scale surface" — "situated medially" is ambiguous between 'in the middle of' and 'toward the midline', and Mirza never states non-contact.

In the embryo the naris forms ventrolaterally on the snout and its vestibule takes a more horizontal orientation than in typical gekkonids; the snout elongates markedly late in development.

-- SOURCE OPENED: yes — I downloaded the full text of PMC7812140 directly (raw HTML from pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, 425 KB, stripped to text and searched), so the quotes below are from the paper itself, not a summarizer. PMCID confirmed correct via the NCBI ID converter (PMID 33169847 -> PMC7812140, doi 10.1111/joa.13312).

TWO OF THE THREE SUB-CLAIMS ARE TRANSFERRED FROM THE OTHER SPECIES IN THE SAME PAPER.

(1) "Naris forms ventrolaterally" — REFUTED, this is Lepidodactylus lugubris. The word "ventrolateral" is used of the naris exactly once in the paper, in section 3.1 under Figure 3, whose caption reads "Early developmental phase of the naso-palatal complex after formation of the vomeronasal pit in L. lugubris": "The primitive naris is now elongated and open on the ventrolateral side of the forming snout (Figure 3B'-D) which corresponds to ventral growth of the nasal prominences." That is L. lugubris at stage 7. What the paper says for E. macularius at stage 30 is plain "ventral", and says it is a SIMILARITY, not a difference: "the presence of the small primordial lateral nasal concha, the lack of the extraconchal space, and the ventral location of the primitive naris are similar in both: E. macularius at developmental stage 30 and L. lugubris at stage 12." The "relatively widely open / no narrowing of the anteriormost part of the oval primitive naris" bit in the DETAIL is accurate, but that is about patency, not direction.

(2) The DETAIL's inference ("independently supports a laterally-to-ventrolaterally directed naris rather than a dorsal one") does not follow, because the primitive naris is not the nostril. The paper explicitly treats them as different structures: "the division of the primitive naris into the external naris and primitive outer choana, and the formation of the vestibulum may start at this stage", and in the Discussion "Initial fusion of the facial prominences is involved in the division of the primitive naris into the external naris and choana (called here the primitive outer choana) (Parsons, 1959a)". The primitive naris is a transient embryonic opening into the stomodeum that is later partitioned; its ventral position is a statement about facial-prominence growth, not about where the definitive nostril ends up. I searched the whole text: "nostril" occurs 0 times, and none of the 21 occurrences of "external naris" assign it a direction (lateral/ventrolateral/dorsal) in E. macularius. The paper describes embryos only, up to an "adult-like stage" (st. 42), and makes no adult external-naris orientation claim for either species.

(3) "Vestibule more horizontal than in typical gekkonids" — PARTLY true at one matched stage, but misstated as a standing species difference, and "typical gekkonids" is n=1. The supporting sentence exists: comparing L. lugubris st. 20-22 with E. macularius st. 34_II, "The vestibulum of the L. lugubris remains vertical, while in E. macularius it attains more horizontal orientation." But the paper then shows the two converge. L. lugubris st. 26: "The vestibulum takes on a more horizontal orientation than previously." L. lugubris adult-like st. 50-60: "The vestibulum takes on an almost horizontal orientation." E. macularius adult-like st. 42: "As in L. lugubris at stage 50-60, the vestibulum of adult-like stage of E. macularius takes an almost horizontal orientation." So this is a heterochronic difference at intermediate stages, and both species finish almost horizontal. Only ONE gekkonid was examined (L. lugubris, Gekkonidae), so "typical gekkonids" is unsupported extrapolation from a single comparator; the paper's own Discussion (4.2) notes gekkotan vestibulum form is variable — "in Gekkota this part of the nasal cavity is usually moderately long, but it may be elongated as in Stendactylus [sic] and Tarentola".

(4) "The snout elongates markedly late in development" — REFUTED, and inverted. The "markedly late" elongation is L. lugubris. L. lugubris at the start of the late phase (st. 26): "The snout and the entire nasal cavity are now much more elongated compared to the stage 20-22." E. macularius at the start of its late phase (st. 35): "The snout and each component of the naso-palatal complex are SLIGHTLY more elongated than at stage 34_II" — and "The vestibulum has a similar orientation to previously", i.e. it had already attained it. E. macularius is the species whose snout is comparatively elongated EARLY, in the middle phase: "The snout as well as the entire nasal cavity and the outer choana in L. lugubris at stage 20-22 is not so elongated as in E. macularius at stage 34_II." The DETAIL's own wording ("the snout and nasal cavity end up much more elongated") is closer to the paper than the CLAIM's "elongates markedly late in development", which contradicts "slightly more elongated".

SPECIES CONFUSION CHECK (requested): yes, confirmed. The confusion is with Lepidodactylus lugubris, the comparator species in the very same paper. Distance: L. lugubris is Gekkonidae, E. macularius is Eublepharidae — different families within Gekkota, deeply divergent, and the paper's whole point is to contrast them.

MORPH CHECK (requested): could not verify. Methods 2.1 states the eggs came from animals "kept in the breeding room of the Faculty of Natural Sciences of the University of Silesia in Katowice" — a captive colony, incubated at 30 C in a ReptiBator. The paper does not state the morph, does not state the animals were wild-type, and gives no provenance for the founder stock. So whether these were normal/wild-type-phenotype animals is UNVERIFIED from this source. I have no opened source showing that leopard gecko morphs differ in snout or nasal-capsule morphology, so I am not asserting that this matters — only that it is undocumented here.

Janiszewska is NOT an author of this 2021 paper; she is a co-author on the companion 2020 study of Anolis sagrei (Frontiers in Zoology), which the 2021 paper cites as "Kaczmarek et al., 2020". A web search result independently flagged the same discrepancy. Journal, volume, issue, year, DOI and PMCID are otherwise correct (J. Anat. 238(2): 249-287, 2021).

STATISTICAL WEAKNESS: Table 1 gives 20 E. macularius embryos total (11 microCT + 9 LM) across 9 stages, i.e. typically n=1 per stage per method. So the single-stage vestibulum contrast rests on one specimen per species per stage.

CORROBORATION: one source only for the substance, which is appropriate here because the claim is a claim ABOUT this source and I checked it against the primary full text; the author-list error is corroborated twice (Europe PMC API + search result). I did not find or open any independent study of E. macularius nasal-capsule embryology.

COULD NOT VERIFY: (a) morph/wild-type status of the E. macularius colony; (b) any adult or hatchling external-naris orientation in E. macularius — this paper simply does not address it, so it cannot be used as evidence for or against a dorsal vs lateral nostril; (c) whether L. lugubris is representative of "typical gekkonids" for vestibulum orientation. - correction: Accurate version, restricted to what Kaczmarek, Metscher & Rupik (2021, J. Anat. 238(2): 249-287; note: three authors, no Janiszewska) actually report:

In E. macularius embryos the PRIMITIVE naris (the transient embryonic opening of the nasal pit into the stomodeum, later partitioned into the external naris plus the primitive outer choana) is described as lying VENTRALLY on the forming snout at stage 30, and the authors present this ventral position as SIMILAR to Lepidodactylus lugubris at stage 12, not as a difference. The "ventrolateral" description belongs to L. lugubris at stage 7, not to E. macularius. It remains relatively widely open at stage 30, with no narrowing of the anterior part — that part of the detail is correct.

The nasal vestibule of E. macularius attains a more horizontal orientation EARLIER than in L. lugubris (E. macularius st. 34_II vs L. lugubris st. 20-22, where the latter is still vertical), but both species reach an "almost horizontal" vestibulum by their adult-like stages (E. macularius st. 42; L. lugubris st. 50-60). This is a heterochronic, intermediate-stage difference, based on one gekkonid comparator, not a standing E. macularius-versus-gekkonids character.

Snout elongation in E. macularius is comparatively EARLY, not markedly late: its snout and nasal cavity are already more elongated at middle-phase st. 34_II than L. lugubris at st. 20-22, and at the start of its late phase (st. 35) the snout is only "slightly" more elongated than before. The "much more elongated" late-phase jump described in the paper is L. lugubris at st. 26.

Confidence: the above is VERIFIED against the opened full text. Confidence UNVERIFIED for: the morph/wild-type status of the captive E. macularius colony (not stated), and any implication about adult nostril direction — this paper studies embryos and never describes the orientation of the definitive external naris in E. macularius, so it cannot be cited for or against a dorsally versus laterally directed nostril. Sample size is roughly one specimen per stage per method (20 E. macularius embryos total), with no assessment of individual variation.

The rostral is a single large plate at the tip of the snout, roughly twice as wide as it is high, and it bears a median cleft or suture.

FINDING 1 — Boulenger never states this for E. macularius, and there is no genus-level bridge. Confirmed: the phrase "rostral subpentagonal, twice as broad as high, with median cleft above" sits in the Eublepharis hardwickii account in BOTH works (1885 p. 231; 1890 p. 107, OCR "median deft"). In both works the E. macularius account is a bare differential diagnosis — 1885 p. 232 and 1890 p. 108 both open "Differs from the preceding by the smaller and less numerous tubercles…" and go on to tubercle size, body/digit proportions, preanal pore counts (9–14) and colour pattern ONLY. I grepped both macularius blocks: zero occurrences of the rostral scale (the single 1890 hit is "canthus rostralis", a different structure, and it belongs to the following account). The claim's phrase "that E. macularius inherits" is the claimant's own inference, not an assertion Boulenger makes. Critically, I also read the genus diagnoses to test whether inheritance is licensed: Boulenger 1885 p. 230 gives only "Digits with a row of lamellae inferiorly; claw-sheaths small, the claws only partially retractile"; Boulenger 1890 p. 107 gives only digits/claws/pupil/preanal pores. Neither genus diagnosis contains any rostral character. So there is no documented basis for transferring it.

FINDING 2 — Smith 1935 repeats the same structure and quietly DROPS the cleft. Smith's E. macularius account (p. 127) is again purely differential: "Closely allied to E. hardwickii, differing in the following particulars: enlarged dorsal tubercles smaller, as broad as or smaller than their interspaces; male with from 9 to 14 preanal pores" — no head scalation, no rostral. And Smith's own hardwickii description (p. 126) gives the rostral as "rostral broader than high, not in contact with the nostril" — NOT "twice as broad as high", and with NO mention of a median cleft. So the leading 20th-century redescription, working the same BMNH material, declined to corroborate the cleft even for hardwickii. The cleft is therefore single-sourced to Boulenger; the 1890 text is verbatim self-repetition of 1885, not independent corroboration.

FINDING 3 — Blyth's original description contains nothing. I read Blyth 1854 p. 738 (the footnote establishing Cyrtodactylus macularius, from the Punjab Salt Range, via Theobald). It is almost entirely colour pattern plus "tail granular beneath" and throat/abdomen scale gradation. There is no head-shield description at all, hence no rostral.

FINDING 4 — The Reptile Database attribution in the DETAIL is wrong, and I can quote the structure. The RDB Diagnosis field is built in two parts: Anderson 1999: 120 supplies subdigital lamellae with small tubercles, mid-dorsal tubercles vs intertubercular spaces, chin shields in contact with first lower labials, and non-linear colour-pattern elements. Then a separate clause reads "Additional diagnostic characters (Grismer, 1988:442-450; 1991: 251-252):" and it is INSIDE that Grismer list that "rostral twice as wide as high" appears. So the character is credited to Grismer, not to Anderson 1999. Equally important: the RDB diagnosis says nothing whatever about a median cleft or suture in the rostral. The second "independent line" therefore supports at most the proportion, never the cleft — and it is not independent of a primary source I have opened, since it is a secondary page quoting Grismer, which I did not open.

FINDING 5 — SPECIES-CONFUSION CHECK (this is the one the claim most needed). Anderson 1999 is a poor vehicle for E. macularius characters in the first place. The RDB synonymy line reads "Eublepharis cf. macularius — ANDERSON 1999" — Anderson himself hedged the identification. The RDB Comment states "No confirmed records from Iran fide RASTEGAR-POUYANI et al. 2008." The Iranian Eublepharis is principally E. angramainyu, and RDB's Comment further records that E. macularius and E. angramainyu can be crossed with viable, fertile F1s (Jančúchová-Lásková et al. 2015). Building an E. macularius scale character on an Iranian source, for a species with no confirmed Iranian records, is exactly the cross-species contamination risk flagged in the task.

FINDING 6 — The Mirza wording is about a DIFFERENT SPECIES, and that resolves the claimant's "unresolved discrepancy". I located the passage: Mirza 2024 p. 9–10, "rostral quadrangle much wider than deep, divided by a median suture for its entire length; rostral in contact with nasal, first supralabial and internasals". This sits in the Description section of Eublepharis madarensis (Sharma, 1980), written from the female holotype SMF 60980 of E. macularius smithi Börner 1981 (Delhi) — i.e. a taxon Mirza 2024 explicitly revalidates OUT of E. macularius ("differs from E. macularius… vertebral stripe present on anterior part of trunk (absent in E. macularius); feebly tuberculate lamellae (strongly tuberculate in… E. macularius)"). So the "entire length" wording is not an E. macularius statement and never was. Note also the shape conflict the claim smooths over: Boulenger "subpentagonal" (hardwickii) vs Mirza "quadrangle" (madarensis). And RDB's Comment records that Mirza 2024's madarensis is itself contested — no type information or proper specimen sources for his sequences — so it is weak ground regardless.

FINDING 7 — RELATED-SPECIES DISTANCE, stated explicitly as the standing rules require. The cleft character is transferred from E. hardwickii, a congener, not a conspecific. Per the phylogeny summarised inside Mirza 2024 (attributed there to Agarwal et al. 2022, which I did NOT open): E. angramainyu is sister to all other Eublepharis, and the E. hardwickii group is sister to the E. macularius clade. So hardwickii is a sister-clade congener — close, but a separate species-group, and Boulenger, Smith and Mirza all treat hardwickii and macularius as diagnosably distinct on scalation and tuberculation.

CAPTIVE-MORPH CHECK — negative, and I say so rather than leaving it implied. I found no sign this claim is morph-derived. Every rostral statement I traced runs to wild-collected museum material (Boulenger's Hardwicke/Traill/Beddome/Tufnell/Riddell specimens; SMF 60980; BMNH types). The failure mode here is species confusion and character transfer, not captive-bred morph contamination.

COULD NOT VERIFY: (a) whether Grismer 1988 or 1991 states the proportion for E. macularius on measured macularius material, and what sample he used — I did not open Grismer; (b) whether Anderson 1999 p. 120 independently mentions the rostral at all; (c) whether any modern source describes a median cleft in verified wild-type E. macularius — I found none in six opened sources; (d) the E. pictus paper (ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403) and Mirza et al. 2014 on E. satpuraensis, either of which might carry a comparative rostral statement.

CONFIDENCE: "rostral roughly twice as wide as high" for E. macularius — LOW / single-source, secondary, attribution in the claim misstated. "Median cleft or suture" for E. macularius — UNVERIFIED, and actively undermined by Smith 1935 dropping it and by RDB omitting it. - correction: What the opened sources actually support:

1. For E. macularius, no primary description I opened — Blyth 1854 (original), Boulenger 1885, Boulenger 1890, Smith 1935 — states any rostral character at all. All four treat macularius as a differential diagnosis against E. hardwickii built on dorsal tubercle size, body/digit proportions, preanal pore count (9–14 vs 13–18) and colour pattern. The rostral is simply not part of the species' documented description in the classical literature.

2. The "twice as broad as high, with median cleft above" wording belongs to E. HARDWICKII (Boulenger 1885: 231, repeated verbatim by the same author in Boulenger 1890: 107 — self-repetition, not corroboration). E. hardwickii is a congener in the sister clade to the macularius clade, not a conspecific. Transferring the character is undocumented: neither Boulenger's nor Smith's genus diagnosis of Eublepharis includes any rostral character, so nothing licenses inheritance.

3. Smith 1935: 126, redescribing E. hardwickii, gives only "rostral broader than high, not in contact with the nostril" — no "twice", and no cleft. The cleft is not corroborated a second time even for hardwickii.

4. The Reptile Database DOES carry "rostral twice as wide as high" for E. macularius, but attributes it to GRISMER 1988: 442-450 / 1991: 251-252, not to Anderson 1999 as the claim states. That attribution in the DETAIL should be corrected. The RDB diagnosis contains no mention of a median cleft or suture. I did not open Grismer, so this proportion rests on one unopened secondary-quoted source.

5. "Divided by a median suture for its entire length" is Mirza 2024's description of EUBLEPHARIS MADARENSIS (from the SMF 60980 holotype of E. macularius smithi, Delhi) — a taxon Mirza revalidates out of E. macularius. It is not a statement about E. macularius, so there is no genuine Boulenger-vs-Mirza discrepancy "about E. macularius" to resolve; the two statements are about two different species (and describe different shapes: subpentagonal vs quadrangular).

6. Anderson 1999 is an unsafe source for this species regardless: RDB lists the entry as "Eublepharis cf. macularius — ANDERSON 1999" and comments "No confirmed records from Iran fide Rastegar-Pouyani et al. 2008." Iranian Eublepharis is principally E. angramainyu, which hybridises with E. macularius.

Defensible restatement: "The rostral of Eublepharis macularius is reported as about twice as wide as high (Reptile Database diagnosis, crediting Grismer 1988/1991 — single source, not opened by me; confidence low). Whether it bears a median cleft or suture is UNVERIFIED for this species: no description of E. macularius I opened mentions the rostral at all. The 'median cleft above' wording is Boulenger's for the congener E. hardwickii, and 'divided by a median suture for its entire length' is Mirza 2024's for E. madarensis, a taxon split out of E. macularius." Do not assert the cleft for E. macularius without opening Grismer 1988/1991 and Anderson 1999 directly, or a modern description based on identified wild-type macularius material.

WHY THE CLAIM FAILS AS WRITTEN:

(a) The Smith 1935 attribution is wrong, and it is the load-bearing error. The passage the claimant quotes — mental "subtriangular or pentagonal, twice as broad as the adjacent labials", then a pair of large postmentals "usually present and in contact with one another" — sits entirely inside species account 86, Eublepharis hardwickii, on p. 126. It is not a joint hardwickii/macularius statement and it is not in Smith's genus diagnosis (p. 125-126), which says nothing about the mental at all. Smith's macularius account (no. 87, p. 127) opens by saying it is closely allied to hardwickii and differs in only two named particulars: smaller dorsal tubercles and 9-14 preanal pores in the male. Everything else, including the whole head scalation, reaches macularius purely by inheritance. So the DETAIL's premise — that this is a head character stated "explicitly rather than by inheritance" — is false for Smith. It is true only of Boulenger's 1885 key couplet.

(b) "Meet on the midline" is supported by one source, about a different species. Boulenger 1885 says only "followed by a pair of chin-shields" — no midline contact. Smith is the only source asserting contact with one another, and (i) he says it of hardwickii, (ii) he qualifies it "usually present", i.e. it is variable, not a fixed character. The Reptile Database/Anderson 1999 line the claimant offers as independent corroboration — chin shields usually in contact with the first lower labials — describes contact with the LABIALS, a different contact entirely; it says nothing about the two postmentals touching each other. The claimant's "Three sources" for the midline element is really one, and that one is about hardwickii and hedged.

(c) Boulenger himself dropped the character. In Boulenger 1890, the same author's synopsis of Indian Eublepharis separates hardwickii from macularius on dorsal tubercles alone; the mental/chin-shield wording survives only in the hardwickii account, and macularius again inherits. An author abandoning his own key character within five years is evidence against treating it as a stable macularius diagnostic.

(d) Congener overlap: it is not diagnostic of macularius. In Boulenger 1885 the couplet's contrast partners are dovii, variegatus and fasciatus — all now referred to Coleonyx, i.e. Central/North American animals, where dovii has "no chin-shields". Against its actual congener E. hardwickii the character does NOT separate, since Boulenger's own hardwickii account (1885 p. 231, repeated 1890 p. 107) gives the mental as broadly pentagonal and in contact with two enlarged chin-shields. So the character is a genus-level eublepharid condition being read as a species diagnosis.

(e) Species-concept contamination (the "confused with another species" check, and it does fire). "E. macularius" in Boulenger and Smith is a much broader taxon than the modern one. Smith's range for it runs to S. Transcaspia and Mesopotamia and he explicitly cites a Persian BM specimen; Boulenger 1885 footnotes a Nineveh specimen he examined personally. Material from that western range is now referred to E. angramainyu. Since 1935 the old macularius concept has also had fuscus, montanus and pictus split out, and the Reptile Database records the contested revalidation of madarensis (Mirza 2024). The Reptile Database further notes no confirmed Iranian records (fide Rastegar-Pouyani et al. 2008) — which undercuts source 3 specifically, because Anderson 1999 is a lizards-of-IRAN key, so its macularius diagnosis rests on a fauna whose inclusion of the species is doubted, and its "additional diagnostic characters" are themselves taken from Grismer 1988/1991 rather than from Iranian macularius.

(f) The morph check is clean and I say so rather than leaving a gap: this is not a captive-morph artefact. All four sources are museum-specimen-based and pre-date the hobby trade, and mental/postmental scalation is not a selectable morph trait. The live risk runs the other way — modern hobby and breeder descriptions of "leopard gecko" head scales describe captive stock of mixed and often undocumented provenance, and should not be used to corroborate any of this. I used none.

COULD NOT VERIFY: I could not open Anderson 1999 itself (only the Reptile Database's transcription of its diagnosis), so I cannot see Anderson's Fig. C or confirm whether his chin-shield character is a couplet against E. angramainyu. I could not open any post-1935 primary redescription of E. macularius (Mirza 2018/2024, Grismer 1988/1991) — my web-search budget was exhausted before I reached them — so I have NO modern taxonomic confirmation that any part of this mental/postmental character still stands for E. macularius sensu stricto. Confidence on the modern status of the whole character: unverified. - correction: Keep the reduced core, drop the midline element and the "three sources" framing, and re-attribute Smith.

DEFENSIBLE (two independent sources, both opened): the mental of E. macularius is broader than long — Boulenger 1885 p. 231 key, "much broader than long"; Reptile Database/Anderson 1999, "mental shorter than wide" — and is followed by a pair of enlarged chin shields (postmentals), Boulenger 1885 p. 231. Confidence: moderate, and only for the broad pre-split macularius concept.

SINGLE SOURCE, SO LABEL IT: "pentagonal" comes from Boulenger 1885 alone. Smith 1935 gives the shape as subtriangular OR pentagonal, so shape is variable, and he gives it for hardwickii. Do not state "pentagonal" flatly.

UNSUPPORTED FOR E. MACULARIUS — DROP OR RELABEL: "that meet on the midline". No source I opened states this for macularius. It is Smith 1935 p. 126 writing about E. HARDWICKII — a congener, close but a distinct species, which macularius reaches only through Smith's "differs in the following particulars" shortcut — and even there he hedges it as "usually present". If you keep it, you must write it as: transferred from E. hardwickii (Smith 1935 p. 126), where the postmentals are only "usually" in midline contact; unverified for E. macularius.

ALSO DROP: "large" as a standalone descriptor — no opened source calls the macularius mental large; Smith's size statement is relative to the adjacent labials, not absolute and not about its own length.

CORRECT A MIS-QUOTE OF PURPOSE: Anderson 1999's "chin shields usually in contact with first lower labials" is contact with the LABIALS, not between the two postmentals. Stop citing it as corroboration of midline contact.

CORRECT THE DETAIL'S PREMISE: this is not a character stated for macularius independently of hardwickii. Only Boulenger's 1885 key couplet states it for macularius directly, and Boulenger deleted it from his own 1890 key. Smith 1935 and Boulenger 1890 both deliver it by inheritance from hardwickii.

ADD THE CAVEAT: all three cited sources use a pre-split E. macularius that included material now assigned to E. angramainyu (Smith's Transcaspian/Mesopotamian range; Boulenger's Nineveh specimen) and lineages since named fuscus, montanus and pictus. Before using this character on a wild-type E. macularius sensu stricto, check it against a post-2000 redescription — which I was not able to open.

There is one distinct, enlarged row of labial scales on each jaw; counts run about 9–11 supralabials and 9–11 infralabials per side.

Eublepharis hardwickii," and it is there that the phrase "about ten upper and as many lower labials" occurs. Boulenger gives NO labial count for E. macularius anywhere.

2. Boulenger 1890, Fauna of British India, Reptilia and Batrachia (archive.org, TheFaunaOfBritishIndiaReptiliaAndBatrachia). Same structure: p. 107 = E. hardwickii, "about 10 upper and as many lower labials." p. 108 = E. macularius, again purely differential, no labial count.

3. Smith 1935, Fauna of British India, Reptilia and Amphibia vol. II — Sauria (archive.org, in.ernet.dli.2015.62460). Page 126 is "86. Eublepharis hardwickii," and that account contains "9 or 10 upper and as many lower labials." E. macularius is species 87, beginning p. 127, described as "Closely allied to E. hardwickii, differing in the following particulars" — enlarged dorsal tubercles, 9–14 preanal pores, colour. No labial count is given for E. macularius.

So the two page numbers in the claim (Boulenger 1885 p. 231; Smith 1935 p. 126) are precisely the hardwickii pages. In each work macularius starts on the very next page and is given no labial data at all.

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION of that misattribution: Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 (Evolutionary Systematics 6: 77–88, doi 10.3897/evolsyst.6.83290, PDF opened) list in their synonymy of Eublepharis hardwickii: "Boulenger 1885: 231 (in part); Boulenger 1890: 107 (in part); Smith 1935: 126 (in part)." Those exact three page citations are formally assigned to hardwickii by a modern redescription. Two independent lines of evidence, per the standing rule.

4. Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022 gives labial counts only for E. pictus and E. hardwickii; its data table has no E. macularius column, and its diagnosis against E. macularius uses dorsal scalation and banding, never labials.

5. Mirza 2024 (Taprobanica 13(1): 9–15, doi 10.47605/tapro.v13i1.318, PDF opened) gives labials only for E. madarensis: Sup 9&10 and 10&10; Inf 11&10 and 9&9. No E. macularius counts.

6. Rawat et al. 2019 (Reptiles & Amphibians 26(1): 58–61, PDF opened, Table 1 read). This is the ONE source that attaches labial counts to an animal called E. macularius, and the quoted values are accurate: SL 10 and 9, IL 10 and 9, SVL 119 and 109 mm, two males, Kamdi Biological Corridor, Banke District.

CONSEQUENCES: (a) "Four sources, one of them measured" collapses to one source, n=2. That breaches the one-source rule. (b) The range is wrong. Only 9 and 10 are attested for E. macularius in anything I opened. The value 11 is unattested for the species and appears to have been imported from congeners (E. pictus SL 11, E. hardwickii IL 11, E. madarensis IL 11). (c) Counting convention is unstated and it matters. Mirza's protocol counts supralabials two ways — to mid-orbit and to the angle of the jaw — giving 11/9 vs 12 in the same hardwickii holotype. Rawat et al. report a bare "SL"/"IL" without saying which. A flat "9–11" is method-ambiguous. (d) Identification security of the sole source is weak. Rawat et al. captured, measured and RELEASED both animals: no voucher specimen, no tissue, no genetics. They identified against only the three Indian congeners recognised in 2019 (E. satpuraensis, E. fuscus, E. hardwickii). E. pictus (2022) and E. madarensis (2024) were described afterwards, and Agarwal et al. 2022 recovered unnamed lineages inside the E. macularius clade (E. sp. Himalayas / E. cf. afghanicus, E. sp. Pakistan). Critically, Rawat et al. cite Delhi as the nearest previously documented locality — and Delhi is the type locality of E. macularius smithi Börner 1981, which Mirza 2024 refers to E. madarensis. The Nepal animals' assignment to E. macularius sensu stricto is therefore not secure.

CONGENER FIGURES IN THE DETAIL — CHECKED: E. hardwickii 11/9 supralabials, 12 to jaw angle, 9 infralabials — CORRECT (hardwickii holotype NHMUK 1946.8.26.67, Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022). E. pictus 10 supralabials, 11/10 infralabials — CORRECT (pictus holotype NCBS NRC-AA-0015, same paper). E. madarensis "10/11 SL, 10 IL" — GARBLED; actual is Sup 9&10 / Inf 11&10 (SMF 60980) and Sup 10&10 / Inf 9&9 (SMF 60979).

FIRST SENTENCE, separately: the existence of one discrete supralabial and one discrete infralabial row is consistent with every description I opened (all treat them as countable discrete rows; Smith describes the mental as "twice as broad as the adjacent labials"), but I opened no source that states this for E. macularius specifically, nor that calls the labials "enlarged" in that species. Unverified as worded.

CAPTIVE-STOCK CHECK, as requested: the claim is not built on a morph, but note that Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022's sequence table includes captive-line animals in this complex — "Eublepharis sp. Himalaya German line" and "Eublepharis sp. Himalaya female, Germany bloodline" — so reference data for "leopard gecko" in this literature is not uniformly wild-caught. Flagged, not load-bearing here.

COULD NOT VERIFY: any E. macularius labial count from a vouchered, genetically confirmed specimen. Mirza et al. 2014 (Phyllomedusa 13: 75–90), which may hold comparative E. macularius scalation, I could not obtain — the Phyllomedusa server returned nothing and my web-search budget was exhausted. I have not opened it and do not cite it. Confidence in that gap: unverified. - correction: Corrected statement, restricted to what an opened source actually supports for E. macularius:

"Eublepharis macularius has a discrete row of supralabial and a discrete row of infralabial scales on each side, as in its congeners. Hard counts attributable to E. macularius are extremely sparse: the only ones I could locate are from Rawat et al. (2019, Table 1), two adult males from the Kamdi Biological Corridor, Banke District, Nepal — SL 10 and 9, IL 10 and 9 (SVL 119 and 109 mm). On that basis the attested range is 9–10, not 9–11, from a sample of two. The counting convention (to mid-orbit vs. to the angle of the jaw) is not stated in that source and materially affects the number. CONFIDENCE: low/unverified — single source, n=2, no voucher specimens (both animals were released), no tissue or genetic confirmation, and the identification was made against only the three Indian congeners recognised in 2019, before E. pictus (Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022) and E. madarensis (Mirza 2024) were described. Delhi, the nearest locality Rawat et al. cite for the species, is now referred to E. madarensis."

Do NOT cite Boulenger (1885 p. 231), Boulenger (1890 p. 107) or Smith (1935 p. 126) for E. macularius labials. Those pages are the E. hardwickii accounts — a congener in the sister clade to the E. macularius clade (Mirza 2024, Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022), i.e. a different species group, not a close population variant. In all three works E. macularius is described only differentially against hardwickii (tubercle size, 9–14 preanal pores, colour pattern) and is given no labial count whatsoever. If the 9–10/"about ten" figure is used at all, it must be labelled as E. hardwickii data transferred from a congener, with that transfer stated explicitly.

The adult dorsal ground colour is a pale, desaturated yellow at its most saturated, and in many wild animals is much paler — cream, greyish-white, pale yellow-green or pinkish-lilac.

-- SOURCES I ACTUALLY OPENED (full OCR text downloaded and read, not summaries):

1. Günther 1864, Ann. Mag. Nat. Hist. (3) 14: 429-430 — archive.org item dli.ernet.24635 ("The Annals And Magazine Of Natural History Vol-xiv"). The identifier the claimant gave is correct and the article is real. BUT: it is titled "Description of a new Species of Eublepharis" and the taxon described is Eublepharis fasciolatus Günther, 1864, type locality Hyderabad, Sindh, based on TWO specimens (one adult ~5.5 in, one young ~3 in) sent by R. T. Riddell. It is not a description of E. macularius; it is a name later synonymised with it (confirmed in Boulenger 1885: 232 and Smith 1935: 127, both opened). The claimant presents it as "describing wild Sindh material" without disclosing it is a synonym/subspecies name and a two-specimen museum lot. The phrase "brownish yellow" appears in the paragraph on the YOUNG ("These bands and rings are broader than the interspaces of the ground-colour, which is brownish yellow"); the adult paragraph only says "the space between the bars being of the ground-colour", carrying the juvenile term over by reference. So the transfer to adults is defensible but implicit — and "brownish yellow" is a warm, brown-tinged yellow. It does NOT support "pale, desaturated yellow at its most saturated", and it supports none of "cream, greyish-white, pale yellow-green or pinkish-lilac". This source cuts against the claim.

2. Boulenger 1885, Cat. Lizards Brit. Mus. vol. 1: 232 — archive.org catalogueoflizar01brituoft. The quoted wording is accurate: "In the adult these bands become more indistinct, and the head and body become spotted or largely vermiculated with chestnut-brown and whitish". Two problems. (a) Boulenger gives no ground colour for the adult at all — "whitish" is the colour of the pale element of a vermiculated pattern, not a stated ground colour, and for the young he says the interspaces are "whitish" where Günther, from the same Sindh series, called them brownish yellow. The two sources disagree about the same population, which the claim does not disclose. (b) This is a catalogue of spirit-preserved British Museum specimens (the accession list on the same page reads "e-f. male & young. Hydrabad, Sind"). A preserved-specimen colour note is not evidence of colour in life. [The specific mechanism — loss of yellow pigment in alcohol — I did not verify from a source I opened; treat that as unverified reasoning, not a cited fact.]

3. Smith 1935, Fauna Brit. India, Reptilia & Amphibia II Sauria: 127-128 — archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.207328. Quoted accurately: "The young are light brown or yellowish or pinkish above..." and "the centres of the dorsal bands fade, leaving only their edges or a series of spots". Critically, Smith's colour words are explicitly about THE YOUNG. His adult text gives no ground colour whatever — only that markings break up, and that one Khandesh specimen had "a broad, pale, median interspace" from coalesced bars. So Smith cannot be cited for an adult ground colour, and "pinkish" is a juvenile descriptor being promoted to adults.

NET ON LITERATURE: none of the three sources states an adult dorsal ground colour. The claim's "three literature sources agree" is not true — it rests on juvenile descriptions transferred to adults, on preserved museum material, and on two sources (Günther "brownish yellow" vs Boulenger "whitish") that actually disagree.

PHOTOGRAPHS (iNaturalist API records opened, and the full-size images downloaded and viewed): All four observations exist, are Research Grade, flagged not-captive, identified E. macularius, and the localities match what was claimed (387949230 Jhampir PK; 361924223 Harsh, Sikar dist., Rajasthan; 271474107 Birhu Kalan, Una, Himachal Pradesh; 287027399 Kirthar PK). That much checks out. The inferences drawn from them do not:

- MISCOUNT / PSEUDOREPLICATION. 287027399 is ONE observation containing four photos (516066042, 516066087, 516066128, 516066161) of plainly the SAME individual — same pale animal, same regenerate-looking tail, same session. The claim counts it as "three Kirthar, Sindh animals". Likewise 387949230 is one observation with two photos of one animal, counted as "two adults, Jhampir". The four cited records document at most FOUR individuals, not the seven implied, and cannot support "in many wild animals". - THE "PALE YELLOW-GREEN (RAJASTHAN ADULT)" IS A ROADKILL. Photo 660548306 (obs. 361924223) shows a dead, flattened, tail-detached animal on tarmac being dismembered by ants. Its yellow-green cast is a post-mortem/desiccation artefact. It is not evidence of living ground colour at all. This is the single most serious defect in the claim. - THE "NEAR-WHITE PINKISH-LILAC" IS A FLASH ARTEFACT. The Kirthar frames are close-range direct-flash night shots over pale grey limestone gravel. In the same frames the animal's head renders blue-grey — leopard geckos do not have blue heads, so the frames carry an obvious colour cast. The animal also looks chalky and opaque, consistent with pre-shed condition [pre-shed diagnosis is my inference from the image, unverified]. Either way, one flash-lit individual does not establish a lilac wild ground colour. - THE "PALE CREAM (HIMACHAL ADULT)" IS NOT CREAM AND MAY NOT BE ADULT. Photo 488325279 shows distinct, moderately saturated yellow blotches along the nape and dorsum on a whitish ground, and the animal still carries broad juvenile band structure.

DIRECT COUNTER-EVIDENCE, SAME EVIDENCE CLASS. I pulled 30 further wild, Research Grade, non-captive E. macularius records from the same region (iNat API, bbox 23-37N / 60-80E) and viewed a sample. Photo 480077493 shows a deeply saturated egg-yolk yellow band ground, well beyond "pale, desaturated"; 504771252 shows bright yellow banding; and the claimant's own Jhampir animal (712990681) is a fairly strong mustard/ochre, not a pale wash. The stated ceiling does not survive. Caveat: 480077493 and 504771252 are juveniles/subadults, so they refute the ceiling for the species but not, on their own, for adults.

ON THE SPECIFIC CHECKS ASKED FOR. Species confusion: the cited photo records are Research Grade E. macularius and I found no evidence they are another Eublepharis; whether the Indian records could be E. fuscus or another congener I could not verify (Smith 1935 does not recognise fuscus) — unverified. Morph confusion: the risk runs opposite to the claimant's assumption. "Pinkish-lilac" and "greyish-white" are the vocabulary of captive lines (lavender/snow/blizzard); in the cited material those appearances trace to one flash-lit animal and one corpse, not to documented wild-type variation. The claimant is right that wild animals do not look like selectively bred "high yellow" stock, but has over-corrected into an equally unsupported pale/desaturated ceiling.

COULD NOT VERIFY: any adult ground-colour statement in the three cited works (there is none); pre-shed status of the Kirthar animal; pigment loss in spirit as the explanation for Boulenger's "whitish"; species identity of the Indian records beyond community ID; the existence of the 8 further photographs implied by "12 photographs" (only 4 observations totalling 8 photos were cited). - correction: Supported version, restricted to what the opened sources actually say: "No adult dorsal ground colour is given for E. macularius in Günther (1864), Boulenger (1885) or Smith (1935). Günther and Boulenger disagree on the pale element from the same Sindh material. Confidence: the literature wording is verified from the original texts; the range of living colour is based on a small photographic sample and should be treated as provisional."

The ground colour is not uniform over the animal: the trunk carries the yellow, while head, lower flanks and tail are markedly paler and whiter.

-- REFUTED as stated, on the claimant's own evidence. I opened both iNaturalist records via the API, downloaded the full-size photos and measured them, and opened the PNAS paper. Species/morph confusion is NOT the failure mode here — both observations are Research Grade E. macularius with agreeing IDs (obs 387949230, Jhampir, Sindh, 2026-08-03, 2 agreeing IDs, 2 photos that show two different individuals — different spot architecture; obs 271474107, Birhu Kalan, Una, Himachal Pradesh, 2025-04-19, 5 agreeing IDs, 1 photo). The claim fails on four other grounds.

(1) "MARKEDLY PALER" IS FALSE — the head is never lighter than the trunk. I sampled the pale interspot ground (pixels above regional median luminance, excluding the dark blotches) and converted to CIELAB. Jhampir animal B: head L*=54.2 vs trunk L*=54.2 (identical); Jhampir animal A: crown L*=81.2 vs trunk L*=88.0 (head DARKER); Himachal: head L*=66.9 vs trunk L*=75.7 (head DARKER). Distal tail likewise equal or darker (Jhampir B 46.6, Himachal 61.3, both below their trunks). What actually differs between regions is yellowness, not lightness: b* head 3.1 / 12.3 / 8.6 vs trunk 9.3 / 31.1 / 23.7. So the observation being reported is "less yellow on the head", and the claim has relabelled that as "paler and whiter", which is a different and measurably wrong statement. Caveat: these are flash photographs at night, not photometry — but the direction of the lightness result is consistent across all three animals and two cameras.

(2) "THE WHOLE TAIL" IS FALSE — the tail base carries yellow. Jhampir animal B: tail base b*=7.9 against a trunk of 9.3, i.e. essentially as yellow as the trunk, while only the distal tail drops to 4.2. Himachal: tail b*=17.0 against trunk 23.7 — yellow-tinged, not "cream-white to pale grey". Jhampir animal A has visibly yellow tubercles on the tail base. The yellow/white transition on the tail is proximodistal, not a head-trunk-tail partition.

(3) THE LIMBS BREAK THE PARTITION. The claim's architecture (trunk = yellow, everything else = pale) omits the limbs, which are the most yellow parts of two of the three animals: Jhampir A hindlimb b*=31.4 vs trunk 31.1; Himachal hind foot b*=28.2 vs trunk 23.7 (i.e. yellower than the trunk). "The trunk carries the yellow" is not a correct description of where the yellow sits.

(4) THE HIMACHAL ANIMAL IS MIS-DESCRIBED. Zoomed, its dorsal ground is white/cream, the same white as its head, flanks and tail; the yellow is not a trunk ground colour at all but discrete bright-yellow patches forming a broken reticulum around the dark blotches, plus yellow on the nape, forelimb and hind foot. Calling the head "markedly paler and whiter than the trunk" is circular there — the trunk ground IS white; the head merely carries denser dark reticulation, which is why it measures darker.

(5) THE MECHANISTIC BASIS DOES NOT SAY WHAT THE CLAIM SAYS IT SAYS. Opened: Ullate-Agote & Tzika 2024, "The dynamic behavior of chromatophores marks the transition from bands to spots in leopard geckos", PNAS, PMC11260152 (note: two authors, not "et al."). The first half of the transfer is accurate — the paper does describe the hatchling as a white head band, then a black band over the shoulder blades, then alternating yellow and black bands to the tail base, with white and black bands on the tail; the yellow body bands as xanthophore-rich with a few contracted melanophores and deeper iridophores; the white head band as a dense full-depth iridophore network with dense collagen. But: (a) it describes ONE transverse white band on the head, not a white head. The rest of the hatchling head is dark. I checked this against wild animals: iNat 29623825 (Jaipur, 23 agreeing IDs) and 267159284 (D.I. Khan, Pakistan) both show a chocolate-black head bearing a single pale occipital/nuchal band — and in the D.I. Khan animal the snout, jaw and limbs are bright yellow-orange. So the head carries yellow even at the banded stage. (b) The paper nowhere states that xanthophores are absent from head or tail skin — it reports iridophore density in the white band, which is not the same claim. (c) The paper nowhere describes adult head or adult tail colour. The word "never" in the claim is the claimant's extrapolation, not the paper's finding. (d) The paper's central result actively undercuts the extrapolation: all bands fade during the first year and are replaced by spots, iridophores gradually perish in adult dermis while xanthophores persist — so hatchling band identity cannot be carried forward as a fixed adult topography, and if anything the paper predicts the iridophore-white zones become LESS white with age. (e) Provenance: the animals were housed and bred at the LANE facility (Univ. Geneva); "wild-type" there means normal-morph captive stock in contrast to the Mack Super Snow PAX7 mutant, NOT wild-caught. No wild populations and no geographic variation were examined. A captive research colony cannot underwrite a statement about wild adults in Sindh or Himachal Pradesh.

(6) SAMPLE. "Every yellow-ground wild adult I looked at" is three photographs of three individuals from two localities, one of which (Himachal) is not a yellow-ground animal by its own appearance. Wild E. macularius ground colour is highly variable: of the Research Grade records I opened, a Pakistani adult (obs 54390450, 18 agreeing IDs) is grey-lavender with no yellow at all, and a Karachi/Sindh juvenile (obs 235312839) is white-lavender with purple-grey bands and no yellow anywhere.

Punjab and Jammu, Nepal; type locality Salt Range, Punjab — but no head/body/tail colour description, so it neither supports nor refutes); iNat obs 29623825, 267159284, 54390450, 235312839, 18537233 (photos examined directly).

COULD NOT VERIFY / UNVERIFIED: (a) I found no herpetological field guide, museum specimen description or taxonomic redescription that gives a regionalised colour account of E. macularius (head vs trunk vs tail). The Reptile Database account carries none. So the claim's core proposition has, as far as I could open, ZERO corroboration in descriptive taxonomic literature in either direction — it rests entirely on photographs. (b) Whether the Jhampir animals are of wild origin rather than escaped/released captive stock: the observer flagged them not-captive and the community accepted it, but Pakistan is a source country for the leopard gecko trade and I cannot verify origin from an observation record. (c) I did not verify the PNAS volume/issue/page (121(29): e2400486121) independently of the claimant. (d) Side caution, unverified: several Research Grade "E. macularius" records in the same iNat result set come from Maharashtra and Gujarat, which fall within the ranges of E. fuscus / E. satpuraensis; I did not check those IDs against a taxonomic revision, so iNat IDs should not be treated as taxonomic authority for colour claims generally. This does not affect the two Sindh/Himachal records at issue. - correction: A defensible replacement, confidence "moderate for the yellow gradient, unverified for anything beyond these photographs": In wild E. macularius that carry yellow, the yellow is not spread evenly and is not confined to the trunk either. It is strongest on the dorsum of the trunk, the limbs and the tail base, weaker on the head, and weakest on the distal tail; the ventrolateral zone and venter are pale cream to lavender-white (ordinary countershading). Measured on three wild adults from Sindh and Himachal Pradesh, head and distal tail are LESS YELLOW than the trunk (CIELAB b* roughly 3-12 vs 9-31) but are NOT lighter — they are equal in lightness or darker, because the head carries denser dark reticulation. The limbs are as yellow as the trunk or yellower, so "the trunk carries the yellow" is wrong as a partition. Ground colour itself varies enormously between individuals: some wild animals have a white or grey-lavender ground with the yellow present only as discrete patches surrounding the dark blotches, and some have no yellow at all. Do NOT cite Ullate-Agote & Tzika 2024 (PNAS, PMC11260152) as a mechanism for adult regional colour: that study describes a single transverse white band on the head of hatchlings (the head itself is dark), does not describe adult head or tail colour, does not report absence of xanthophores from head or tail, used a captive-bred research colony where "wild-type" means normal-morph rather than wild-caught, and its main finding — bands fade entirely within the first year while iridophores perish and xanthophores persist — argues against reading adult topography off the hatchling band map.

The adult spotted pattern is the broken-up remains of the juvenile banded pattern; the spots are not a separate pattern laid on top.
