It does NOT say "in place". The claim's added words "in place" are not in the paper. - Spots also arise in the former LIGHT interbands, not only where black bands were: "The black spots in the white and yellow bands can form in three different ways: i) the migration of melanophores, ii) the proliferation of existing melanophores, or iii) the expansion of existing melanophores"; "melanophore division and state transition are the main drivers of black spots formation on the white and yellow bands." Their Fig. 3C time-lapse marks "a region where no melanophores are visible at week 0 and gradually appear and expand in 12 wk." - Spots form with no band precursor at all: on the regenerated tail, "melanophores directly form black spots as in the adult dorsal skin, rather than yellow and black bands as seen in hatchlings", and "spots form even on the regenerated tail of juveniles, despite the presence of bands on their body"; and in the Mack Super Snow morph, which hatches uniformly black (no bands) and still develops adult spots. Their conclusion: "black spot formation is an intrinsic capacity of melanophores in the postembryonic skin." So the correct picture is two concurrent processes — band fading (iridophore loss, melanophore contraction) plus spot formation from melanophores that are already dispersed through the whole skin — not fragmentation of one pattern into another. Only the within-old-black-band spots fit the claim ("black spots form as the melanophores in the surrounding areas contract"); the interband spots do not.

"FOUR INDEPENDENT SOURCES" IS FALSE. Günther 1864 is the original description of Eublepharis fasciolatus, a nominal taxon later sunk into E. macularius (Reptile Database entry opened, local file rdb_emac.txt: "Eublepharis fasciolatus GÜNTHER 1864: 429 (fide SMITH 1935)"; types BMNH 1946.8.26.65-66, "Hydrabad, Sind... donor R T. Riddell"). Boulenger 1885: 232 lists fasciolatus in the synonymy and his specimen series includes "e-f. male & young. Hydrabad, Sind" — i.e. Günther's two types. Boulenger's "in some only the brown edges of the dorsal bands remain" is therefore, at least in part, a re-description of the same adult specimen Günther described. Smith 1935 cites both Boulenger and Günther. Historical evidence collapses to roughly one museum series (plus a Khandesh specimen Smith adds); genuinely independent lines of evidence are about two, not four.

SPECIES-CONFUSION CHECK: not a different species in the fatal sense — fasciolatus is a synonym/subspecies of E. macularius. But Boulenger's and Smith's macularius concept was broader than the current one: Boulenger p. 232 gives the range as "North-western India, probably ranging through Baluchistan and Persia to the Euphrates" and footnotes a Paris Museum specimen from Nineveh; Smith p. 128 gives "NW India to S Transcaspia and Mesopotamia" and a Persian BM specimen. Moradi & Shafiei 2011 (Amphib. Reptile Conserv. 5(4):88-91, opened, local file arc_angramainyu.txt) place E. angramainyu Anderson & Leviton 1966 in the Tigris–Euphrates basin of Iran and Iraq — a species described long after both works. Whether Boulenger's Nineveh / Smith's Persian and Mesopotamian material is E. macularius as now defined is UNVERIFIED by me; their colour-pattern generalisations may pool more than one taxon. The Sindh and Punjab material central to this claim is within current E. macularius.

MORPH CHECK: the PNAS work is entirely captive stock (Methods: animals housed and bred at the LANE facility, Geneva, cantonal permit 1008) — no wild-caught Pakistani/Afghan animals. The wild-type time-lapse used normal-patterned (+/+) captive-bred juveniles, so that part is wild-type phenotype; but the strongest "spots need no bands" evidence comes from Mack Super Snow, a captive-bred PAX7-deletion morph, and from regenerated tail skin. That does not invalidate the refutation (regenerated tail in ordinary wild-type animals shows the same thing), but the claim's phrase "confirm experimentally" overstates what a lab colony of captive morphs establishes for wild populations.

COULD NOT VERIFY: Whimster (PNAS's ref. 7, the 180-degree skin-graft study) — not opened; I only have PNAS's characterisation of it, which says black spots formed across graft boundaries with no melanophore migration observed. Also unverified: any field/wild-population documentation of the band-to-spot transition. Minor citation error: the PNAS paper has two authors (Ullate-Agote & Tzika), so "et al." is wrong; volume/issue/e-number given are correct (2024 Jul 8 online, 121(29): e2400486121). - correction: Corrected version that the opened sources support: "In E. macularius the juvenile transverse bands fade with age, and in partly transformed animals the band centres fade while the dark band margins persist, so that some adult dark markings are genuinely band remnants — Günther (1864: 430) describes an adult from Hyderabad, Sindh (the type of his E. fasciolatus, now a synonym of E. macularius) retaining one pair of brown cross bars on the neck and three pairs on the trunk; Boulenger (1885: 232) and Smith (1935: 128) repeat this, Smith adding 'a series of spots corresponding to them'. Note that these three accounts are not independent: Boulenger's Sindh specimens are Günther's types and Smith follows both. However, the adult spotted pattern as a whole is NOT simply the fragmented band pattern. Ullate-Agote & Tzika (2024, PNAS 121(29): e2400486121) show that black spots also form in the former white and yellow interbands, by expansion and proliferation of melanophores that are already present throughout the hatchling skin in a contracted state, and that melanophores form spots with no banded precursor at all — on regenerated tail skin (including in still-banded juveniles) and in the bandless Mack Super Snow morph. Band fading and spot formation are two concurrent processes; spot formation is an intrinsic capacity of postembryonic melanophores, not a by-product of bands breaking up."

Adult spots are dark brown / chestnut-brown rather than jet black.

-- The four quoted sources are accurately quoted — I opened all of them — but the inference they are used to support is refuted by a fifth source the claim omits, and the "three independent historical sources" framing is wrong.

VERIFIED, source by source (all opened as full text, not abstracts): 1. Boulenger 1885, Cat. Lizards Brit. Mus. 2nd ed. vol. I, p. 232 (Internet Archive scan catalogueoflizar01brituoft). Exactly as claimed: young with five chestnut-brown transverse bands; in the adult the bands become indistinct and head and body become spotted or vermiculated with chestnut-brown and whitish, in some only the brown band-edges remaining. CONFIRMED. 2. Günther 1864, pp. 429-430. CONFIRMED, but the citation needs correcting: this is Ann. Mag. Nat. Hist. ser. 3, vol. 14, "Description of a new Species of Eublepharis" (E. fasciolatus), NOT Günther's 1864 Reptiles of British India, where the Eublepharis account sits around p. 110-119. Günther's adult: only the brown edges of the bands remain; ground colour brownish yellow. No "black" anywhere. 3. Smith 1935, Fauna Brit. India, Sauria, pp. 127-128. CONFIRMED: young with broad dark brown cross-bars and sometimes intervening dark brown spots; with age the band centres fade, leaving edges or a series of spots. Smith gives no colour word at all for the adult spots — the claim represents this correctly. 4. Ullate-Agote et al. 2024, PNAS 121(29):e2400486121, "The dynamic behavior of chromatophores marks the transition from bands to spots in leopard geckos" (read via PMC full text). CONFIRMED: "black spots" used consistently for adults of their captive colony. 5. iNaturalist 387949230 (Jhampir, Sindh, Pakistan, 2026-08-03) and 271474107 (Una, Himachal Pradesh, 2025-04-19), checked through the iNat API: both research-grade, both flagged not captive, both E. macularius. I also viewed wild Sindh/Kirthar photos: spots read dark brown to blackish-brown, not flat black — but a flash photo's white balance is weak evidence for a colour claim.

WHAT REFUTES THE INFERENCE: (a) Blyth 1854, J. Asiat. Soc. Beng. 23: 738 — the ORIGINAL description of the species, from wild Salt Range (Punjab) material collected by Theobald, decades before any captive stock existed — describes the animal in black throughout: black crown, broad black band across the nape, black tail tip, black tubercles, and, for the very transition the claim is about, "the interior of the black bands is pale and speckled with black, the margins continuing black", with the dark hue expected to disappear from the band interiors with age. So the earliest wild-material source describes the persisting adult marks as black. The claim's key move — "three historical sources on wild material agree on brown" — fails: the first and most directly wild-derived source says black. (b) The three brown sources are not independent. Boulenger's specimen list on p. 232 includes entries e-f from Hyderabad, Sind, presented by R. T. Riddell, marked as the types of E. fasciolatus — i.e. Boulenger re-described Günther's own two specimens. Boulenger 1890 (Fauna Brit. India, p. 108, also opened) repeats his 1885 wording almost verbatim. Smith 1935 defines macularius by difference from hardwickii following Boulenger and cites him. This is one British Museum descriptive lineage, not three observations. (c) All three brown sources describe spirit-preserved museum specimens, where melanin-based black commonly reads brown and ground colour fades. Günther's own "brownish yellow" ground colour is the tell — Blyth's collector reported the living animal as strikingly rosy-carneous. Preservation state, not wild-vs-captive origin, is the more parsimonious explanation of "chestnut-brown". (d) The brown/black split does not track adults or captivity. Ullate-Agote et al. call the HATCHLING bands black, where Günther/Boulenger/Smith call the juvenile bands brown. The terminological difference runs through the whole ontogeny, so it cannot be attributed to adult captive stock. (e) Neither side of the contrast measures anything. Ullate-Agote's "wild-type" is a lab line of unstated wild provenance in a colony maintained alongside the Mack Super Snow morph, so their "black" is not a wild-animal observation either.

SPECIES-CONFUSION CHECK (asked for explicitly): the historical macularius is a broader composite than today's. Boulenger's footnote on p. 232 covers a Paris Museum specimen from Nineveh, Iraq — that is E. angramainyu, not described until 1966. Smith's range runs to southern Transcaspia and Mesopotamia (now E. turcmenicus and E. angramainyu), and the one adult he describes in detail is from Khandesh, Bombay Presidency, in the region now occupied by E. fuscus / E. satpuraensis-grade lineages. Of the two iNat records, 271474107 is from Una, Himachal Pradesh, in the north-Indian foothill area where recent phylogenies (Mirza; Agarwal et al.) carry an unnamed "Eublepharis sp. Himalaya" lineage inside the macularius clade; it is a community-ID photo record, not a voucher, so its identity to species is not secure. The Jhampir, Sindh record is in the core range and is safe. No captive-morph confusion detected in the claim itself — the claim correctly flags Ullate-Agote's animals as a captive colony.

COULD NOT VERIFY: no source I opened reports an actual colour measurement (reflectance, standardised photography, or fresh-specimen colour chart) of wild adult spots; whether the Ullate-Agote lab line has documented wild provenance; and whether the Himachal Pradesh animal is true E. macularius. Any statement about the spots' true hue in life is therefore unverified. - correction: Weaker, defensible version: "Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century descriptions based on spirit-preserved museum specimens call the adult marks chestnut-brown or brown (Boulenger 1885: 232, repeated in Boulenger 1890: 108; Günther 1864, Ann. Mag. Nat. Hist. ser. 3, 14: 429-430, as E. fasciolatus; Smith 1935: 127-128, of the juvenile bars). These are not independent: Boulenger re-described Günther's fasciolatus types and Smith follows Boulenger, and preserved melanin commonly reads brown. Blyth's original description of wild Salt Range material (1854: 738) calls the same bands and their persisting margins black. Modern work on a captive colony (Ullate-Agote et al. 2024) uses 'black spots' for adults and 'black bands' for hatchlings alike. In wild animals I examined, the spots were a warm dark umber to blackish-brown with soft edges rather than a flat black — but that is a field impression, uncorroborated, and the brown/black difference in the literature tracks author and preservation state, not wild versus captive stock." Also fix the citation: Günther 1864: 429-430 is Annals and Magazine of Natural History ser. 3 vol. 14, not The Reptiles of British India. Drop the claim that jet-black spotting is a captive-stock impression; it is refuted by Blyth 1854 and is not supported by anything I could open. Confidence: the quotations are confirmed; the hue conclusion is unverified.

Spots are irregular rounded-to-oval blobs and short bars of variable size, several tubercles across, largest on the trunk and clearly bigger than a single tubercle.

-- PARTLY SUPPORTED, BUT FALSE AS STATED — it describes one point in a documented range as if it were the species pattern, and its tubercle-scale content is in no source.

WHAT I OPENED (all read directly, not summarised from memory): 1. Ullate-Agote A. & Tzika A.C. 2024, PNAS 121(29):e2400486121, "The dynamic behavior of chromatophores marks the transition from bands to spots in leopard geckos" — full text read (PMC11260152; I grepped the article text myself, not just an abstract). source_opened = true. 2. iNaturalist obs. 387949230 (api.inaturalist.org) plus both photos (712990630, 712990681) downloaded and re-magnified by me at 4x and 8x. source_opened = true. 3. Boulenger G.A. 1885, Catalogue of the Lizards in the British Museum vol. 1: 232 (E. macularius account, museum specimens). source_opened = true. 4. Minton S.A. 1966, Herpetology of West Pakistan, Bull. AMNH 134, E. macularius account. source_opened = true. 5. Mirza et al. 2022 (E. pictus description; tubercle-row definition, Sindh sequence). source_opened = true.

A. CITATION ERROR. "Ullate-Agote et al. (2024)" is a TWO-author paper: Ullate-Agote & Tzika. Cite it as such.

B. THE PAPER SUPPORTS ONLY THE FIRST CLAUSE. Verified in its text: "black spots of variable sizes and shapes" and "irregularly shaped black spots"; also "only black spots of variable sizes are clearly distinguishable" in adult skin. It says NOTHING about short bars, about spot size relative to tubercles, or about spots being largest on the trunk. Its one pigment-vs-tubercle sentence is EMBRYONIC: chromatophore precursors "aggregate around the developing tubercles, which are the largest scales seen on the dorsal skin" (stage 33-35 embryos, wild-type and Mack Super Snow). If anything that points toward per-tubercle registration, not away from it. Its spot-area measurement is four wild-type plus four MSS animals via Fiji "Analyse particles", with no absolute values in the main text (SI Fig. S10) — so there is no published size number to check the claim's fractions against.

C. PROVENANCE CAVEAT (this is the morph-vs-wild-type trap, and the claim half-falls into it). Every animal in the PNAS paper was captive-bred at the LANE facility under Swiss permits (experimentation permit GE24/33145). "Wild-type" there is the morph-trade/lab sense — the non-mutant phenotype contrasted with Mack Snow, Mack Super Snow and Super Lemon Frost — NOT a wild-caught E. macularius. So the only published prose behind the claim comes from captive lab stock; the wild anchor is a single amateur photograph.

D. THE DECISIVE REFUTATION — the pattern range is wider than the claim, from two independent primary sources I opened: - Boulenger 1885 (museum specimens): in the adult the juvenile bands become indistinct and "the head and body become spotted or largely vermiculated"; in some individuals only the brown edges of the dorsal bands remain. - Minton 1966 (West Pakistan, including Sindh material; the synonym E. fasciolatus Günther 1864 has type locality Hyderabad, Sind): adult dorsum straw yellow to pale violaceous grey, "usually showing trace of juvenile bands", with blue-black spots "in some cases discrete and sparse, in others fusing into a reticulum". So wild adults run sparse-discrete-spots -> blobby -> vermiculate/reticulate, and commonly retain a trace of juvenile banding. Rounded-to-oval blobs and short bars are one end of that continuum, not the description.

E. THE CITED PHOTO REFUTES ITS OWN GENERALISATION. On the same Jhampir animal, magnified myself: the trunk does show irregular blobs and some short merged bars (their own counts — roughly 4-6 per transverse rank, ~10-15 ranks between limbs, typical marks about a sixth to a fifth of visible trunk width — are in the right ballpark, though I read typical marks slightly larger than their eighth-to-sixth). BUT the head and nape of the same individual are plainly VERMICULATE: narrow curved, C-shaped and ring-like strands forming a labyrinth, roughly one to two tubercles wide — exactly Boulenger's "largely vermiculated". And at 8x on the flank, a substantial share of the dark marks are single-tubercle-sized dots the same size and bead shape as the neighbouring pale tubercles. So "clearly bigger than a single tubercle" fails inside the very animal cited, and "blobs and short bars" mis-describes its head. (Those two readings are my own observations from one photograph, magnified by me — unverified against any publication.)

F. TUBERCLE-SCALE CONTENT IS UNVERIFIED EVERYWHERE. No source I opened states spot width in tubercles. The only published anchor for tubercle spacing is Boulenger 1885: in E. macularius the tubercles are smaller and less numerous than in E. hardwickii, "the granular interspaces being as wide as the tubercles themselves". Minton 1966 adds that the dorsal tubercles are conical and "irregularly arranged on body" (in annuli only on the tail) — so there is no regular tubercle grid on the trunk to count spots against in the first place. My own 8x measurement of the cited photo puts the LARGEST trunk blotches at roughly 3-5 tubercles across; confidence: unverified, one photograph, one individual, hand-held curved posture, phone optics.

G. SPECIES/MORPH CONFUSION CHECK — no confusion found, with one caveat. Jhampir (Thatta district, lower Sindh, 25.024 N 68.009 E) is inside the E. macularius range: Minton 1966 treats E. fasciolatus (type locality Hyderabad, Sind) as a synonym of E. macularius, and Mirza et al. 2022 sequenced an E. macularius from Pakistan, Sindh, Dadu. The iNat record is wild (captive flag false), and the animal shows a wild-type phenotype with an unregenerated, whorled, banded-spotted tail — nothing suggesting a released captive morph. Caveat: research grade rests on two community IDs (observer ameer12372 + supporter danielb138), no voucher and no genetics, and the E. macularius clade in Mirza et al. 2022 contains poorly supported lineages including an undescribed "Eublepharis sp. Pakistan" (from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, not Sindh).

COULD NOT VERIFY: any published statement that trunk spots are the largest on the body; any published spot-size measurement in absolute units or in tubercles; any published description of "short bars" in adults. - correction: Use this instead: "In adult E. macularius the juvenile bands break up and the dorsum carries dark brown to blue-black markings of variable size and irregular shape (Ullate-Agote & Tzika 2024, on captive-bred laboratory 'wild-type' animals: 'black spots of variable sizes and shapes'). Across wild adults the pattern spans a documented range rather than one geometry: from discrete, sparse spots, through irregular rounded-to-oval blotches and short coalesced bars, to markings 'largely vermiculated' (Boulenger 1885) or 'fusing into a reticulum' (Minton 1966), with a trace of the juvenile bands usually still visible (Minton 1966). Vermiculate/reticulate markings are typical of the head and nape even in individuals whose trunk is blotchy. On the trunk of a well-spotted individual, the larger blotches are several tubercles across and much larger than a single tubercle, but the same animal also carries dark marks only one tubercle wide, and E. macularius tubercles are irregularly arranged on the body (Minton 1966) with granular interspaces about as wide as the tubercles (Boulenger 1885), so there is no regular tubercle grid to index spots to." For a texture or generative model, sample the spotted-to-vermiculate continuum rather than a single blob rule, put vermiculation on the head/nape, and treat any blotch-size-in-tubercles figure (including 4-6 blotches per rank and 10-15 ranks) as an unpublished single-photo estimate, confidence: unverified.

Spots are solid, with NO pale halo. But a large minority of wild adults show the inverse: dark rings and vermiculations enclosing pale or yellow centres.

-- SOURCES I ACTUALLY OPENED (BHL itself was unreachable — Cloudflare bot-check; I did not attempt to bypass it, I used Internet Archive scans instead): (1) Boulenger 1885, Catalogue of the Lizards in the BM(NH), 2nd ed., Vol. I, the E. macularius account, which the OCR page-breaks confirm sits on p. 232 (running heads "232 EUBLEPHARIDAE" before it, "EUBLEPHARIS. 233" after) — archive.org item catalogueoflizar01brituoft, _djvu.txt. (2) Gunther 1864, "Description of a new Species of Eublepharis", Ann. Mag. Nat. Hist. ser. 3, vol. 14, article starting p. 429, colour description on p. 430 — archive.org item annalsmagazineof3141864lond, _djvu.txt. (3) The Reptile Database species account for E. macularius (reptile-database.reptarium.cz), for synonymy and range. (4) iNaturalist API records AND the full-size photographs for obs. 361924223, 387949230, 271474107 (all three are research-grade, captive=false, current taxon Eublepharis macularius). Files saved at C:\Users\ziyad\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-ziyad\920e259d-472d-4210-945a-591bc20b749a\scratchpad\ (inat_raj.jpg, inat_jha_a.jpg, inat_jha_b.jpg, inat_him.jpg, plus crops crop_raj_body.jpg, crop_jhab_head.jpg, crop_him_body.jpg, crop_him_head.jpg).

WHAT CHECKS OUT - The Boulenger quotation is verbatim and correctly placed. p. 232: young with five chestnut-brown transverse bands, "In the adult these bands become more indistinct, and the head and body become spotted or largely vermiculated with chestnut-brown and whitish; in some only the brown edges of the dorsal bands remain." That last clause is genuine independent support for a dark-outline / pale-interior geometry in some adults. - The Gunther phrase is verbatim: "a pair of brown rings on the crown of the head" (p. 430). - No species mix-up in the citations. Gunther's taxon is Eublepharis fasciolatus (types from Hyderabad, Sindh, coll. R. T. Riddell), which Boulenger 1885: 232 lists in the synonymy of E. macularius and which the Reptile Database carries as E. macularius fasciolatus. All three iNat animals are wild (captive=false), not captive morphs, and Rajasthan, Sindh and the Punjab/Shivalik foothills all fall inside the Reptile Database's stated range ("E Afghanistan, Pakistan, NW India (Rajasthan, Ajmer, Madar foot hills, Punjab, Jammu), Nepal"). So the pet-morph and wrong-species traps are not what breaks this.

WHY IT STILL FAILS — three separate defects 1. "A large minority" is unsupported by anything opened. Boulenger writes "spotted OR largely vermiculated" with no frequency at all; Gunther describes exactly one adult specimen; three iNaturalist photographs cannot establish a rate. This is the kind of number that has to come from a scored series of specimens, and I found none. Mark it unverified rather than stating a proportion.

2. The Gunther citation is doing work it cannot do. His "pair of brown rings" is explicitly a HEAD marking, listed among head markings ("a pair of brown rings on the crown of the head, one cross band between the eyes, and two on the snout; a longitudinal streak runs from the eye to the nostril"). His adult BODY pattern is neither spots nor rings nor vermiculation: "In the adult only the brown edges of these bands remain; so that there is one pair of brown cross bars on the neck, and three pairs on the trunk, the space between the bars being of the ground-colour." Paired transverse bars. So Gunther supplies zero evidence for pale-centred rings on the trunk, and in fact describes an adult trunk pattern that the claim's framing ("spots", solid or annular) does not cover at all.

3. Two of the three photographs do not show what the detail says they show. I examined them at up to 7x: - Rajasthan (361924223) — this one DOES support the claim: the neck and anterior/mid trunk are an extensive dark reticulum with several closed annuli enclosing yellow-green centres. Caveat worth stating: it is a road-killed, sun-dried, flattened animal on tarmac, so its colour rendition is not that of a live gecko, and the observer's own note is "not sure about the id." - Second Jhampir animal (387949230, photo 2) — REFUTED. The neck and anterior trunk are solid, discrete, round dark spots on a yellow-olive ground. The only ring-shaped figures are on the crown of the head. Calling these "dark-edged, yellow-centred rosettes over the neck and anterior trunk" is wrong. (Separately: the two photos under that one observation look like different individuals under different lighting; I could not verify either way, so "the second Jhampir adult" may not be a second verified adult.) - Himachal (271474107) — OVERSTATED. At high zoom the head, neck and anterior trunk are solid dark-brown blotches on a white ground, some partly fused. The yellow is a dorsolateral wash of ground colour lying BETWEEN the blotches, occasionally enclosed where blotches merge — yellow as interstitial ground, not a ring drawn around a pale centre. And the enclosure effect is strongest on the mid/posterior trunk and around the hindlimb, i.e. the opposite of the claim's proposed "pale-centred rings anteriorly and on the head" gradient.

4. Terminological slippage. "Vermiculated with chestnut-brown and whitish" (Boulenger) states that the two colours interdigitate in worm-like fashion; it does not state which colour encloses which, and it is not a synonym for "annuli with pale centres." The claim merges the two.

ON THE FIRST HALF ("solid, NO pale halo"): I could not refute it, but note it is only weakly established. Neither Boulenger nor Gunther mentions any pale ring or halo around the dark marks, and none of the four photographs shows one — but two 19th-century descriptions saying nothing is an argument from silence, not a positive finding. Treat "no pale halo" as consistent-with-sources, not as documented.

ALSO WORTH FLAGGING (not a refutation, an open risk): the Reptile Database notes that Mirza 2024 proposed revalidating Eublepharis madarensis, whose type locality is the Madar foothills, Ajmer, RAJASTHAN — the same state as the strongest supporting photograph. The Reptile Database disputes that revalidation (no type information, unverifiable sequence vouchers) and still keeps Rajasthan inside E. macularius, so I did not treat the Rajasthan animal as a different species. But the one image carrying the claim comes from the population whose identity is currently contested, which is a thin base for a general statement about the species. - correction: Adult dorsal marks are dark blotches on a pale ground with no pale halo around them — consistent with every source and photograph I opened, though "no halo" rests on silence in the two historical descriptions rather than on a positive statement.

Some adults instead carry an open pattern in which the brown breaks up into vermiculation and closed annuli enclosing pale or yellow ground. The documented basis for this is Boulenger 1885: 232 alone: the adult head and body become "spotted or largely vermiculated with chestnut-brown and whitish", and "in some only the brown edges of the dorsal bands remain". I verified this geometry in one wild animal, iNaturalist obs. 361924223 (Rajasthan) — a road-killed, dried specimen, from the population Mirza 2024 proposed to split as E. madarensis (a revalidation the Reptile Database rejects as unverifiable).

Do NOT state a frequency. Nothing I opened quantifies how many wild adults show the open pattern; "a large minority" is unverified.

Do NOT cite Gunther 1864 for body rings. His "pair of brown rings" is on the crown of the head (p. 430), listed among head markings. His adult TRUNK is described as one pair of brown cross-bars on the neck and three pairs on the trunk — the retained edges of the juvenile cross-bands, with ground colour between. That is a third adult pattern, paired transverse bars, which neither "solid spots" nor "pale-centred rings" describes, and it should be recorded as such.

Do NOT state an anterior-to-posterior gradient. No source I opened describes one, and the claimant's own photographs contradict it: in obs. 271474107 (Himachal) the head, neck and anterior trunk are solid blotches while the enclosed yellow appears mid-body and toward the hindlimb, and in obs. 387949230 (Jhampir) the neck and anterior trunk are solid round spots with ring figures confined to the crown of the head.

Part 23 · continued

Surface anatomy — what could not be verified at all

Gaps, stated rather than filled. Anything built into these areas is a modelling decision and has to be tagged as one.

tubercles

1) MEASURED TUBERCLE DENSITY (tubercles per unit area) - not found anywhere, for any body region, in any source I opened. Russell et al. (2014) is the only quantitative study of leopard gecko skin surface I located, and it measures sensilla per mm2 and mean scale AREAS, never tubercle density or tubercle spacing. If you need a number, the only route is arithmetic I did not verify against any source: ~18-20 longitudinal tubercle rows across the dorsum (from Mirza 2024 on the Rajasthan/Delhi population) spread over the dorsal arc of an adult, with tubercles ~1.1-1.3 mm wide and interspaces at least one tubercle wide, implies centre-to-centre spacing of roughly 2-3 mm and therefore on the order of 0.1-0.25 tubercles per mm2 (roughly 10-25 per cm2). Treat that as my estimate, not a literature value.

2) TUBERCLE HEIGHT / PROTRUSION - no source measures how far a tubercle stands above the surrounding scale pavement, in mm or as a ratio. Only adjectives ("cone-like", "subconical", "pronounced", "dome shaped"). The height of the bumps in your model is an artistic decision.

3) WHERE TUBERCLES ARE DENSEST - I could not verify this for any body region. Russell et al. establish where tubercles are LARGEST (thigh > crus > pes > hips > tail base > head), which is not the same thing, and their prose says nothing about spacing varying by region. Any claim that the tubercles are densest along the mid-dorsum, or on the flanks, or at the tail base, is unsupported by what I read.

4) FORELIMB TUBERCULATION - unverified. Russell et al. sampled only hindlimb (thigh, crus, pes); Mirza (2024) mentions only the hind limbs. No source I opened states whether the upper arm and forearm carry tubercles. Do not assume symmetry with the hindlimb without checking a specimen or a high-resolution photograph.

5) THE INTERSPACE CONFLICT - three sources I opened (Boulenger 1885, Smith 1935, Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022) say the intertubercular gaps are as wide as or wider than the tubercles; the diagnosis that The Reptile Database attributes to Anderson (1999, The Lizards of Iran, p.120) says mid-dorsal tubercles are generally LARGER than intertubercular spaces. I could not open Anderson 1999 to check context (it may be a comparison against E. angramainyu specifically), so the conflict is unresolved. I weighted the three opened sources.

6) DORSAL TUBERCLE ROW COUNT FOR E. MACULARIUS SENSU STRICTO - not obtained. Mirza et al. (2014) Phyllomedusa 13(2):75-90, the likeliest source, is gold open access but revistas.usp.br refused all connections from this network (ECONNREFUSED on repeated attempts, via both WebFetch and curl, direct and via DOI); OpenAlex lists no mirror PDF. I did not cite it. Also not opened: Grismer 1988 and 1991 (in Estes & Pregill, Phylogenetic Relationships of the Lizard Families; and Grismer 1991), which are the primary source for the "widely spaced, pronounced and pointed dorsal tubercles" wording I quote at second hand from The Reptile Database.

7) SOURCES I TRIED AND FAILED TO OPEN, so nothing in this report rests on them: Peacock, Gilbert & Vickaryous (2015) J. Anat. 227:596-610 on leopard gecko cutaneous wound healing (Wiley returned HTTP 403, no PMC copy); Szydlowski, Madej & Mazurkiewicz-Kania (2016) Acta Zoologica, on chromatophore ultrastructure in leopard gecko skin (paywalled) - it may contain histological thickness data for tubercle vs interscale skin; Anderson (1999) The Lizards of Iran; Szczerbak & Golubev (1996) Gecko Fauna of the USSR.

8) A TABLE ERROR YOU SHOULD KNOW ABOUT - Russell et al. (2014) Table 2 prints the "between shoulders" tubercle area as 0.141 mm2, which is smaller than every other tubercle measurement and equal to the granular scale in the same row; it contradicts the paper's own statement that the smallest tubercles are on the head. I rendered the published page to confirm the printed value. It is almost certainly a decimal-point error (probably 1.41). I excluded it rather than guess.

9) NO SOURCE OPENED describes tubercle arrangement on the neck, in the axilla/groin, on the eyelid margin, or around the cloaca/precloacal pore region, beyond the note that tubercles extend "up to the caudal constriction" (Mirza 2024, madarensis population). Those areas are unmapped.

eye

Gaps I did not fill, rather than guess at:

1. WHICH LID DOES THE CLOSING IN E. MACULARIUS. No source I opened states it for this species. Smith 1935 says both lids are movable in Eublepharis; the lower-lid-does-the-work claim is a general lizard/reptile rule (Smith 1935 p.10; Wyneken 2012 ARAV). Treat as likely, not established.

2. LID EXCURSION. No measurement of how far, how fast, or at what angle the lids travel; "connivent" in Boulenger/Smith establishes full closure but nothing quantitative. Sleeping-with-eyes-closed and blink-rate claims appear only in pet-care sources, which I did not accept.

3. WHETHER THE SLIT IS DENTICULATE / BREAKS INTO PINHOLES. Smith's general Gekkonidae text mentions denticulated slits and pin-point openings, but his Eublepharis diagnosis says only "pupil vertical". The famous four-pinhole result (Roth et al. 2009) is Tarentola chazaliae, a different family, and does not mention Eublepharis at all — as is the "350x better than human" sensitivity figure. Both are misattributed to leopard geckos across the popular web. My photographic read suggests a smooth-margined slit, but n=1.

4. A FORMAL PUBLISHED DESCRIPTION OF THE WILD-TYPE IRIS. None found in any taxonomic, field-guide or veterinary source I opened. The reticulated dark-with-silver-veining description is my own reading of high-resolution photographs, and the best-resolution eye I could find was a captive high-yellow animal, not a wild-caught wild-type. Wild-type iris colour may be cooler/greyer. Only weak (breeder) corroboration that the "normal" iris is patterned.

5. GLOBE AND CORNEAL DIAMETER. Camacho-Luna et al. 2020 measured ocular dimensions in 26 leopard geckos but the values are not in the abstract and the full text is paywalled. The 19-21% eye/head ratio I report is the exposed aperture, not the globe.

6. EYE-SIZE SAMPLE IS THIN. The ED/HL ratio rests on ONE publication and TWO specimens, with ED rounded to whole mm. A congener (E. angramainyu) gives 0.29 rather than 0.19-0.21, and I could not resolve whether that is a species difference or a difference in measurement convention.

7. NICTITATING MEMBRANE. Bellairs 1948 reportedly found "probably a small nictitating membrane" in Coleonyx — a different eublepharid genus — but that paper is paywalled and I did NOT open it; I have only a search-engine summary, so I am not asserting it. Nothing at all for Eublepharis.

8. SCLERAL OSSICLE COUNT. Present (DigiMorph CT), but the commonly quoted "20 or more" traces to a hobbyist page I could not open (TLS certificate failure). Uncounted for E. macularius.

9. SOURCES I TRIED AND FAILED TO OPEN: Bellairs 1948 Proc. Zool. Soc. Lond. 118:420-425 (paywalled); Mirza et al. 2014 Phyllomedusa 13(2):75-90, the modern E. macularius comparative description (revistas.usp.br refused connection repeatedly); "Ophthalmology of Gekkota: Geckos" in Wild and Exotic Animal Ophthalmology (Springer, login wall); the Reptile Database full diagnosis (deliberately withheld by the site). Any of these could sharpen points 1, 3 and 4.

ear

Several things I looked for and could not document, listed so you do not mistake inference for evidence.

(1) There is no modern redescription of E. macularius giving its own ear-opening shape, orientation and EL/OD ratio. Every Eublepharis description with those numbers (Mirza et al. 2014; Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022; Mirza 2024; Mohapatra et al. 2026) is for a congener. For E. macularius the only species-specific figure I found is Grismer's 'height of auditory meatus 1.5 times internostril distance', and I read that in the Reptile Database compilation, not in Grismer (1988), which is a Stanford University Press book chapter I could not obtain. The classical descriptions (Boulenger 1885, 1890; Smith 1935) write the head and ear characters in the E. hardwickii account and then list E. macularius as differing only in tubercle size, preanal pore count and body/digit proportions — so those ear statements reach macularius by the authors' own 'differs from the preceding by...' construction, not as direct observations of macularius. I have flagged that everywhere it applies.

(2) No absolute dimensions. I found no published ear-opening length or height in millimetres for E. macularius. Mirza (2024) does tabulate EL and OD in mm, but the columns in the extracted PDF table are misaligned against their row labels and I will not quote numbers I cannot align with confidence. Werner & Wever (1972), 'The function of the middle ear in lizards: Gekko gecko and Eublepharis macularius', does report tympanic membrane areas for this species, but Wiley returned HTTP 403 and I could not read it; I am therefore not quoting any membrane area.

(3) Meatus depth. I could not find a measured depth for the E. macularius external auditory meatus. 'Ear opening deep' is Mirza et al.'s wording for E. satpuraensis; 'a shallow external ear canal' is Christensen-Dalsgaard & Manley's for Gekko gecko. Those two are not obviously consistent, and neither is about macularius. Treat the recession as qualitative: present, a few millimetres, not quantified.

(4) See-through head. The red-laser-through-the-head demonstration is published for Gekko gecko only. Gekko is in Gekkonidae, a different family from Eublepharidae; the split between them is deep within Gekkota, so this is a distant transfer, not a near relative. I found no peer-reviewed source showing or stating it for E. macularius. Pet-care and hobbyist pages assert it confidently; those are weak sources and I did not count them.

(5) Exact anatomical direction of the extracolumella bar. The leopard gecko photograph caption places the pale extracolumella protrusion at the 'top-left' of the tympanum, but that is an image coordinate and I cannot tell which side of the head was photographed or how it was oriented, so I cannot say whether that is anterodorsal or posterodorsal on the animal.

(6) Whether E. macularius has the three conical tubercles on the anterior wall of the ear opening that Mirza (2024) describes for E. madarensis. Unrecorded either way.

(7) I could not open: Grismer (1988); Wever (1978) The Reptile Ear; Werner & Wever (1972); Werner et al. (2005, 2008); Anderson (1999) The Lizards of Iran. Several of these are the actual primary sources behind statements I have cited at one remove, and each is flagged as such in the relevant finding.

One correction to the premise in the brief: geckos do not have unusually open or superficial ear canals. The opposite is the case. Evans's lepidosaur ear chapter treats the flush, near-surface tympanum as the common lizard condition and singles out geckos as a group in which the membrane is recessed more deeply below the surface and protected by a meatal closure muscle. What is true is that geckos have a large, conspicuous, unscaled external ear opening — visible, but set at the bottom of a short funnel.

feet

Five things I could not document and am explicitly NOT filling in:

1. WEBBING. No source I opened — Boulenger (1890), Smith (1935), the Reptile Database diagnosis, or any of the three modern Eublepharis species descriptions — mentions interdigital webbing for Eublepharis, in either direction. Gecko genus diagnoses do routinely mention webbing when it is present (e.g. Smith's treatment of digit form across genera is detailed), so silence is weak evidence of absence, and Zhuang et al. (2019) measure free interdigital angles in the E. macularius pes, which implies separate digits. But no source states "webbing absent". Treat as: almost certainly no significant webbing, formally undocumented. Model toes as free, with at most a low basal skin fold.

2. TOE PATTERNING / BANDING. I found no description of digit or foot colouration for E. macularius. Boulenger (1890) and Smith (1935) describe head, body and tail pattern in detail and say nothing about the limbs or feet. The closest datum is the congener E. jhuma: "Limbs paler than body color with whitish spots on the legs" (Mohapatra et al. 2026) — and that refers to the legs, not the toes. Whether E. macularius toes are banded, speckled or plain is unverified. Do not invent body-style banding on the toes.

3. E. MACULARIUS-SPECIFIC DIGIT MEASUREMENTS. Powell, G.L., Osgood, G.J. & Russell, A.P. (2018) "Ontogenetic allometry of the digital rays of the leopard gecko (Gekkota: Eublepharidae; Eublepharis macularius)", Acta Zoologica 99:331-356, DOI 10.1111/azo.12215 is exactly the paper for toe proportions — metapodial and digit scaling in manus and pes across ontogeny. It is paywalled at Wiley; the Wiley page is behind a bot-verification wall which I did not attempt to bypass, ResearchGate returned 403, and no open repository copy exists. I confirmed its existence and full citation via the Crossref API only. All my digit-proportion figures are therefore transferred from congeners. If you want E. macularius numbers, this is the paper to obtain.

4. SUBDIGITAL LAMELLA COUNT FOR E. MACULARIUS. I have counts for congeners (E. jhuma 22-25 on the fourth toe; E. hardwickii 17; E. pictus 19; E. satpuraensis 18-22; E. turcmenicus 20-23; E. madarensis 17-19) but the diagnoses I opened never state the E. macularius range, because tuberculate-vs-smooth texture rather than count is the character used to separate it. A figure in the 15-25 range is a reasonable interpolation but I am not asserting it.

5. WHICH SPECIES KOPPETSCH ET AL. (2020) EXAMINED. The abstract says "three species of Eublepharidae" without naming them; full text paywalled. Search-engine summaries asserted the genera were Aeluroscalabotes, Goniurosaurus and Eublepharis, but I did not open a source confirming that, so I have not treated it as established.

PROCESS NOTE ON SOURCE QUALITY: the two strongest sources here are Boulenger (1890) and Smith (1935), both read as full scanned text from the Internet Archive. They are old but are formal taxonomic diagnoses and they agree with each other independently and with modern osteological work (Russell & Gamble 2019). No pet-care or breeder sites were used for any claim. The single most important correction to the common framing: leopard geckos DO have subdigital lamellae — a row of transverse tuberculate plates — they lack adhesive pads, scansors and setae. Sources that say "no lamellae" are wrong.

head_scales

Gaps, stated plainly rather than filled in.

1. NO MODERN FULL REDESCRIPTION OF E. MACULARIUS EXISTS THAT I COULD OPEN. This is the central problem. Every detailed modern Eublepharis head description I found (Mirza & Gnaneswar 2022; Mirza 2024) is of a congener — E. hardwickii, E. pictus or E. madarensis. The only full head scalation text that applies to E. macularius is Smith (1935) and Boulenger (1885/1890), and in both works the E. macularius account is written purely as a short list of differences from E. hardwickii (dorsal tubercle size, preanal pore count, proportions, colour) — so every head character is inherited by taxonomic convention rather than written out for the species. I have flagged each inherited statement.

2. EXTENT OF THE ROSTRAL'S MEDIAN GROOVE IS CONTRADICTORY. Boulenger 1885/1890 say the cleft is 'above' (upper part only); Mirza's congener descriptions say the rostral is 'divided by a median suture for its entire length'. I could not determine which applies to E. macularius. If the groove depth matters to your model, treat it as a choice.

3. NO MALE-vs-FEMALE HEAD WIDTH NUMBERS FOR E. MACULARIUS. I could not obtain any paper reporting mean head width by sex in millimetres for this species. Kratochvíl & Frynta (2002) is the right source and I read its abstract, but the species table is paywalled, so I never saw the E. macularius row confirming male-biased HSD for this species specifically. Several search-result snippets asserted 'males have wider heads than females' attributing it to Gutzke & Crews 1988, but the aggregator page carrying that claim returned HTTP 403 and I never opened it, and the Gutzke & Crews 1988 Nature abstract I did read is about temperature-dependent sex determination and does not mention head width. I have therefore NOT cited it. The male head widening is reported as 'likely', resting on the family-level combat/HSD argument plus verified male-male aggression in E. macularius.

4. THE JAW-ANGLE LOCATION OF THE WIDENING IS INFERRED, NOT DOCUMENTED. No source I opened says 'the head widens at the jaw angle in mature males'. The inference chain is: morphometric protocols define head width as the largest width of the head; enlarged male heads function as biting weapons; bite force comes from the jaw adductor chamber, which lies at the jaw angle. Reasonable, but it is my reasoning, not a citation.

5. THE VISIBLE MOUTH LINE IS NOT DOCUMENTED ANYWHERE I LOOKED. Marked unverified above. Only indirect support (labials counted separately per jaw, 'to angle of jaw').

6. NO SOURCE STATES WHETHER E. MACULARIUS LABIALS ARE PALER AS A RULE. The closest is a single statement about E. madarensis labials lacking the head's reticulation, plus the verified negative that E. macularius lacks the pale supralabial stripe that E. satpuraensis and E. hardwickii have. Single-source, transferred, flagged.

7. COULD NOT ACCESS: Anderson, S.C. 1999, The Lizards of Iran (the key modern source for E. macularius head scalation — I only read the Reptile Database's quotations of it); Mirza et al. 2014, Phyllomedusa 13: 75–90 (the E. satpuraensis description with its E. macularius comparison table — the journal host refused all connections); Kratochvíl & Frynta 2002 full text; Grismer 1988; Szczerbak & Golubev 1996. ScienceDirect, Wiley, ResearchGate and the Biodiversity Heritage Library all returned 403 to automated fetches.

8. NOT USED: no pet-care blog, breeder site, care sheet or hobbyist magazine contributed any fact above. I found a Khan article in Reptilia 45 (a hobbyist magazine) that would have had morphology notes but did not cite it, since it is a weak source and I could not open it anyway.

pattern

SOURCES I COULD NOT OPEN: (1) Blyth 1854, J. Asiatic Soc. Bengal 23: 737–738, the original description of Cyrtodactylus macularius from the Salt Range, Punjab — the relevant JASB volume was not retrievable from archive.org (the biostor item matching the title turned out to be a different 1855 Blyth paper). So I never read the original description and cannot say what Blyth himself wrote about colour. (2) The Reptile Database species account deliberately withholds roughly half a page of descriptive text from automated retrieval, stating it is available only to contributors — so I could not read its description or coloration section. (3) Mirza et al. 2014, Phyllomedusa 13(2): 75–90 (E. satpuraensis), which would contain a modern comparative colour diagnosis — revistas.usp.br refused connection and the ResearchGate copy returned 403. (4) Whimster 1979, J. Exp. Zool. 208: 153–160, the primary grafting study of leopard gecko pattern ontogeny (cited as ref. 7 by the PNAS paper) — paywalled. (5) Börner's 1970s revision naming the subspecies afghanicus, fasciolatus, montanus and smithi — not opened, so I make no claim about geographic subspecific colour differences. (6) Khan's Pakistani natural-history account — both the ResearchGate PDF and academia.edu copies were blocked.

SPECIFIC GAPS: (a) No published quantification of spot size, count or density for WILD adult E. macularius exists among the sources I read. The only quantification I found (Jančúchová-Lásková et al. 2015) covers HEAD spots only and reports square-root- and log-transformed values whose underlying table I could not extract. My spot-size figures are my own estimate from one magnified photograph and are flagged unverified. (b) No source I opened states in words that the adult tail is paler than the body; I inferred it from the chromatophore histology plus photographs. (c) No source gives the relative TIMING of body-band versus tail-band breakup; the observation that the tail retains bands longer rests on three photographs of subadults. (d) I found no statement about whether wild adults ever retain complete tail rings into full adulthood. (e) I could not verify whether ground colour shifts with the shed cycle, time of day or temperature — three Kirthar animals looked strikingly pale pinkish-lilac compared with the Sindh lowland animals and I do not know whether that is population, shed state, or flash photography at night. (f) I did not verify geographic variation in adult ground colour across the range in any systematic way.

SOURCE-STRENGTH CAVEATS: The iNaturalist observations are wild animals in the native range, and I opened and viewed every photograph I cite — but they are community-identified, not expert-vouchered museum specimens, so they are weaker than the taxonomic literature. I weighted the Pakistani records (including one from Chiddru in the Salt Range, effectively the type locality) above the Indian ones. Günther 1864 describes his material under the name Eublepharis fasciolatus; I treat it as E. macularius only because both Boulenger 1885 and Smith 1935 — which I opened — place fasciolatus in the synonymy of macularius, and its type locality (Hyderabad, Sindh) is well within the range. No fact in this report has been transferred from a different Eublepharis species; where E. hardwickii or E. angramainyu appear above it is only as an explicit contrast, never as a substitute.

Part 23 · continued

Lateral spine bending — the 18 numbers that survived

24 agents, four search angles, then verifiers told to refute each number from the opened source. The one that matters is the second card: a SAME-SPECIES measurement of pelvic girdle yaw on a level trackway, which is what the walker's spine was eventually fitted against.

geckos · verified

Maximum lateral trunk bending of ~20 degrees per step during level trotting; trunk is straight (rectilinear) at midstance and bends alternately left/right, peaking near footfall of each diagonal couplet.

Value: Lateral flexion greatest at step phase 0.03 +/- 0.04 (initial footfall), magnitude 20.1 +/- 6.32 deg; rectilinear through midstance; second maximum at phase 0.81 +/- 0.08, magnitude 19.4 +/- 5.60 deg (means +/- s.d.). Fig. 4A y-axis 'Lateral bending (deg.)' spans -40 to +40 with 0 = straight; representative trace for a 2.3 g animal at 0.50 m/s. Conditions: level balsa-wood track over a force platform, trotting gait (diagonal limb phase 0.92 +/- 0.06), speeds 0.28-0.75 m/s (mean 0.47 +/- 0.13 m/s), stride frequency 13 +/- 2 Hz. Body: mass 2.55 +/- 0.27 g, SVL 5.57 +/- 0.27 cm, N = 5. Measured from three dorsal-midline paint marks (pectoral point, second of three trunk points i.e. mid-trunk, pelvic point) filmed by 3 cameras at 1000 frames/s; the paper does not state the exact geometric formula (presumably the angle between the pectoral-midtrunk and midtrunk-pelvic segments, deviation from straight).

Species: Hemidactylus garnotii (Gekkonidae), same infraorder (Gekkota); different family from Eublepharidae

Source: Chen J.J., Peattie A.M., Autumn K., Full R.J. (2006) Differential leg function in a sprawled-posture quadrupedal trotter. J. Exp. Biol. 209: 249-259. doi:10.1242/jeb.01979

What was actually opened: JEB HTML full text (journals.biologists.com) read twice; PDF downloaded from polypedal.berkeley.edu (081_Chen_...pdf) and text-extracted: Materials and methods (Animals, Kinematics, GRF), Results paragraph 'Lateral flexion was greatest...', Fig. 4 caption and axis labels.

geckos · verified

In the target species, lateral rotation (yaw) of the pelvic girdle during level locomotion has a mean angular excursion of roughly 50 degrees per stride with the intact tail, falling to roughly 33-34 degrees when tail undulation is restricted or the tail is autotomised. This is girdle yaw, not a trunk-curvature angle; the paper does not report a mid-trunk bending angle.

Value: Fig. 4B (means +/- s.e.m., n = 10): angular excursion of pelvic girdle in yaw approx. 51 deg (error bar ~48-54) original tail; approx. 33 deg (~28-38) restricted; approx. 34 deg (~31-37) autotomised - values read off the axis of the downloaded figure, not stated numerically in text or Table 1. Fig. 4A representative stride (original tail): pelvic girdle rotation swings from approx. -38 deg (near 5% stride) to approx. +46 deg (near 63% stride); negative = rotated toward the observed right hind limb. Stats in text: restricted vs original t = 2.287, P = 0.048; autotomised vs original t = 3.129, P = 0.012. Conditions: level 1.0 x 0.13 m sandpaper trackway; speeds 0.59-3.36 SVL/s across all trials, mean 1.23 +/- 0.16 SVL/s (original tail), 1.50 (restricted), 1.85 (autotomised); hind-limb duty factor 0.77-0.78 (Table 1), i.e. walking-type gait, gait not formally classified. Body: SVL 104.6 +/- 2.1 mm, mass 36.3 +/- 1.9 g, 10 adults. Markers: dorsal midpoint of body, centres of pectoral and pelvic girdles, right limb joints, five tail points; two Edgertronic cameras at 250 frames/s. Methods define the variable only as pelvic girdle rotation 'in the yaw axis'.

Species: Eublepharis macularius (Eublepharidae), same species

Source: Jagnandan K., Higham T.E. (2017) Lateral movements of a massive tail influence gecko locomotion: an integrative study comparing tail restriction and autotomy. Scientific Reports 7: 10865. doi:10.1038/s41598-017-11484-7 (PMC5589804)

What was actually opened: PMC full text (read twice); Europe PMC full-text XML (Methods, Results, Table 1 in full, captions of Figs 2 and 4); Fig. 4 image (41598_2017_11484_Fig4_HTML.jpg) downloaded from Springer Nature static media and inspected.

geckos · verified

In the target species the tail (caudal vertebral column) is laterally undulated during level locomotion with tail-tip excursions of up to ~3 cm (~0.3 SVL) relative to the pelvic girdle at slow speed, decreasing with speed.

Value: Fig. 2 (per-individual means +/- s.e.m., original tail): lateral displacement of tail tip relative to pelvic girdle approx. 0.034 m at 0.6 SVL/s, approx. 0.019-0.021 m at 0.8-1.1 SVL/s, approx. 0.003-0.007 m at 1.9-2.3 SVL/s; regression y = -0.0127 x + 0.0279 (m vs SVL/s), R^2 = 0.423, P = 0.042. Restricted tail: approx. 0.002-0.005 m. Measured from top-view video (250 frames/s) as lateral distance of the tail-tip marker from the pelvic-girdle marker, left side of the body; yaw plane only. SVL 104.6 +/- 2.1 mm, mass 36.3 +/- 1.9 g. Values read off the figure axis.

Species: Eublepharis macularius (Eublepharidae), same species

Source: Jagnandan K., Higham T.E. (2017) Scientific Reports 7: 10865 (as above)

What was actually opened: Fig. 2 image (41598_2017_11484_Fig2_HTML.jpg) downloaded from Springer Nature static media and inspected; Fig. 2 caption and Results text from the Europe PMC XML.

geckos · likely

Maximum one-sided rotation range of the pectoral and pelvic girdles of the Tokay gecko trunk during one trot cycle is about 33-34 degrees (secondary citation of a motion-capture study of trunk lateral undulation on horizontal, 45-degree and vertical planes).

Value: Pectoral girdle angle: maximum unilateral fluctuation range 33.56 +/- 3.01 deg; pelvic girdle angle: 33.22 +/- 1.72 deg, 'during one trot gait cycle'. Plane (horizontal / 45 deg / vertical), speed and body size are NOT stated in the citing paper. The primary study (Wang et al. 2020) used an optical motion-capture system, 29 reflective markers (10 on trunk, 5 on tail, 12 on legs, 2 on head per the Manoonpong-group description of the same dataset), found a standing-wave trunk waveform at low speed changing to a head-to-tail travelling wave at high speed, and states the lateral undulation pattern results from girdle rotation plus axial muscle activity. Wang et al. 2021 (Zoology 145: 125892) additionally measured 13 angular variables including trunk flexion, girdle rotation and trunk deflection on the vertical plane, but the numerical values are behind a paywall and were not read.

Species: Gekko gecko (Gekkonidae), same infraorder (Gekkota); different family from Eublepharidae

Source: Primary: Wang W., Ji A., Chen G., Ravi S., Shen H., Gorb S.N., Dai Z. (2020) Kinematics of gecko climbing: the lateral undulation pattern. Zoology 140: 125768. doi:10.1016/j.zool.2020.125768. Numbers taken from the secondary source: 'A Gecko-Inspired Robot with a Flexible Spine Driven by Shape Memory Alloy Springs', Soft Robotics 2023 (PMC10442688), section 'Collaborative model of flexible spine and limbs', citing Wang et al. 2020 as its ref. 39.

What was actually opened: PMC10442688 full text (read twice, including the paragraph containing the 33.56/33.22 deg values and its reference list); Europe PMC abstract records for PMIDs 32279015 and 33550221; ADS/Crossref/Semantic Scholar/figshare (RMIT 27530589) records for Wang 2020 - no accessible file; ScienceDirect and ResearchGate pages returned 403. Primary full text NOT read.

lizards_general · verified

Sceloporus clarkii walking/trotting on a treadmill uses a standing wave of lateral bending with two nodes (pectoral girdle; penultimate trunk vertebra just anterior to the pelvis). Lateral excursion of the mid-trunk landmark was ~18 mm at 0.27 and 0.48 m/s and ~13 mm at 0.83 m/s (means +/- SD: 18.0+/-2.0, 17.6+/-1.2, 13.4+/-2.2 mm); pectoral node 10.5, 9.5, 5.5 mm; pelvic node 10.0, 9.7, 9.7 mm; snout 20.8, 15.2, 11.0 mm; tail peak 18.0, 21.2, 24.2 mm. Only the snout displacement changed significantly with speed (P=0.028); trunk peak and node amplitudes did not (P>0.067). Node positions did not shift with speed. Trunk excursion is therefore roughly 0.15-0.20 SVL peak-to-peak and speed-invariant over a 3-fold speed range (walking trot; duty factor approaching 0.5 at the top speed). Note the paper reports lateral DISPLACEMENT of dorsal landmarks (mm, from the dorsal video y-coordinate, Fig. 4 stick-figure overlays), not a trunk bending angle.

Value: Mid-trunk lateral excursion 18.0 / 17.6 / 13.4 mm (~0.20 / 0.19 / 0.15 SVL) at 0.270 / 0.476 / 0.833 m/s; no significant change with speed. SVL 90-92 mm. Gait: walking trot. Measured at 4 equally spaced trunk landmarks between pectoral girdle and pelvis, dorsal view, 200 fields/s.

Species: Sceloporus clarkii (Phrynosomatidae (Iguania)), other (different infraorder; Iguania vs Gekkota)

In the same S. clarkii study, maximum pelvic rotation relative to the direction of travel (dorsal-view angle between the pelvic line and travel direction; one-sided maximum, PELVMAX) was 16-25 degrees across all individuals and speeds and did not vary with speed; peak pelvic rotation occurred at 44-51% of stride duration (just before foot-up, i.e. 81-85% of stance). The authors state this range matches values for 'several other lizard species (Ritter, 1992)', for alligator (Gatesy 1991) and salamander (Ashley-Ross 1994).

Value: PELVMAX (mean +/- SE, degrees): 16+/-7 (ind. 3, 0.270 m/s); 25+/-3 and 21+/-2 (inds. 1, 2 at 0.476 m/s); 21+/-2 and 19+/-2 (inds. 1, 2 at 0.833 m/s). One-sided maximum of pelvic yaw from travel direction; SVL 90-92 mm; walking trot.

Species: Sceloporus clarkii (Phrynosomatidae (Iguania)), other

lizards_general · verified

Across 44 lizard species in four families (320 dorsal-view video sequences, DeepLabCut tracking of 22 points), in-vivo 'spine apex ROM' (sum of the maximum deviations of the mid-spine marker to either side of the shoulder-girdle-to-hip-girdle axis, expressed in degrees; thoraco-lumbar spine only) clusters between 15 and 30 degrees; the most common strategy is 10-30 degrees of spine ROM with 60-130 degrees of limb ROM. Family means: dragons (Agamidae) 20.3, geckos (Gekkota) 23.6, skinks 27.6, varanids 19.6 degrees. Direction means: upward climbing 24.8, downward 16.4, level walking 16.6 degrees (level trials were varanids only, n=51). Speed classes: slow 22.7, medium 24.0, fast 19.4 degrees, i.e. faster trials had decreased spine ROM and increased leg ROM. Caveat for the target: the gecko data (n=154 sequences) are from vertical climbing, not level ground, and I could not read the abbreviated gecko species labels in Fig. 6a at the rendered resolution; Eublepharis is not identifiable among them.

Value: Spine apex ROM 15-30 degrees (cluster); family means 19.6-27.6 degrees; level walking (varanids) 16.6 degrees; slow/medium/fast 22.7/24.0/19.4 degrees. Speed classes are categorical (thresholds not given in main text); body sizes not given per species in main text (Supplementary S1, Fig. D1, not accessed).

Species: 44 species: Agamidae (n=74 seqs), Gekkota (n=154), Scincidae (n=21), Varanidae (n=71) (Agamidae, Gekkota (multiple gecko families), Scincidae, Varanidae), same infraorder for the gecko subset (Gekkota); other for the rest

Walking S. clarkii uses a 'rough/loose standing wave' of axial bending with two nodes; node positions and node/peak amplitudes do not change across a 3-fold speed increase (only snout displacement falls). The trunk antinode lies between the nodes.

Value: Nodes: pectoral girdle (axial landmark 3) and axial landmark 8 = penultimate trunk vertebra, dorsal to pubic symphysis (just anterior to pelvis). Table VI lateral displacements (mm, mean ± SD; dorsal-view treadmill video, landmark lateral range from stick-figure superposition of all frames of a stride; paper does not state whether this is peak-to-peak or half-amplitude): trunk max 18.0±2.0 / 17.6±1.2 / 13.4±2.2 mm at 0.270 / 0.476 / 0.833 m s-1 (≈0.20, 0.19, 0.15 SVL; n.s. vs speed, P>0.067); pectoral node min 10.5±6.4 / 9.5±2.3 / 5.5±2.0 mm (n.s.); pelvic node min 10.0±0.1 / 9.7±2.0 / 9.7±1.7 mm (≈0.11 SVL; n.s.); snout 20.8±2.4 / 15.2±3.1 / 11.0±2.6 mm (decreases, P=0.028); tail 18.0 / 21.2 / 24.2 mm (tends to rise, n.s.). Conditions: SVL 90–92 mm; 0.270, 0.476, 0.833 m s-1 (≈3.0, 5.2, 9.1 SVL s-1); walking trot (hind duty factor 0.64→0.52); stride freq 3.4→5.8 Hz; 27–30 °C; 200 fields s-1; axial data from 1 individual per speed (n=2 strides slow; n=5 at each faster speed).

standing_wave · verified

The original standing-wave/travelling-wave paper: fully-limbed lizards show a standing wave of trunk lateral bending at low speed that is replaced by a travelling wave as velocity rises; short-limbed lizards use a travelling wave even at the lowest speeds.

Value: Abstract only. Species: Cnemidophorus tigris (Teiidae) and Dipsosaurus dorsalis (Iguanidae) = standing wave at low speed → travelling wave at higher speed; Gerrhonotus kingii (Anguidae) and Eumeces multivirgatus (Scincidae) = travelling wave at all speeds recorded. High-speed video + computerized motion analysis. NO numeric amplitude, node location, transition speed or phase could be verified — full text is paywalled. Second-hand only (unverified against the original): Reilly & DeLancey 1997 (p. 429) say Ritter's lizards showed standing waves with nodes near the girdles, pelvic rotation in the same 16–25° range, and snout displacement decreasing with speed; Suzuki et al. 2021 Front. Neurorobot. attribute to Ritter 1992 that D. dorsalis uses 'intermediate' waves at intermediate speeds.

phase · verified

Forelimb footfall coincides with maximum lateral convexity of the trunk on that side; onset of the same forelimb's swing (start of protraction) coincides with maximum lateral concavity on that side. Stride defined from right-forelimb touchdown; propulsive phase ~0-50% of stride, swing ~50-100%.

Value: Max concavity toward the forelimb at ~0.5 of its stride cycle (its lift-off), max convexity toward it at 0/1.0 (touchdown). Fig. 3a: mean lateral rotation per intervertebral joint (10 joints Vert1-11 in Varanus; 5 joints Vert3-8 in Salvator) runs from about -1.5 deg at footfall, through zero at ~0.25, to a peak of ~+1.8 to +2 deg at ~0.45-0.6, back to -1.5 to -2.5 deg at 1.0 (values zeroed about their mean; ~3-4 deg peak-to-peak per joint). Slow treadmill walking; stride durations 1.5-1.85 s (monitors) and 1.5-3.25 s (tegus); 1 stride per individual, n=3 per species; measured with XROMM at intervertebral joints along the trunk. Body mass/SVL not stated in this paper (deferred to earlier ventilation papers on the same animals).

Species: Varanus exanthematicus and Salvator merianae (Varanidae (Anguimorpha) and Teiidae (Lacertoidea)), other (same order Squamata, different infraorders from Gekkota)

phase · verified

In a walking trot the trunk is a standing wave with nodes on the pectoral girdle and just anterior to the pelvis; peak pelvic yaw occurs late in hindlimb stance, just before foot-up, and this timing does not change with speed.

Value: Time of peak pelvic rotation = 0.44-0.51 of the stride (0 = right hind footfall), just before hind foot-up (0.54-0.60 of stride) = 81-85% of the stance phase. Max pelvic rotation from the direction of travel 16-25 deg (all individuals and speeds). Standing-wave amplitudes (peak lateral displacement, mm): trunk 18.0+/-2.0, 17.6+/-1.2, 13.4+/-2.2 at 0.270, 0.476, 0.833 m/s (~0.15-0.20 SVL); snout 20.8 -> 11.0 mm (decreases with speed); caudal 18-24 mm; pectoral and pelvic nodes ~5-10 mm minimum. SVL 90-92 mm; treadmill; gait a walking trot at all three speeds (diagonal couplets). Pelvic angle = angle between caudal-lumbar line and travel direction; companion JEB abstract: pelvic rotation 'to the opposite side' begins before foot-up.

Species: Sceloporus clarkii (Phrynosomatidae (Iguania)), other (same order Squamata, different infraorder from Gekkota)

phase · verified

In the leopard gecko the pelvic girdle yaws through the hindlimb stride with a peak late in stance; the trunk carries a standing wave that becomes a caudally travelling wave in the tail. Only pelvic-girdle yaw vs the hindlimb cycle was reported; trunk curvature vs forelimb cycle was NOT measured.

Value: Fig. 4A (representative right-hindlimb stride, original tail): pelvic yaw about -38 deg at hind footfall (negative = rotated toward the observed hindlimb), zero crossing at ~0.33, peak ~+47 deg (rotated toward the opposite hindlimb) at ~0.60-0.65 of the stride, hindlimb stance ending at ~0.75 (swing 0.75-1.0), returning to ~-40 deg at 1.0. Mean yaw excursion of pelvic girdle ~50 deg with intact tail, ~32-34 deg after tail restriction or autotomy (Fig. 4B). n=10 adults, mass 36.3+/-1.9 g, SVL 104.6+/-2.1 mm; level trackway with sandpaper; 250 fps; speeds 0.59-3.36 SVL/s (treatment means 1.23-1.85 SVL/s); markers on dorsal midpoint of body, centre of pectoral/pelvic girdles, hip/knee/ankle. Inference (mine, not the authors'): peak pelvic yaw at ~80-85% of hindlimb stance matches the Sceloporus timing, and in a trot-like gait this is just before the diagonal forelimb lifts off.

Species: Eublepharis macularius (Eublepharidae), same species

phase · verified

At each foot touchdown the local trunk segment (shoulder for forelimb, hip for hindlimb) reaches maximal curvature, convex toward the touching-down limb; hip bending is in phase with hindlimb movement (forelimb/shoulder relation weaker in field video). Fully limbed lizards on firm substrate use an almost pure standing wave with nodes at shoulder and hip.

Value: Fig. 4A right: Hilbert-transform phase of hip bending vs hind-leg phase falls along the 1:1 diagonal (approximately zero phase offset, i.e. in phase). Limb sequence in Brachymeles FR-HL-FL-HR, hindlimb leads ipsilateral forelimb by 0.38+/-0.07 of a period (lateral couplet), duty factor ~0.5. Curvature quantified as body curvature kappa(s,t) in units of 1/SVL from 21 DeepLabCut midline points; field videos on soil/poppy seeds (Brachymeles) and lab trials on sandpaper / granular media (Uma, Sceloporus). Absolute SVL and speeds not given in main text (relative hindlimb length per species given in Fig. 2). Precise phase definition (what constitutes phase zero of 'leg movement') is not spelled out in the main text.

Species: Brachymeles kadwa, B. taylori, B. muntingkamay; Uma scoparia; Sceloporus olivaceus (Scincidae (Brachymeles); Phrynosomatidae (Uma, Sceloporus)), other (same order Squamata, different infraorders from Gekkota)

Gekko gecko (same infraorder as the target) uses a diagonal (trot-like) gait with a standing wave of trunk bending at low speed (single-peak waveform, nodes near the girdles) that becomes a travelling wave at high speed; the pattern is produced by girdle rotation plus axial muscle activity. Trunk flexion, pectoral and pelvic girdle rotation angles were measured, but no numeric phase of trunk bending relative to forelimb touchdown/lift-off was available in the parts I could read.

No phase fraction or bending amplitude reported in the accessible abstract/snippets.
